en: The Ritual Manual for the Maṇḍala Named Vajrāvalī, Volume One.
[Oṃ, homage to Śrī Vajrasattva.]
I pay homage to the glorious Lord of the Vajra. O Māras, remember the feet of the Enemy of Existence!
O wrathful ones, run in all directions! Let the Vajra-women sing songs of auspiciousness.

May the circle of vajras here close together through the splendor of the fearless one, so that the world may be established without obstacle within the great mandala of the glorious Vajradhara’s majesty.
Let this [wisdom] be held within the heart by means of a succession of vajras, like one who wields a vajra both internally and externally;
for that light, having dispelled internal darkness, bears the very form of the illustrious Vajradhara.
The extensive ritual procedure for the mandala and so forth of the Teacher has been set forth in the two *Kamalī* [Tantras].
We shall now state it here clearly in a concise form, arranged in sequence, such that it can be easily performed.

Furthermore, while other teachers have presented incomplete systems, lacked originality, or were unclear in their expression, this [work] has been adorned by us with various virtues: being complete in its methodology, presenting novel insights, possessing lucid exposition, and being both traditionally authoritative and logically sound in various respects.

0.2 (p.49) Rituals to be set forth in the *Vajrāvalī*: Here, indeed, out of a commitment to supreme compassion for embodied beings— who, their intellects bound by a succession of fetters such as ignorance that is difficult to abandon, are generally driven by the force of the waves of karma that are hard to resist, and thus remain without rest through repeated sinking and surfacing in the exceedingly deep and difficult-to-cross whirlpools of the river of saṃsāra within the three lower realms and the two higher realms, and are consequently lacking in autonomy— the [author], wishing to uplift them, first [describes] the sequence beginning with the preparation of the ritual implements such as the *argha* offering.

In the construction and consecration of monasteries and other such works, as well as in the performance of empowerments (*abhiṣeka*), hearing, reflection, and so forth, the preceptors—being compassionate, possessing great learning, a mind skilled in the methods of mantra, endowed with wisdom, fortitude, lack of envy, and persevering energy—should properly encourage [the practitioner] in the accumulation of merit and the accumulation of gnosis. Accordingly, they should perform, in due order: the offering of honorific water (*argha*) for the monastery and other sites; the preliminary service characterized by the giving of *argha* and other offerings; the gathering of disciples; the digging of the ground; the purification of the site; the appropriation of the ground; and the ritual staking of obstacles (*vighnakīlana*).

The consecration of the site (*vasundharādhivāsana*), the consecration of the vase (*kalaśādhivāsana*), the consecration of the deity (*devatādhivāsana*), the drawing of the mandala lines (*maṇḍalasūtraṇa*), the scattering of colored powders (*rajaḥpātana*), the placement of the vases (*kalaśanyāsa*), the accomplishment of the mandala (*maṇḍalasādhana*), the consecration of the deity (*devatādhivāsana*), the consecration of images and so forth (*pratimādipratiṣṭhā*), the consecration of lotus ponds and so forth (*puṣkariṇyādipratiṣṭhā*), the consecration of mango groves and so forth (*āmrārāmādipratiṣṭhā*), the consecration of the disciple (*śiṣyādhivāsana*), the entrance of the master (*ācāryapraveśa*), the entrance of the disciple (*śiṣyapraveśa*), the empowerments of the garland, water, crown, vajra, bell, and name (*mālodakamukuṭavajraghaṇṭānāmasekāḥ*), the bestowal of the three pledges (*trisamayadāna*), the empowerment of the master (*ācāryaseka*), the transmission of the mantra (*mantrasamarpaṇa*), the collyrium (*añjana*), the mirror empowerment (*darpaṇaseka*), and the casting of the arrow (*śarakṣepa*).

The secret, the wisdom-knowledge, and the fourth initiations; the vow of knowledge (*vidyā-vrata*), the vajra-vow, the conduct-vow (*caryā-vrata*); the prophecy, the authorization, the breathing-instruction, the self-initiation, the fire-offering, the dissolution of the mandala, the mental mandala, the bali-offering, the warding off of obstacles, and the characteristics and maintenance of the vajra and vajra-bell—these fifty procedures are to be performed.
1. The ritual for the offering of honor (*argha*) at monasteries and other sites.
1.1 The Rite for the Offering of Honor to Monasteries, Perfumed Chambers, Shrines, Dwellings, and Hermitages.
Regarding the examination of the ground:
on an auspicious day, in the forenoon, the ground for a monastery or similar structure should be examined, preceded by the offering of a bali-oblation.

Therein, one should avoid an *aśvattha* tree in the east, an *arjuna* in the southeast, a *plakṣa* in the south, a *palāśa* in the southwest, a *nyagrodha* in the west, a *śālmali* in the northwest, a *bakula* in the north, and an *udumbara* in the northeast; as well as ground shaped like the back of a tortoise, which is a cause of death or loss of wealth. Having avoided ground that is elevated in the north out of fear of the destruction of one's lineage, elevated in the east out of fear for the practitioner's destruction, and depressed in the center, one should select ground that is the cause of sovereignty, the state of a *vidyādhara*, or similar attainments.

Thus, having dug a pit one span (vitasti) deep in a four-cornered plot that slopes toward the northeast, with its center slightly raised, its course flowing clockwise, and its soil soft, and having quickly filled that pit with that very earth— if there is more earth remaining— [then it is auspicious].
Then that ground should be known as pure; furthermore, one should take the earth from that pit.
Having made this pit, one span in measure, and filled it with water, [one should perform the rite].
Some say that when [the water] is joined with a *śītalī* plant and a living fish,
one should go a hundred paces and, having returned properly, examine it.
A ground that is auspicious when filled with water should be avoided by those seeking their own welfare if it is deficient.
If the water here makes a sound, it portends danger from the nagas.

1.1.2 (p.53) Thus, the teacher who has understood the characteristics of the site, having bathed, having prepared the articles for worship, having dressed himself in whatever garments and ornaments he obtained, and having well-cultivated the yoga of the deity, should— in the evening— cause a square mandala measuring four cubits (as stated by the phrase "the size of a cowhide") to be made in the center of that site with clay and cow dung. Having meditated upon the wheel of the mandala therein, worshipped it, and offered the *digbali* oblation, he should— with his right knee placed on the ground and palms joined in reverence—
supplicate the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, World-Protectors, and others residing in the ten directions for the sake of the site.
Those lords who dwell in this triple world, the great and most magnificent ones—
the gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, and so forth—
I inform you all of this for the sake of accomplishing the welfare of all sentient beings,
and for the purpose of establishing a monastery on this auspicious site.
Through the virtuous practice of hearing, reflection, and so forth, for the sake of realizing the true nature of phenomena (dharmatā),
I, [name], am striving to establish the good reputation of [name].
"If it is acceptable to you, I shall do so; otherwise, certainly not.
You must grant me this auspicious land on the basis of signs such as dreams."

Thus one should recite three times. Thereafter, having consecrated his face twenty-one times with the left hand using this *svapnamāṇavaka* mantra— namely, "Oṃ mucili svāhā / Oṃ mohani svāhā / Oṃ dattili svāhā"— he should, after first performing worship before the Blessed One Lokeśvara, lie down in the southern direction with his head toward the north, facing east, adorned with pure ornaments, in a clean place, and sleep according to his desire.

In the case of a bad dream, one should perform what is described below either by reciting the Amṛtakuṇḍalin mantra or by resolving that all phenomena are ultimately devoid of intrinsic nature; furthermore, having fashioned a boy made of clay in a dream, one should act upon a ground that has been granted or not forbidden by the deities. If it is forbidden, one must certainly not do so.

On the second auspicious day, during a good dream, in the forenoon, one who possesses the yoga of Vajrasattva, seated in the vajraparyaṅka posture with the earth-touching mudrā, should contemplate the ground as empty by means of the mantra *oṃ bhūḥ khaṃ*. Then, having visualized the earth as consisting of vajra-paramāṇus with *hūṃ laṃ hūṃ*, one should consecrate it with *oṃ medini vajrībhava vajra bandha hūṃ*.

Having recited three times the syllable *hūṃ* with the moon upon the left hand, and by means of the rays [emanating] from it, the striking of the fingertips, and those sounds, one should invoke the Earth Goddess from the ground—either emerging with half her body or her entire body—yellow in color, holding a golden vase and the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*) in her two hands, and well-adorned. Having worshipped her with water for the feet, water for rinsing the mouth, and the respectful offering (*argha*), as well as flowers and other offerings, one should say:
"O Goddess, you are the witness of all the Buddhas, the Protectors, regarding the specificities of the conduct and methods (*caryā-naya*), and the stages (*bhūmi*) and perfections (*pāramitā*)."
"Just as the army of Māra was broken by the Protector, the Lion of the Śākyas, so too,
having conquered the army of Māra, shall I establish monasteries and other structures. Having said,
"Let that which was requested three times be done," one should contemplate [the earth] as remaining right there, hidden, established in the form of the earth.

Then, on that ground, one should visualize a peaked pavilion (*kūṭāgāra*) produced from *bhrūṃ* and arising from *bhrūṃ*. According to some, it is the abode of the Victors (*jinālaya*) produced from *bhrūṃ*, situated upon the wind, fire, water, earth, and Mount Sumeru, which have been transformed from *yaṃ*, *raṃ*, *vaṃ*, *laṃ*, and *suṃ*.

There, within the interior of the peaked pavilion (*kūṭāgāra*), upon a fragrant mandala that has been prepared, one should summon the mandala-circle and the guardians of the directions (*dikpāla*) and others by means of light rays from the seed-syllable at one’s own heart. Preceded by the offering of water for the feet (*pādya*), water for sipping (*ācamana*), the respectful oblation (*argha*), worship, and sacrificial cakes (*bali*), one whose tongue is a vajra produced from the syllable *HŪṂ* and who holds an incense burner should ring a bell and, with the verses to be recited hereafter beginning with “O Blessed One” and ending with “you ought to grant your presence,” effect the presence (*saṃnidhāna*) of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, as well as the gods, nāgas, and so forth, by substituting words such as “monastery” (*vihāra*) in place of the word “consecration” (*pratiṣṭhā*).

Having visualized the sky as completely full, one should place the jars of Victory and the others to be described according to the patron's means—or in their absence, other jars containing living fish—in due order. Then, having fashioned the ritual assistants into the forms of all-acting deities such as Vighnāntaka and the rest, one should have them dig a square pit two cubits wide and half that deep. To the northeast of that, one should dig a circular pit of the same measurement or half that size. Both of these should be smeared with clay and cow dung.

Then, having offered the *argha* into the square pit using the *argha* vessel itself with the *argha* mantra to be described later, one should offer water from the *vijayā* and other jars in due order; just as the square [pit] is filled, one should fill the circle by means of a stream [of water].

Thereafter, having observed water flowing in a clockwise direction containing cool living fish, and having offered a sprig of a milky tree, one should meditate upon oneself as Jāṅgulī—yellow in color, with three faces (yellow, black, and white) on the right, middle, and left; possessing seven hoods, a jeweled crown, and six arms; holding a vajra and an arrow in her two right hands, and a bow, a noose, and a raised index finger in the other two; embraced by her own consort as the means (*upāya*); adorned with variegated garments and nāga ornaments; seated upon a solar seat on a double lotus (*viśvābja*) with a radiant aura. Thus one should contemplate oneself as Jāṅgulī.

Having divided the lotus-array (*kamalāvarta*) into five parts and visualized the ground as consisting of universal vajras by looking down as far as the subterranean realm (*rasātala*), one should worship the spectators with betel nuts, garlands, and sandalwood. Then, having visualized Indra and the other lords of the ten directions together with their servants, sons, and wives in the northeast, one should dig ten stakes—described below—which have been consecrated one hundred and eight times with the *sarvakṛt* mantra and the mantra beginning with *oṃ gha gha*, for the sake of protection and success. 1.1.7 (p.59) % Examination of the Site-Serpent (*vāstunāga*).

Then, having dispelled the intention of obstacles, one should examine the Vāstunāga. On whatever ground a monastery or similar structure is to be built, one should measure that ground, including its surroundings, as a square; then, having determined the characteristics of the Vāstunāga’s sleeping position in the center of that ground, the preparation of the site (bhūsaṃskāra) should be performed.

In this regard, according to the movement of the sun, during the three successive months beginning with Bhādrapada, the Vāstunāga is said to sleep on the ground in its center with its head respectively toward the east, south, west, and north, while facing toward the south, west, north, and east.

Having observed that, taking up the cord with a vajra-fist together with the assistant practitioner, he should move clockwise while stationed in the southeast (fire) and northwest (wind) directions; having laid out the lines for the east, west, north, and south, starting from sunrise, he should dig the pit to fill the depression by moving clockwise. Some say that on the side of the serpent's belly, one should leave a space of one cubit for the belly and [the same for] the sight-staff.

For if [the earth] is dug at the head, the father, son, and others perish; on the back part, however, there is the destruction of oneself or the abandonment of one's country; at the tail, cattle, buffaloes, and so forth perish; and if there is a stone in that ground, there will be wind.

There is pain in the bones, muteness in the pebbles, fever in the husks and charcoal, and minor afflictions in the hair-roots, wood, and so forth. Having removed the stumps, roots, withered grass, skeletons, charcoal, and the like, and having gratified the Earth and Fire, the Tathāgatas, the local lords of those places, the directional guardians (dikpālas), the world guardians (lokapālas), and the field guardians (kṣetrapālas) by means of a propitiatory fire-oblation (śāntikahoma), one should perform a rite for the pacification of the king and the patron. One should also offer the remaining sacrificial oblation (śeṣabali). In subsequent rites as well, a festival should be held according to one's ability, a communal meal (saṃghabhojya) should be provided, and a fee (dakṣiṇā) should be given to the preceptor.
One should satisfy the artisans and laborers; this is the rule for the offering of honor to monasteries, perfumed chambers, shrines, dwellings, and hermitages.
1.2 The Rule for the Offering of Honor to Lotus Pools and the Like. (p. 62)

Regarding the construction of lotus ponds, tanks, wells, and so forth, one should first perform offerings and worship; then, as previously described, having prepared the *argha* water, one should visualize Vairocana in the form of Vajravaruṇa by reciting "Oṃ Vaṃ Vajravaruṇa Hūṃ. One should then perceive that [Vairocana] transforms into a dwelling place for the eight families of nāgas, filled with the water of the nectar of gnosis (*jñānāmṛta*), and completely full of water endowed with the eight qualities, reaching down to the subterranean realm (*ārasātala*), while reciting "Oṃ Vajrasattva, you are the *samaya*. This is the ritual procedure for the *argha* of lotus ponds and the like.
1.3 The Ritual Procedure for the *Argha* of Images and the Like 1.3.1 (p. 62)

However, when making images, books, and so forth, preceded by offerings and worship, one should instantly visualize the sculptors as having the form of the Family Lord (*kulādhipa*) of the deity to be fashioned, and the scribes as having the form of Amitābha; these should be visualized as being respectively joined at the heart, throat, and crown with the syllables *HŪṂ*, *ĀḤ*, and *OṂ* situated upon a vajra, lotus, and wheel, and with a moon and a vajra in their left and right hands. Then, touching the heart and other parts while reciting *HŪṂ ĀḤ OṂ*, one consecrates the materials—such as sacred wood, clay, stone, or cloth.

Through the resolve upon emptiness (*śūnyatādhimokṣa*), one should instantly visualize the form of the deity to be manifested from the seed-syllable in the heart; then, one should recite the passage beginning with "O Blessed One" and ending with "you should grant your presence.

On the leaf, one who has cultivated the intellect should visualize the speech-vajra, brought by the agent, transformed into the form of syllables; having consecrated it twenty-one times with "Oṃ Vajrasattva Hūṃ" and "Oṃ Āḥ Vighnāntakṛt Hūṃ," and having empowered the brush and other writing implements as the nature of the wisdom of insight (*prajñājñāna*), and the ink as the nature of wisdom-nectar through the transformation of vajra-atoms, and furthermore having empowered the pen and the ink with "Oṃ Dhīḥ! O you who are victorious in hearing and memory, O remover of the veil of all ignorance, Hrīḥ Svāhā!"—one should offer them to those [implements].

One should stabilize [the image] with the *śatākṣara* mantra. One should also perform acts such as pleasing the artisans and feeding the Saṅgha. In all cases here, the dismissal (*visarjana*) of the visualized deities must be performed. Furthermore, one who wishes to restore a monastery that is dilapidated or cracked should offer bali-oblations and other gifts, dismiss the forms of the deities installed during the consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*) according to the ritual timing, and then carry out the restoration and so forth in that same manner. This is the procedure for the offering of water (*argha*) to images and the like. 2. The Procedure Characterized by the Offering of Water and Other Gifts (Arghādidānalakṣaṇavidhi) 2.1 (p. 65)
In this context, as appropriate among the procedures to be described,
there should be vessels made of gold, silver, stone, copper, wood, clay, pearl, conch,
or leaf-cups for the water for the feet, for sprinkling, for sipping, and for the arghya offering.

In that regard, having placed barley milk, white flowers, *kuśa* grass, sesame seeds, parched grain, nectar, and scented white water into one of the vessels, one should recite the mantra *oṃ āḥ hūṃ*, as well as the mantra of one’s own sovereign lord and the mantra of Kuṇḍalin, seven times or one hundred and eight times for the sake of pacification (*śānti*). Having placed sesame, curd, yellow flowers, *darbha* grass, nectar, and yellow scented water [into another vessel], one should likewise recite [the mantra] for the sake of nourishment (*puṣṭi*).

Then, on his own left side, he should place the vessel for *argha*, the vessel for *pādya*, and the vessels for sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) and sipping water (*ācamana*); in front of these, he should place three receiving vessels.

There, taking water from the *pādya* vessel with his left fist and a flower with the thumb and forefinger joined like a pair of tongs, he should offer it three times into the vessel while gracefully rotating his fingers, reciting the mantra to be mentioned later, releasing the fingers in sequence: the forefinger, the middle finger, the ring finger, and the little finger.

One should sprinkle three times with water from the second vessel, which is held at the tips of the kuśa grass blades grasped by the right hand, over the second recipient. The same applies when sprinkling with water from the *sārvakarmika* flask. Taking water from that very second vessel with the fist of the right hand and grasping a flower with the thumb and index finger as a pincer, one should offer it three times with the fist turned downward to the second recipient alone for the purpose of rinsing the mouth, while reciting the mantra to be described below, releasing the fingers in sequence: the little finger, the ring finger, the middle finger, and the index finger.

Taking water and so forth from the third offering vessel with the hollowed palms (*añjali*), one should offer it by opening the *vajrāñjali* while reciting: "Oṃ āḥ hrīḥ, accept this most excellent honor-offering (*argha*), hūṃ svāhā. This should be done three times. In the third instance of the recipient, and in the previous triad of rites, one should omit *argha* and instead recite: "the foot-water (*pādya*), the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*), and the sipping of water (*ācamana*). 2.3 (p.67)

This sequence of offering water for the feet (*pādya*), sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*), sipping (*ācamana*), and the respectful oblation (*argha*) is generally observed; however, it is seen elsewhere in different orders. One should perform the sprinkling as appropriate, sometimes placing the *argha* first, and sometimes the *argha* alone, according to the occasion and as is fitting. In that regard, one should contemplate the water for the feet being offered for the washing of the feet of the deities; the sprinkling for all the limbs; the sipping for the hand or the mouth; and the *argha* for the front or the head.

Flowers on the head, incense and a lamp before [the deity], an offering of food before [him] or in the hand or the mouth, and perfume on the heart—this is the procedure for the characteristics of the offering of the *argha* and so forth in all rituals.
3. The Procedure for the Purpose and Observances of Preliminary Service (Pūrvasevā).

Thereafter, having been requested for the purpose of consecrating a monastery or similar structure that has been completed, or for the purpose of initiation—whether for his own sake or for the sake of another who desires the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) and so forth—and perceiving a great benefit for sentient beings, he should, after encouraging others [to participate], perform the preliminary service (*pūrvassevā*) which generates the necessary provisions and destroys obstacles for the drawing of the mandala.

For one who knows the path to omniscience does not attain accomplishment without such service; therefore, sitting down free from dualistic conflict, he who knows the reality of the two-fold excellent method should proceed.
Having visualized the circle of deities, when weary, one should recite their mantra;
one should recite one hundred thousand times the mantra of the Lord of the Circle, or one hundred thousand times that of one's own tutelary deity.
And ten thousand discus-bearers—this is called prior service.

69) Furthermore, since the stages of meditation (*bhāvanākrama*) and the mantras for those deities of the generation and completion stages have been explained extensively according to the rules elsewhere, they are not elaborated upon here. Even if one were to describe for each of the many dust-mandalas (*rajo-maṇḍala*) to be discussed below their respective configurations, colors, faces, arms, weapons, and mantras alone, the text would become overly voluminous; thus, fearing that those of limited inclination might not engage with it, we shall not mention even their mere configuration and so forth.

In the *Niṣpannayogāvalī*, however, for those of superior intelligence, we have here stated a concise essence of the sequence of meditation on the deities of the mandala; this must certainly be practiced. For this very reason, the *Niṣpannayogāvalī* is the necessary supplement to the *Vajrāvalī*, just as the *Jyotirmañjarī* is to it.

Thus, having performed the preliminary service (*pūrvasevā*) in detail, one who is capable of manifesting the yoga of the deity mandala—which is instantly and perfectly accomplished in all its aspects, and which both radiates forth and reabsorbs—may, while remaining within the wheel itself, perform the consecration of the mandala and the gathering of disciples by the command or through the accumulation of merit, provided there is no prohibition from the lords of the wheel. This concludes the procedure for the purpose and rules of the preliminary service.
4. The Procedure for Gathering Disciples.

Regarding the procedure for consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*), according to the *Kālacakra*, it should be performed during the months of Māgha, Phālguna, Vaiśākha, Jyeṣṭha, Āṣāḍha, or on the full moon of Caitra; however, according to other sources, it may be performed in Caitra or in Kārttika or Āśvina, on the second, third, fifth, seventh, tenth, thirteenth, or full-moon days.

On the days of the Moon, Mercury, Jupiter, and Venus, there is gain of wealth in Rohiṇī; in Mṛgaśiras, peace; in Ārdrā, good fortune; in Puṣyā, victory; in Uttarā, increase of progeny; in Hastā, success; in Anurādhā, the desired object; in Jyeṣṭhā, happiness; in Mūla and Śravaṇa, knowledge of the scriptures; in Āṣāḍhā, increase of sons; and in Bhādrapadā, general prosperity. When the ascendant is occupied by benefic planets, auspicious undertakings succeed.

The *yogas* free from *viṣkambha*, *atigaṇḍa*, *śūla*, *gaṇḍa*, *vyāghāta*, *vajra*, *vyatīpāta*, *parigha*, and *vaidhṛti* are the causes of success for auspicious rites; likewise, the *karaṇas* must be free from *viṣṭi*. Thus, having ascertained an auspicious *muhūrta* during any of the twelve months—according to the sequence of one's own or another’s established tenets (*siddhānta*), or by the method of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*)—and having been requested two or three times by the disciple for the purpose of drawing the mandala, [the master should proceed].

If the ritual implements have not been gathered, then one should expel the sin—black, deformed, naked, with pendulous testicles, upraised hair, and like a Piśāca—by means of rays from the syllable *HŪṂ* situated upon the sun-disk placed on that [image], which has emerged from the syllable *KAṂ* located in the heart; having drawn that *HŪṂ* back into the heart and transformed it, one should visualize the Great Wrathful One Vajrahūṃkāra as described below and cast him out, reciting: *OṂ SUMBHA NISUMBHA HŪṂ HŪṂ PHAṬ*.

"Oṃ gṛhṇa gṛhṇa hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ! Oṃ gṛhṇāpaya gṛhṇāpaya hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ! Oṃ ānaya ho bhagavan vidyārāja, destroy all the sins of [name], hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā! Reciting this, one should visualize that the sin, having been expelled by the blazing vajra held in the hand, is rendered void. 4.3 (p.74)

Having driven in the stakes against the obstacles in the disciple’s mind by means of the Amṛtakuṇḍalī—shaped like a stake below the navel while reciting himself, "Oṃ vajrakīla, nail down all his obstacles! Bind, bind! Hūṃ phaṭ! as commanded by the Vajrahūṃkāra—one should burn away all the wicked ones with extremely fierce rays from the stakes. Then, having visualized that disciple in the form of Samantabhadra through the syllable *saṃ*, one should contemplate for the sake of protection a moon disc arising from the syllable *a* in the heart, presided over by a double-vajra (*viśvavajra*) produced from the final vowel.

Having reflected thus, one should visualize on the crown of the head a five-pronged vajra arising from the syllable *hūṃ* situated upon a moon, with its prongs pointing upward and its center trampled by Māmakī. Then, having meditated upon oneself as armored, with all limbs pervaded by the radiation of subtle yellow vajra-rays produced from the mantra-garland located within the hub (*varaṭaka*) of the vajra on the moon at the heart of the Wisdom Goddess (*Jñānadevī*), one should provide protection while reciting: *oṃ āḥ śaṅkare śāntikare ghuṭa ghuṭa ghuṭṭini ghātaya ghātaya ghuṭṭini amukaṃ rakṣa svāhā hūṃ*. One should thus protect [the practitioner].

And one should give him the Kuṇḍalī-mantra to recite. When this has been done, obstacles do not prevail over him and the necessary materials are obtained with ease; such is the procedure for gathering disciples.
5. The Procedure for Digging the Earth 5.1 (p. 76)

Then, having gathered the collection of necessary materials and being accompanied by highly skilled assistants, he should perform the rite of the mandala starting from either the full moon until the next full moon, or beginning on the first day of the waxing moon—or the fifth, eighth, tenth, thirteenth, or fourteenth—and continuing until the full moon, starting from the morning. On the day of entering the mandala, however, the master should remain without food along with his disciple.

In that regard, however, if the mandala is being drawn in the forenoon during an auspicious day, lunar mansion, and muhūrta, by one who is learned (*savidya*), properly engaged in the yoga of the Lord of the Mandala and the deities, and has performed prior service (*pūrvasaṃsevā*): if it is drawn in the eastern direction, there will be the death of the king and various calamities for the people; in the southern direction, the person for whose sake the mandala was made will die; in the western direction, the preceptor (*ācārya*) will die; in the northern direction, one who has entered [the mandala] there will die; and in the southeastern direction, there will be rain.

Knowing that there will be famine in the southwest, wind and rain in the northwest, death near a shrine (*caitya*), water near water presided over by *nāgas*, and the death of a child in the shade of a tree—one should abandon all these and, in the northeast direction from towns, cities, villages, groves, monasteries, and dwellings, or wherever the mind finds peace, select an excellent mandala site sloping toward the north and east.

Having fashioned the mandala with perfumes and other offerings, having fully worshipped the deities of the mandala, and having given the *bali* offering, one should dismiss them into the sky. Then, with offerings of *bali* and other gifts, [one should address] the local guardians (*kṣetrapāla*) and others situated there:
"Whatever gods, *nāgas*, *yakṣas*, or *rākṣasas* are present here, I entreat them; may they grant me this ground for the sake of the mandala."

Having thus requested three times, and having ascertained through a dream or other means that she has been granted [permission] by them or is unopposed, one should, on the morning of the following day, pray to Śrī Vajradhara and the others situated in the expanse of the sky; having caused them to grant mental permission, one should at midday dispel obstacles either through the meditation on the protection wheel and the nailing down of obstacles (*vighnakīlana*) or through a wrathful fire-offering (*krūrahoma*). In the case of the fire-offering, for the sake of protecting the disciple, one should perform a pacifying fire-offering (*śāntikahoma*) in the afternoon in a hearth located in the southeast direction. Then, [one consecrates] that ground with: *oṃ āḥ vighnāntakṛt hūṃ*.

Having sprinkled [the site] with mustard seeds, water, and ashes over which the *sarvakṛnmantra* beginning with "ityādi" has been recited, one should sit in the vajraparyaṅka posture and meditate there upon the Earth Goddess (*pṛthivīdevatā*) in the form that will be described. Preceded by the offerings of water for the feet (*pādya*), water for sipping (*ācamana*), and the respectful oblation (*argha*), one should entreat her three times with the words "Come, come! and so forth, or "O Goddess, you... and so forth. Having mentally raised her as she replies, "Let it be done thus," one should establish her in the sky.

Then, considering that ground to be free from obstacles and having offered the *bali* as before, one should cause it to be excavated in the region of the belly of the *vāstu-nāga*—measuring either one *vyāma* or reaching the depth of the neck, or down to the water level or the bedrock, according to the distinction of inferior, middling, or superior success; or else, measuring up to the knees, the hips, or the navel. This is the procedure for digging the earth.
6. The Procedure for Purifying the Ground in Three Ways. 6.1 (p. 80)
Then, from [eating] stone, there arises a great wind; from bone, the occurrence of colic;
from gravel, muteness; and from husks or charcoal, fever.

Thinking that minor disturbances may arise from wood containing hair or roots and the like, one should remove ashes, charcoal, hair, husks, stones, bones, gravel, bricks, potsherds, and so forth. Then, having filled the pit with that very same earth moistened with fragrant water, and if there is a deficiency, having added more earth as well, one should sprinkle it with scented water consecrated by the *sarvakṛt* mantra and the syllable *HŪṂ*. One should then prepare the ground to be half a cubit high, level, slightly raised in the center like the back of a tortoise, and slightly sloping toward the northeast.
Moreover,
if one is unable to extract all the defects of the arrow-heads;
Having placed the hand [upon it], one should recite the mantra; that indeed is the most excellent purification.
On the stone terraces of palaces, in cow-pens, in hermitages and similar places, or on the banks of rivers;
Purification occurs even without digging, or in a place that has already been consecrated in the past.

But that [place] should first be cleared of evil beings by Amṛtakuṇḍalin alone, and then one should sprinkle it with mustard seeds, water, and ashes over which that mantra has been recited; beginning from the eastern direction, one should smear it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) over which that mantra has been recited.

One should sprinkle this ground, which has been dug and pounded, with scented water; reciting "Oṃ bhūḥ khaṃ," one should make it into space. Then, having visualized it as consisting of vajras by means of "Hūṃ laṃ hūṃ," one should empower it by placing the hand upon it and consecrating it with the mantras: "Oṃ medini vajrībhava vajra bandha hūṃ," "Oṃ hana hana vajrakrodha hūṃ phaṭ," and "Oṃ āḥ hūṃ śodhaya śodhaya rakṣa rakṣa hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ. One should then preside over it.

On that ground, having filled its center with all-creating five-jeweled medicinal herbs and grains as appropriate, and having sprinkled it with scented water consecrated by those same mantras, one should incorporate the terrestrial deities residing in the sky through the offering of bali, pādya, and so forth; then, reciting "Oṃ Āḥ Hūṃ," one should perform the *kamalāvarta* and recite the hundred-syllable mantra.

Furthermore, through the firm resolve (*adhimokṣa*) that the entire universe is of a single flavor with emptiness, one should resolve that the ground has the nature of suchness (*tathatā*) and is utterly pure; this is the unsurpassed purification.

Then, having determined the directions such as the east according to the sequence to be described, one should have that site for the maṇḍala constructed so that it is well-sheltered, contains a four-doored peaked pavilion (*kūṭāgāra*) within which the expansion of one’s wishes proceeds, is surrounded by archways (*toraṇa*) and boundary-poles (*akṣavāṭa*) on the four sides, is variegated in every respect, hung with garlands of flowers and bells, and provided with banners and spread canopies. This is the threefold procedure for purifying the ground. 7. The Procedure for Taking Possession of the Ground.

There, having sat down in the center of the mandala ground strewn with flowers, holding a vajra and a vajra-bell, possessing the yoga of the mandala to be drawn, having destroyed obstacles by means of the protection wheel and other rites, holding an incense burner, and with a tongue [empowered] by the *hūṃ*-born vajra, he should say:
"May all the Buddhas residing in the directions without exception attend to me!
Here, I, the Vajra-holder named so-and-so, shall draw the mandala."
All the Buddhas and others who have arrived shall grant you this accomplishment.

Having thus invited and honored the Perfectly Awakened One and the others, [the preceptor] proceeds— either with the four disciples Vairocana and the rest stationed in the directions starting from the east, each appropriately joined with the yogins of Vairocana and so forth while holding the vajra and bell, or even with a single disciple— moving sequentially to each respective location and saying:
"Teach the supreme maṇḍala, which is the peaceful state of all Tathāgatas, the abode of all Tathāgatas, and the foremost selflessness of all phenomena."
Complete with all the marks and devoid of all unmarked characteristics,
speak of the supreme mandala, the foremost body of Samantabhadra.
Proclaim the supreme maṇḍala, born from the foremost of peaceful dharmas, which purifies the conduct of gnosis, and which is the pinnacle of Samantabhadra’s speech.
The great mind of all sentient beings is pure and naturally stainless;
O Charioteer of the Mandala, speak of the supreme Samantabhadra-mind!
Thus, one should exhort oneself with each of these four verses.

Through the application of the five colors, the dust-mandala (*rajomaṇḍala*) is also a *maṇḍala*, for it consists of all Tathāgatas, is produced from the great peaceful samādhi of Vairocana and the others, is inhabited by all Tathāgatas, and is the form of the lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*) of the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) and so forth; because it illuminates the attainment of the essence of great bliss, which is inseparable from emptiness and compassion, and because it possesses characteristics such as being square and is free from defects such as being too thin or too thick, it is the supreme body (*kāyāgra*), having the nature of the Body-Vajra (*kāyavajra*). Thus, it is "the supreme body."

It has manifested in the form of pure dharmas. That which purifies the conduct for the sake of such gnosis is, by virtue of its illuminating nature, of the essence of the Vajra of Speech (*vāgvajra*). Because it radiates as the intrinsic nature of all phenomena, it is the Great Mind (*mahācitta*); in reality, it is the nature of the Vajra of Mind (*cittavajra*), being free from all conceptual impositions. Addressing the Charioteer with the words "Speak!", he brings this meaning directly before him. However, the traditional teaching (*āmnāya*) is that in the absence of an actual petitioner, one should likewise perform [the request] through meditative absorption (*dhyāna*). 7.2 (p. 87)

Then, preceded by the emanation of the maṇḍala circle and so forth, having visualized the maṇḍala, and holding two vajra-fists with the two index fingers extended, their tips joined and facing downward upon his head, he utters "HŪṂ VAJROTTHA" and rises up into the sky. Breaking his cross-legged posture and standing up, facing east, he plants his feet evenly and pays homage to the Tathāgatas with his palms joined at his crown. Then, beholding sentient beings enveloped in the darkness of ignorance and possessed by Māras, [he addresses] the Māras.

In order to instantly dispel [obstacles], one should assume the form of the Vajra-Hūṃkāra to be described below, possessing a fierce, haughty demeanor with furrowed brows and bared fangs due to the possession of wrath. With the syllable *ma*, the right eye is made into the sun; with the syllable *ṭa*, the left eye is made into the moon; and with the syllable *hūṃ*, both pupils are made into the fire at the end of an aeon. With this "vajra-vision," one should gaze upon the entire world in all directions and generate the following pride:
"I myself am the Vajra-holder; I myself am Vajrasattva.
I am the Buddha, the Great King; I am the Vajra-holder of great power."
I am the Lord of Yogins, the King; I am Vajrapāṇi, the steadfast one.
Thus.

7.3 (p.89) Then, with a blazing vajra visualized on the soles of his feet, performing the graceful *kamalāvarta* movement as the occasion required, brandishing the vajra and ringing the vajra-bell, he proceeded toward the northeast by means of the vajra-step itself.

Beginning from that [point] and proceeding clockwise on the mandala ground together with the disciples, one should dance in vajra-steps, [placing the weight] successively on the eyes, the hands, the hips, the feet, and the sides.
One should rotate it with the application of the *tāla* gesture, and likewise again with the reverse movement.
Then, having performed the *dhārā-nṛtya*, one should have the practitioner dance with a creeper;
likewise, having danced to rapid beats, one should whirl about like a wheel.

May those who are here—whether they be gods, asuras, yakṣas, rākṣasas, pretas, piśācas, apasmāras, bhūtas, ḍākas, ḍākinīs, male or female stars, elders, their wives, attendants, retinues, garuḍas, kimpuruṣas, or mantra-adepts—depart from this spot on earth. This is for the sake of the fulfillment of perfect awakening by me, the teacher so-and-so, for such-and-such a disciple, and for the purpose of causing all sentient beings to attain unsurpassed knowledge.

"The glorious [mandala of] such-and-such must be drawn; therefore, having heard this command of the Great Vajradhara, depart immediately! Whoever does not depart, his head I shall shatter into a hundred pieces with this blazing *hūṃ*-syllable vajra, a great and intensely flaming wisdom-vajra!
Or rather: "Let all the hosts of obstacles dwelling in body, speech, and mind listen!
I am the glorious Vajradhara, the executor of the wheel of commands."
With my vajra of blazing form, I shall shatter those born of the three bodies;
if anyone should transgress against me, they shall be destroyed here, and not otherwise.

Or, reciting "iti" three times, one should dispel obstructing spirits with infinite wrathful deities whose eyes are wide open. One should then consecrate the site of the mandala, down to the netherworlds (*pātāla*), as consisting of the swift vajra of the syllable *hūṃ*.

91) Here, while rotating, one should insert the vajra into the bell held by the disciple standing to one's left at each door, and that vajra into one's own bell. In this same manner, one proceeds to the front, the right, and the back.

Therein, having visualized a single-pronged vajra born from the syllable *hūṃ* on the sole of the foot, one should dance and move about while striking that vajra upon the ground with the sole of the foot. Thereafter, likewise with a three-pronged [vajra]; thereafter, likewise with a five-pronged [vajra]; and thereafter, likewise with a universal [vajra]. However, these are performed by moving about while turning back. These four, which mark with the vajra and are themselves vajras as they strike, are the "vajra-steps" (*vajrapada*).
Each should be performed once, proceeding clockwise, with the *ālīḍha* and other postures. 7.5 (p.92)

In that regard, bending the left calf and placing the right foot gracefully and straight at a distance of five *vitastis* constitutes the *ālīḍha* stance. Bending the right calf and placing the left [foot] in the same manner constitutes the *pratyālīḍha*.
The *vaiśākha* stance has a width of twenty-six finger-breadths (*aṅgula*), with the toes of the outer feet pointing outward and both knees held stiff.
The *vaiśākha* posture itself, with the two hands at a distance of one cubit and shaped like the wings of a swan, is the *maṇḍala* posture.
The *sama* posture arises from the mutual contact of the toes of both feet.
Regarding these five postures, some say that for each posture one should perform one complete circumambulation to the right.
Others say that the *pratikaraṇa* consists of three circumambulations; others say there is no fixed rule in this matter.

Having placed the two heels with a space of four finger-breadths between them and keeping the left foot straight, one should place the right foot across at a distance of one span (*vitasti*), gracefully, like the position of the Vaiśālī star—this is the *jātapada*.
Likewise, having kept the right foot straight and placing the left foot across, this is the *pratyājātapada*.
Having placed the feet together, one should hold the right foot three *vitastis* ahead of the left; this is the *vikaṭapada*.
Likewise, having made the right leg straight, one should place the left [foot] three *vitastis* ahead of the right; this is the *prativikaṭapada*.
One may also join the two soles of the feet together even while seated; this is the *sampuṭapada*.
One should step upon the left foot with the right foot; this is the *kūrmapada* (tortoise-step).
Having lifted one foot, one should move about with the other; this is the *ekapada* (single-step).

One should perform these seven steps according to the fixed rule of positions, as well as the *bhramarījāla* (swarm-of-bees). The *bhramarījāla* consists of moving all around the body by circling to the right and to the left.

While performing these thirteen [postures] beginning with *ālīḍha*, one should execute, as appropriate, the four foot-placements—*sāgarāndola*, *parvatotkṣepa*, *lalitākṣepa*, and *krodhākṣepa*—the nine throws (*akṣepa*), the six [movements] such as *vajrotkarṣa*, and the thirteen symbolic gestures (*abhinaya*) of the sword and other implements.

96) Thereafter, having performed the dance in *ālīḍha*, facing south, one should cast the left index finger toward the heart; then, falling to the ground on the left side while gazing into the sky, one should strike down all the Māras with the right hand holding the vajra. 1/

Having performed the dance preceded by the *kamalāvarta*, one should raise the *vajra* and, threatening with the left index finger, lift the *vajradaṇḍamudrā* with the right hand while standing with feet even. Playfully, one should step forward with the right foot in the *vajrapada* stance, bent slightly, extending two and a half *tālas*, while keeping the left foot steady; then, with both feet positioned like wings, one should bend the right knee and raise the *daṇḍamudrā*. Threatening with the left index finger, one should bend the left side of the torso.
Closing the left eye, one should rotate the face in the mandala; fixing the gaze and knitting the brows—this is the *ākampanākṣepa*. The withdrawal is at the right hip. 2.

Likewise, raising the vajra and standing with feet together, one should extend both feet evenly to a distance of two and a half *tālas* and place them so that they form a triangle. Having struck the ground in front with the hands, one should raise the *daṇḍamudrā* and look out, placing the index finger on the left breast—this is the *trāsanākṣepa*. The withdrawal is at the left hip region. 3.

In the same way, having formed the Vajrotthāna-mudrā and standing with feet even, one should raise the staff-mudrā (*daṇḍamudrā*), close the right eye, and look at the index finger on the breast with the left eye. Having assumed the left vajra-step (*vajrapada*) and bent the right knee, one should lift the foot and, full of wrath, suddenly whirl it with the left like a wheel. Then, bending that foot, one should place it in the half-pratyālīḍha stance; keeping the feet steady and positioned like wings—this is the "Agitation and Casting" (*saṃkṣobhaṇākṣepa*). By means of the application of the Vajra-dance, there is a withdrawal (*saṃhāra*) at the right hip. 4.

Likewise, having performed the *vajrotthāna*, standing with feet even, one should raise the staff-mudrā and look at the forefinger on the breast with the left eye; bending the left knee and placing the right in the *vajrapada* position, one should lift the left foot and suddenly whirl it around with the right, then set it down. Having placed the fallen foot so that it is bent, standing, and triangular, and having placed the right side-stationary, one should stand in the *ālīḍha* posture—this is the "confounding throw. While dancing, the withdrawal is at the region of the left hip. 5.
Having turned around with this same left foot, one should again strike with the hand in front and then raise the staff once more; this is specifically the "swift throw" (kṣiprākṣepa).

The "confounding throw" (vimohanākṣepa) is indeed the "turned-face throw" (vyāvṛtāsyākṣepa), but with the mouth opened, the tongue placed in the manner of licking a bell, and one should whirl like a wheel. 6–7.

In the same manner, having raised the *vajra* and placed the two feet at a distance of one *tāla*, one should form a triangle. One should slightly bend the right knee and incline the left knee; one should also incline the region of the breast and the left side of the abdomen. Following the movement of the staff-like arm with the index finger upon the breast, and immediately after casting the gaze upon the staff, the face is whirled about; this is the throw known as *kelīkila*. The withdrawal [of the hand] occurs on the right hip. 8.

When that very *mahākelīkila* has his gaze fixed on the staff and is led behind his own back by means of the region of his right shoulder—with his left eye closed, enraged, and making a stamping motion with his feet—the withdrawal (*saṃhāra*) is as before.
9/7.7 (p.98). Having assumed the *vāmagarva* posture, one should raise a vajra at the heart with the right hand; this is the *vajrotkarṣa*. 1.

2. *Vajrākṣepa*: With the left *vajra-muṣṭi*, the raised index finger threatens the heart; with the right *vajra-muṣṭi*, one performs the gesture of striking with a *vajra*. 3. *Vajrabhairava*: With the four fingers having their tips contracted, one presses the thumbs; extending both hands upward and downward from the mouth, one makes the mouth, nostrils, cheeks, and eyes wide open and terrifying. 4. *Vajrakuṇḍali*: Having whirled the *vajra* clockwise with the right hand, one places both feet on the ground in succession.
Extending the left arm while holding the base of the right hand—which holds a vajra—at its root, one should dance; this is the Vajra Dance (vajranartana). 5.
Preceded by the Vajra Dance, one should tilt the head to the left with a sense of pride; this is the Strīmāyā gesture (strīmāyākaraṇa). 6. 7.8 (p. 100)

The mudrā of Vajralāsyā from pride is as follows: drawing the right vajra-fist out from the sheath of the left vajra-fist and holding it in the gesture of a sword is the gesture of the sword (1). Threatening at the heart with the right [hand] while brandishing a three-pronged vajra is the gesture of the vajra (2).

The *muṣalābhinaya* (gesture of the pestle) is so called because of the crushing of obstacles with a pestle held in the *vajrabandha* [mudrā]. 3. Having formed the *sampuṭāñjali* (the hollowed palms), one joins the tips of the fingers of each hand together to form the *vajrāñjali*; likewise, at the base, the *vajrabandha* is formed through a firm binding. Having made the two little fingers and the two index fingers of the two *vajramuṣṭis* (vajra-fists) joined as in the *vajrabandha*, one should release them like a wheel; this is the *cakrābhinaya* (gesture of the wheel). 4. One should gracefully extend the index and middle fingers of the right *vajramuṣṭi* and hold them upward; this is the *patākābhinaya* (gesture of the banner). 5.
One should open the joined palms like a lotus; this is the *padmābhinaya* (lotus gesture). 6.
Having formed a right fist with the thumb tucked inside, one should extend the index finger and raise the arm upward like a staff; this is the *daṇḍābhinaya* (staff gesture). 7.
One should hold the right index finger in the manner of drawing [a rein]; this is the *aṅkuśābhinaya* (goad gesture). 8.

Extending and then contracting the fingers of the right hand constitutes the gesture of the hood (*phaṇābhinaya*). (9) Taking a bow with the left hand and drawing the string back to the ear with the right hand to hold the weapon constitutes the gesture of the bow (*cāpābhinaya*). (10) Drawing an arrow with the right index and middle fingers constitutes the gesture of drawing the arrow (*śarākarṣaṇābhinaya*). (11)
From those very two [hands], by means of the gesture of raising an arrow, there is the "gesture of raising an arrow" (12).
By means of the gesture of performing praise, one should hold the joined palms at the heart; this is the "gesture of salutation" (13).

Thereafter, having performed the gestures of prostration (*praṇāma*) and the *kamalāvarta* [turning of the lotus], and dancing with the *vajrapada* while brandishing the *vajra* and ringing the bell, one enters the center of the maṇḍala ground and sits. Having first uttered the syllable *hūṃ*, one should expel the obstacles by means of the infinite wrathful deities who have been emanated through the ten gestures. One should meditate on the maṇḍala ground as being composed of vajras down to the subterranean realm (*ārasātala*). Among these, the gesture of the vajra-throne (*vajrāsana*) is formed by binding the vajra-paryaṅka and the earth-touching mudrā (*bhūsparśamudrā*).
(1) The gesture of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) is formed by binding the samādhi-mudrā. (2)
Placing the left foot between the right calf and thigh, and then placing the right foot upon that between the left calf and thigh— this is the vajraparyaṅka posture.
Placing the left calf upon the right calf so that both knees are bent down— this is the padmāsana posture.
Placing the right foot upon the left thigh and placing the left foot on the surface of the right thigh is the *sattvaparyaṅka* (the hero’s cross-legged posture).

(5) Having bound the half-crossed posture with the left foot, one should place the right knee upright and straight near it; this is the *vīrāsana* (hero’s posture). (6) Some say that the *vīrāsana* consists of making the left half-crossed and placing the right knee fallen upon it, then placing the right foot face-up at the base of the left thigh.
Holding both feet straight while seated on a high seat is the *bhadrāsana* (auspicious posture). (7)
Placing the two feet at a distance of one span (*vitasti*) on the seat and remaining seated with the heels drawn up is the *utkuṭuka* posture (8).
Having placed the right foot in the *sattvaparyaṅka* position, extending the left leg gracefully is the *salīla* posture (9).
Sitting with the two feet joined together is the *svastika* posture (10).

7.10 (p.104) Regarding these vajra-steps and so forth, one should perform the two types of gazing—looking forward with the vajra-gazes and looking backward with the face turned away—as appropriate. One should also practice the nine aesthetic sentiments (*rasas*)—the erotic, the heroic, the loathsome, the furious, the comic, the terrifying, the compassionate, the marvelous, and the peaceful—as explained in the *Āmnāyamañjarī*. Furthermore, one should perform the gestures (*ākṣepas*) beginning with the vajra-steps and ending with the gazes, as taught in the *Māyājāla*, *Paramādya*, *Krodhavijaya*, and other tantras, and as explained here.

The knowers of the tradition maintain that even if one fails to perform all or some of the vajra-positions and so forth due to lack of full understanding, incapacity, a desire for a concise ritual, or simply out of lack of interest, there is no impairment to the present undertaking; for the removal of obstacles is accomplished even by means of circumambulation and other such acts.

Then, having worshipped the mandala ground smeared with fragrant paste with flowers, incense, and so forth, as well as with incense burners at the four corners and four gates, and with dance, song, and the like; and having touched it with one’s hand and recited the mantra of the Lord of the Mandala one hundred and eight times, and the hundred-syllable mantra seven times; and having emanated and reabsorbed the circle of deities right there, one should go to sleep—this is the procedure for the appropriation of the site.
8. The Procedure for Nailing Down Obstacles (Vighnakīlanavidhi) 8.1 (p. 106)

Then, having risen in the morning and reflected, "I shall act so that the world may reach the state of the Vajra-holder without obstacle," one should instantly, following the realization of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), visualize—arising from the syllable *raṃ* and situated upon a double-vajra (*viśvavajra*) born from the syllable *hūṃ*—a vajra-fence, a cage, and a canopy of arrow-nets formed by a single, seamless mass produced by the radiation of light rays from the syllable *hūṃ* located on the double-vajra; and below, a ground consisting of blazing, unbearable flames and universal thunderbolts (*viśvakuliśa*). In the center of that, one should instantaneously manifest oneself through the transformation of one's own being into the form of Vajrasattva.

Vajra-hūṃkāra, also known by the name Trailokyavijaya, stands upon a sun disc atop a multicolored lotus, trampling upon Bhairava and Kālarātri with his two feet in the *ālīḍha* posture. Enraged, blazing like the fire at the end of an aeon, and appearing as a mass of radiant rays, he seems to devour the entire multitude of obstacles in the world. His three faces—the central blue, the right yellow, and the left green—are wide open; his tongue is lolling out fiercely with prominent fangs. Each face has three round red eyes, arched brows, and furrowed brows. He is adorned with the six mudrās.

Adorned with a garland of five skulls on his forehead and a row of heads from which blood flows hanging from his neck as ornaments, wearing a tiger skin garment slipping from a girdle of severed heads, with upward-flaming tawny locks of hair encircled by the blue serpent Ananta, and decorated with the kings of serpents such as Takṣaka; with two hands holding a vajra and a vajra-bell, his two vajra-fists joined at the back, his two little fingers linked together, and his two index fingers extended—thus, in the Trailokyavijaya mudrā, he is in union with his own consort Prajñā.

Holding a goad and a noose with his two right hands and a skull-cup and a khaṭvāṅga with his two left hands, filling the quarters of the sky with the resounding "huṃ" and "haḥ," he draws in the obstructors of the ten directions with rays of light emanating from the "huṃ" syllable at his own heart and delivers them over to the ten wrathful deities manifested from that same "huṃ" syllable.

And those wrathful stakes (kīla), eighteen, twelve, or eight finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) in length respectively, with a thickness of six, four, or two and a half finger-breadths, made of *khadira* wood, bone, or iron, placed in nine vessels, smeared with white mustard seeds and red sandalwood, wrapped with five-colored threads, and worshipped—having visualized each of these ten stakes as being bound with garlands of red flowers—one should [drive them] below the navel...

Upon the form of the single trident, one should visualize a kila in the form of oneself, blazing like the fire at the end of an aeon; with the left hand in the vajra-fist and the right hand, having turned the primary insignia into a mallet bound with a garland of red flowers, one should seize it and, uttering the long-sounding *hūṃ*, drive it into the ten directions of the kūpas, [reciting] "Oṃ vajrakīla kīlaya sarvavighnān hūṃ" or the like, to enter those obstacles.

Reciting "Oṃ gha gha ghāṭaya ghāṭaya sarvaduṣṭān phaṭ phaṭ kīlaya sarvapāpān phaṭ phaṭ hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ vajrakīla vajradharo ājñāpayati sarvavighnānāṃ kāyavākcittaṃ kīlaya hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ," and while visualizing that they are nailing [the stakes] at the head, reciting "Oṃ vajramudgarākoṭaya hūṃ" as they strike them, one begins from the northeast direction and proceeds clockwise outside the vajra-fence of the maṇḍala.
In the circle of light, the preceptor should first perform the ritual of driving in and striking the stakes in the eight directions; if he is unable to do so, then the door-preceptors should do it.
He should drive in the stake of Uṣṇīṣa to the east of the eastern stake, and the stake of Sumbha to the west of the western stake.

Although it is stated in the *Tattvasaṃgraha* and other works that one should "drive in the stakes" within the external mandala-circle, nevertheless, contemporary masters say and do the following: outside the mandala house, one should perform the rite of driving in the stakes; upon the ten lumps of clay placed thereon, one should honor the wrathful deities in the form of stakes with flowers and so forth at each junction of the day, as well as with parasols and offerings of bali. Since even in this way the desired accomplishment is all the more easily attained, there is no contradiction. Thus, through the acts of driving in and striking, one should contemplate the host of obstacles as being of a single flavor with suchness through great bliss (*mahāsukha*).

And one should visualize all remaining obstacles fleeing far away; thus, one should resolutely resolve that the entire world—above, below, and across, as far as the great Cakravāḍa mountains—is in every way free from obstacles and firm. This is the first stage.

Alternatively: OṂ ĀḤ HŪṂ! Yamāntakṛt, nail down all evil Indras and Upendras together with their retinues! HŪṂ PHAṬ! OṂ ĀḤ HŪṂ! Prajñāntakṛt, nail down all evil Yamas together with their retinues! HŪṂ PHAṬ! OṂ ĀḤ HŪṂ! Padmāntakṛt, nail down all evil Nāgas together with their retinues! HŪṂ PHAṬ! OṂ ĀḤ HŪṂ! Vighnāntakṛt, nail down all evil Kuveras together with their retinues! HŪṂ PHAṬ! OṂ ĀḤ HŪṂ! Acala, nail down all evil Īśānas together with their retinues! HŪṂ PHAṬ!

Oṃ āḥ hūṃ! Ṭakki, nail down all evil fires together with their retinues! Hūṃ phaṭ! Oṃ āḥ hūṃ! Nīladaṇḍa, nail down all evil Nairṛtis together with their retinues! Hūṃ phaṭ! Oṃ āḥ hūṃ! Mahābala, nail down all evil winds together with their retinues! Hūṃ phaṭ! Oṃ āḥ hūṃ! Cakravartin, nail down all evil suns, moons, and Pitāmahas together with their retinues! Hūṃ phaṭ!

"Oṃ āḥ hūṃ! Sumbha! All wicked Vemacitrin and earth-deities, together with your retinues, be pinned down! Hūṃ phaṭ! With these mantras, one should perform the pinning and striking against the obstacles in the forms of Indra and the other [guardians] in the east and so forth. All else is as before; this is the second sequence.
Some say that the four stakes should be driven into the four corners, while others say they should be placed at the gates.

The colors, forms, and other characteristics of the wrathful deities and Indra and the others are to be understood from the *Āmnāyamañjarī*. Furthermore, when one so desires, there is the extensive meditation on the *Rakṣācakra* (Protection Wheel). Alternatively, even without wooden stakes of *khadira* wood and the like, one should perform the pinning and striking by means of the aforementioned meditation alone; then, turning the hands upward and reciting "Oṃ Vajra Hūṃ," while lifting the ground, one should resolve [upon it] in that manner. This is the procedure for pinning down obstacles. 9.
The Procedure for the Consecration of Vasundharā 9.1 (p. 113)

Thereafter, having sat down in the center of the mandala ground upon a prepared mandala of perfumes, one should visualize Vasundharā arising from the syllable *vaṃ*. Contemplating three *hūṃ*s on the moon of the right hand, one strikes the ground three times with the tips of the fingers; through those sounds and the rays of light from the *hūṃ* syllables, she is urged forth. Having become one with the Earth Goddess, who has arisen in the form of a Jñānasattva, she is yellow, gentle, dressed in white garments, adorned with various ornaments, and her heart is bound with affection.

Having worshipped her—who stands before him with two hands, the left holding a golden *bhadraghaṭa* vessel and the other extended in the gesture of fearlessness, having one face—preceded by the offering of water (*argha*) and so forth, he should address her with haste: "Oṃ! Come, come, O Great Goddess, Mother of the World of Earth, you who are filled with all jewels and adorned with divine ornaments!"
O you whose sound is the resonance of necklaces and anklets, who are worshipped by Vajrasattva:
having accepted this *argha*, please perfectly accomplish the work of the mandala.

One should perform the consecration (*adhivāsana*) by reciting "hrī hī hī hī haṃ svāhā" three times, including the invocation (*āvāhana*) and the rite for bringing [the deity] into proximity (*sannidhāpana*). By implication, the phrase "well-accomplished" (*susādhaya*) indicates the departure (*visānnidhya*) [of the deity].
Alternatively, [one may proceed as follows].
O Goddess, you are the witness of all the Buddhas, the Protectors,
regarding the specificities of the methods of conduct and the stages and perfections.
Just as the army of Māra was broken by the Protector, the Lion of the Śākyas,
so too, having conquered the army of Māra, I shall draw the maṇḍala.

Having recited this three times, one should perform the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsana*). Having said, "Let it be done thus," one should contemplate that [the earth] has dissolved right there. Then, having formed the *vajrabandha* mudrā with the palms joined together, one should press down upon the ground with it. Having empowered it three times with "Oṃ vajrībhava hūṃ," one should visualize that from the spreading rays of the blazing syllable *HŪṂ* emerging from the *vajrabandha*, the earth is made into a vajra as far as the bottom of the netherworld (*ārasātala*). Reciting "Oṃ vajra dṛḍha tiṣṭha" three times, one should preside over it. Thereby, the earth shall become subject to oneself. This is the procedure for the preliminary consecration of the Earth-Goddess (*vasundharā*). 10. The Procedure for the Preliminary Consecration of the Vase (*kalaśa*)

10.1 (p.117) Then, having had the mandala ground smeared with fragrant substances mixed with the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) consecrated by the three-syllable mantra, and having had it strewn with heaps of flowers, [the practitioner], having bathed in the afternoon, with limbs scented with fragrance, wearing bright red garments, garlanded, with a fragrant face, and adorned with ornaments such as necklaces, anklets, armlets, earrings, bracelets, a girdle, and rings;

Adorned with a crown and red garments consecrated by reciting "Oṃ hūṃ svāhā" and "Oṃ vajroṣṇīṣa hūṃ phaṭ" seven times respectively, he sits in the center of the maṇḍala ground facing east; alternatively, sitting in the eastern part of the maṇḍala facing west, possessing the yoga of the Lord of the Maṇḍala, he prepares maṇḍalas at the locations of the deities using nectar, sandalwood, saffron, and so forth, visualizes his own pledge-circle (*samayacakra*) therein, and invites the wisdom-circle (*jñānamaṇḍala*) situated in space.

Having caused [the disciples] to enter and having performed the worship, praise, and tasting of nectar (*amṛta*), one should consecrate the vases situated in the directions starting from the east outside the visualized maṇḍala; alternatively, however, facing north, one should consecrate those located in the northeast corner.

In that regard, for the jar used in rites of pacification (*śānti*) and nourishment (*puṣṭi*), the interior of the belly is sixteen finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) in circumference; from the bottom of the belly to the edge of the lip, the height is twenty finger-breadths; the two lips hanging down from the mouth to the limit are two finger-breadths each; the neck is six finger-breadths; the mouth is eight finger-breadths from one lip-edge to the other; and of those eight finger-breadths, two parts constitute the opening of the neck, while one part constitutes the length of the two lips.

For the rites of causing enmity (*vidveṣa*) and eradication (*uccāṭana*), the belly [of the vessel] is twelve finger-breadths in circumference and twenty-four finger-breadths in height; the curved neck is eight finger-breadths, and the mouth is six finger-breadths with lips one finger-breadth each. For the rites of subjugation (*vaśya*) and attraction (*ākarṣaṇa*), it is fashioned by the artisan exactly as a jar would be. For the rite of paralysis (*stambhana*), it is short, being sixteen finger-breadths in both circumference and height, with a neck of four finger-breadths and a mouth of six finger-breadths, with thick lips of two finger-breadths.

For all rites, such as those of pacification and so forth, the vessels described [in the *Kālacakra*] should be taken; for it is stated in the *Kālacakra*: "In other tantras, although vessels that have roots at the wrong time, drooping lips, high necks, and large bellies are mentioned, one should nevertheless understand that they must possess the sixteen-finger measurement and so forth.
Here, Nāgabuddhipāda has said:
"Whether made of gold, silver, copper, or even clay..."
Having collected whatever has been obtained, the observer of the vow should place it in the flask.

Therefore, having rendered the golden and other vessels empty according to the described characteristics, one should visualize them as having the form of jewels through the syllable *vaṃ*. For the sake of pacification (*śānti*) and nourishment (*puṣṭi*), they should be whitened with rice, flour, chalk, or sandalwood; marked with the symbols of the deities; filled with the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*), scented water, the five jewels, medicinal herbs, and grains; adorned with shining sprouts at their openings; with their necks bound by pairs of cloths and garlands; and arranged individually in the shape of a mandala beneath a canopy, following the sequence for depositing the signs of the dust-mandala (*raja-maṇḍala*) to be described later.
"Having placed [the disciples], seated upon appropriate seats atop a fragrant maṇḍala, before him, the one skilled in the ritual should place a very white thread upon a cloth.

According to this instruction from the tradition of Nāgabuddhipāda, one should wrap [the area] with seven white threads over which the *hūṃ* has been recited seven times, using the mantra: *oṃ vajraśikhara rūṭamaṭa diśāṃ bandha bandha hūṃ*. According to another tantra, it should be done with five threads of colors corresponding to the specific rites, such as pacification (*śānti*).

10.4 (p.122) The five jewels are pearl, gold, ruby (*padmarāga*), coral, and *rājāvarta* stone. If a ruby is unavailable, silver, copper, conch, or a jewel may be used in place of the *rājapaṭṭa*. When one’s wealth is meager, the *vijaya* and *sārvakarmika* jars must be made with an interior filled with jewels (*ratnagarbha*); other jars are not permitted. Even in that case, the *vijaya* jar must necessarily have its interior filled with jewels. The five medicinal herbs are *bṛhatī*, *kaṇṭakārī*, white and red *daṇḍotpala*, and white *aparājitā*.

The five grains are sesame, barley, mung beans, rice, and wheat; in some places, mung beans (*mudga*) are listed in place of rice. [One should use] the sprouts of any one of the five: mango, *nāgakeśara*, *aśoka*, *aśvattha*, and *udumbara*. In the absence of *nāgakeśara*, [the sprouts of] *nyagrodha* or *jambu* may be used. The cloth should be red, yellow, or white; in some places, green or blue is also prescribed. 10.5 (p. 124)

In the victory vase (vijayakalaśa), which stands upon a lotus in the center of the source of phenomena (dharmodayā), there should be the emblem, seed-syllable, or [name] of the presiding deity, according to the appropriate placement upon either the moon or the sun. In the other vases, upon a lotus, there should be the respective emblems or seed-syllables of the deities upon either the moon or the sun.
As Nāgabuddhipāda has said:
"For all the deities of the maṇḍala, there should be the seed-syllable or else the emblem."
The wise one should draw [the symbols] on the side of the jar.

Thus, in whichever maṇḍala there are as many deities as there are, there should be that many vases for them; or else, [there should be vases] only for the deities of the central chamber (*garbhapuṭa*). In that case, there are four for the Mothers of the Families (*kulamātṛ*), five for the Tathāgatas, or else five for the Tathāgatas alone. Or else, there is one for the Lord (*adhipati*), one for the four Tathāgatas, one for the four Mothers of the Families, one for the six beginning with Rūpavajrā, and one for the four Wrathful Ones (*krodha*)—thus making five. Or else, there is only one for the Leader (*nāyaka*) himself.

Among these positions, an additional "all-purpose" (sārvakarmika) flask should be prepared for the purpose of sprinkling the disciples and others; however, some do not accept this. In the absence of a second flask, one should draw the insignia of the Leader (Nāyaka) on the Victorious Flask (vijayaghaṭa), and the insignia of the All-Purpose [flask] on its left side—this is another position. That insignia belongs to Vighnāntaka.

According to the view that the four emblems of Vairocana and the others should also be drawn in the four directions, it is stated in some places that the emblem of the central leader is situated directly above the emblem of Vairocana, specifically above his face. There is also another view that [the emblems] of Locanā and the others should likewise be in the four intermediate directions.
Alternatively, the five Buddhas, the four goddesses, and the four wrathful deities may be arranged separately.
Each one of the two earrings bears six forms, such as the vajra and other symbols.

"Thus, fifteen"—this alternative position stated by someone, which differs from the positions already mentioned, is incoherent. Thus, in the Mañjuvajra maṇḍala, the arrangement of the number of vases is twenty, ten, six, two, one, and fifteen.

In the Piṇḍīkrama maṇḍala, however, according to the second fivefold system, the distinction is as follows: one for the Tathāgatas, one for the Mothers, one for Caturūpavajrī and the others, one for the eight Bodhisattvas, and one for the ten Wrathful Deities.
There is also one for the two sons of one’s own direction, and one for the six wrathful consorts;
including separately those within the womb, the Vighnas, the Aris, and the door-guarding Wrathful Deities, there are twenty.

Thus say some. Regarding the Vajrasattva maṇḍala described in the *Sampuṭa*, the distinction is as follows: there is one [vase] for those situated in the inner enclosure (*garbhapuṭa*), one for those in the second enclosure, one for the eight goddesses of the cardinal directions, one for the eight goddesses of the intermediate corners, and one for the gatekeepers. There are separate vases for the Mothers of the Tathāgata family and for the gatekeepers. In the second enclosure, there is one for the goddesses of the cardinal directions and one for the goddesses of the intermediate corners. In the third enclosure, there is one for those situated on the left in the cardinal directions and one for those situated on the right.

Some say there are twenty: one for those situated in the corners [of the innermost circle], one outside of them in the corners, and one *sārvakarmika* (all-purpose) [deity]. Alternatively, in the *saṃvara-maṇḍala*, there are five, being one for each of the five wheels (*cakras*). Or rather, there are five belonging only to those situated in the central enclosure (*garbhapuṭa*). Or again, there are nine: five for these [in the center] and four for the four wheels. Or else, there are nineteen: thirteen situated in the central enclosure and the *samayacakra*; one for those in the cardinal directions of the *cittacakra*; and one for those in the intermediate directions; likewise for the *vākcakra* and the *kāyacakra*.
In these systems, even when performing the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) for each respective deity, the *sārvakarmika* [mantra] of Khaṇḍarohā should also be established.
Following this principle, the number of ritual jars (*kalaśa*) in other mandalas should also be understood according to what is appropriate.

Therein, due to its preeminence and the abundance of ritual duties, one should place upon the *vijaya-kalaśa* a conch or a lotus vessel containing water mixed with the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) as obtained, along with fragrant water, and consisting of vajra-atom particles transformed into the nectar of gnosis by reciting seven times the three-syllable mantra: *oṃ vajrāmṛtodaka ṭhaḥ hūṃ*. This vessel should be consecrated with the *hūṃ*-mantra and adorned with a vajra tied with a garland of flowers. In the center, within the water—which is the form of the waters of the Mandākinī drawn forth by the mantra *oṃ tapte mahātapte svāhā*—one should instantly [visualize] the circle of deities together with their seats.

Having reflected thus, one should bring the mandala of gnosis (jñānamaṇḍala) before oneself by means of the rays from the seed-syllable in one’s own heart, and offer water for the feet (pādya), water for sipping (ācamana), and the respectful offering (argha). Then, having entered that pledge-mandala (samayacakra), one should contemplate it as melting through great passion (mahārāga) and becoming the nature of the thought of awakening (bodhicitta), merging into a single flavor with the previously held water. Furthermore, one should contemplate the pledge-deity within the symbol (cihna) as having become one with the gnosis-deity.

Then, having grasped [the water] with the left fist up to the vajra-encircled flower garland while reciting the *hūṃ* mantra, one should consecrate the water one hundred and eight times with the heart-mantra of the Lord of the Maṇḍala, or with *oṃ vajrodaka hūṃ*. Into that [water], one should cast three white flowers consecrated with the *kuṇḍali* mantra.

Furthermore, whichever deity a particular flask belongs to, that flask should be consecrated one hundred and eight times, twenty-one times, or seven times with that deity’s mantra; likewise, having grasped it up to the vajra-encircled flower garland, one should cast a flower into it in the same manner.

Thereafter, having worshipped the jars of Vijaya and the others with flowers and other offerings, and having sprinkled them with water for all-purpose rites using the very same leaf-stalk for the sake of protection, one should say, "Until the completion of the mandala activities here, you shall ward off obstacles. Then, having offered the bali and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), one should ring the bell while preceded by the praise beginning with "Akṣobhyavajra."

Having drawn a small amount of water from each of those jars, one should place it in a conch shell or similar vessel situated on the northern side of the eastern door of the maṇḍala house for the purpose of sprinkling oneself and the disciples. Alternatively, another [teacher] says that one should place the *sārvakarmika* jar itself there, provided with a bundle of *kuśa* grass, for that purpose. One should perform the consecration, worship, and other rites for the jars three times a day or once a day.

The mantras of the Wheel Lord (Cakreśa) and the others are to be known from the *sādhanas* and other such works.
