However, they are presented here in brief because they are widely practiced; some of them are stated therein, specifically for the mandala of Mañjuvajra: Oṃ āḥ maṃ hūṃ: [the mantra] of the Wheel Lord, who is non-different from Akṣobhya. Oṃ āḥ jinajik hūṃ: [the mantra] of Vairocana. Oṃ āḥ ratnadhṛk hūṃ: [the mantra] of Ratnasambhava. Oṃ āḥ ārolik hūṃ: [the mantra] of Amitābha. Oṃ āḥ prajñādhṛk hūṃ: [the mantra] of Amoghasiddhi.

Oṃ āḥ moharati hūṃ, [homage] to Locanā; oṃ āḥ dveṣarati hūṃ, [homage] to Māmakī; oṃ āḥ rāgarati hūṃ, [homage] to Pāṇḍarā; oṃ āḥ vajrarati hūṃ, [homage] to Tārā; oṃ āḥ rūpavajre jaḥ hūṃ, [homage] to Rūpavajrā; oṃ āḥ śabdavajre hūṃ hūṃ, [homage] to Śabdavajrā; oṃ āḥ gandhavajre vaṃ hūṃ, [homage] to Gandhavajrā; oṃ āḥ rasavajre hoḥ hūṃ, [homage] to Rasavajrā; oṃ āḥ sparśavajre khaṃ hūṃ, [homage] to Sparśavajrā.

Oṃ āḥ dharmadhātuvajre raṃ hūṃ, [homage] to Dharmadhātuvajrā. Oṃ āḥ Yamāntakṛt hūṃ, [homage] to Yamāri. Oṃ āḥ Prajñāntakṛt hūṃ, [homage] to Prajñāntaka. Oṃ āḥ Padmāntakṛt hūṃ, [homage] to Padmāntaka. Oṃ āḥ Vighnāntakṛt hūṃ, [homage] to Amṛtakuṇḍalī. When Akṣobhya, inseparable from Mañjuvajra, is the Lord of the Mandala, then [his mantra is]: Oṃ āḥ Vajradhṛk hūṃ. 10.9 (p.134)

In the Piṇḍīkrama Maṇḍala, however, the mantras for Akṣobhya and the others are exactly as previously stated. For Maitreya and the others, they are as follows: Oṃ Āḥ Maitreya Maiṃ Hūṃ; Oṃ Āḥ Kṣitigarbha Dhṛīṃ Hūṃ; Oṃ Āḥ Vajrapāṇe Oṃ Hūṃ; Oṃ Āḥ Khagarbha Oṃ Hūṃ; Oṃ Āḥ Lokeśvara Oṃ Hūṃ; Oṃ Āḥ Mañjughoṣa Hūṃ Hūṃ; Oṃ Āḥ Sarvanivaraṇaviṣkambhin Oṃ Hūṃ; Oṃ Āḥ Samantabhadra Saṃ Hūṃ; Oṃ Āḥ Acala Hūṃ Hūṃ; Oṃ Āḥ Ṭakkirāja Hūṃ Hūṃ.

Oṃ āḥ nīladaṇḍa hūṃ hūṃ / Oṃ āḥ mahābala hūṃ hūṃ / Oṃ āḥ uṣṇīṣa hūṃ hūṃ / Oṃ āḥ sumbha hūṃ hūṃ / When Vajrasattva, inseparable from Akṣobhya, is the Lord of the Wheel, then his mantra is: Oṃ āḥ hūṃ hūṃ.

In the maṇḍala of Vajrasattva as taught in the *Sampuṭa*, "Oṃ vajrāmṛta mahāsukha hūṃ svāhā" is the heart-mantra of Vajrasattva, the Lord of the Wheel. "Oṃ āḥ vajraghaṇṭe hoḥ haṃ svāhā" is the mantra of the vajra-bell, which is effective for all rites (*sārvakarmika*). Other mantras are likewise taught together in the tantra itself.

In the Saṃvara maṇḍala, the heart-mantra of the Lord of the Wheel (Cakreśa) is: *oṃ śrīvajra he he ru ru kaṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ ḍākinījālasaṃvaraṃ svāhā*. The mantra of Khaṇḍarohā, which is effective for all rites (*sārvakarmika*), is: *oṃ khaṇḍarohe hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ*. The mantras of the other deities of the maṇḍala have been written by us, together with their oral instructions (*sāmnāya*), in this *Saṃvarābhisamaya*.

In the Hevajra maṇḍala, the heart-mantra of the Lord of the Wheel is: *oṃ devapicuvajra hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*. The mantra of Ghasmarī is either *oṃ oṃ svāhā* or *oṃ āḥ vajraghasmari oṃ hūṃ svāhā*; this is effective for all rites (*sārvakarmika*). Other mantras are condensed in the *Sampuṭa*.

In the Vajradhātumaṇḍala described in the *Tattvasaṃgraha*, the heart-mantra of the Lord of the Mandala (Cakreśa) is: *oṃ sarvatathāgata mahāyogīśvara hūṃ*. For Vajrayakṣa, however, the mantra is: *oṃ vajrayakṣa hūṃ*; this is the all-purpose (sārvakarmika) mantra. Others are collected in the *Tattvasaṃgraha-tantra*. 10.11 (p.136)

Here, for the sake of employment in the rites of the mandala and so forth, one should first place either the Victorious Vase (*vijayakalaśa*) or the All-purpose Vase (*sārvakarmikakalaśa*) within the pericarp of an eight-petaled lotus drawn with white or other colored powders. On the eastern petal, one should place the five-colored thread (*pañcaraṅgikasūtra*) that has been consecrated according to the procedure to be described; on the southern [petal], the vajra; on the northern, the vajra-bell (*vajraghaṇṭā*); and on the western and the corner petals, the five containers of powder as appropriate.
Reciting the Kuṇḍalī mantra—either *oṃ a ā aṃ aḥ* or [the appropriate mantra]—one should sprinkle the water of that flask upon the dust-line; this is the procedure for the consecration of the flask.
11. The Procedure for the Consecration of the Deity (p. 137).

Then, having had the mandala ground smeared with fragrant substances and the like and strewn with heaps of flowers, one should construct there—according to the circumstances—a square mandala in the squares of the five lords and a circular one for the other deities, using the five nectars and fragrances. Facing west, one should cause the mandala of deities beginning with the Lord of the Circle to descend upon those mandalas, drawn by rays from the seed-syllable in one's own heart, seated appropriately upon moons or suns resting on lotuses; then, having worshipped them preceded by water for the feet and so forth, and having praised them, one should taste the nectar.

Having placed his right knee on the ground, having placed the syllable *HŪṂ* on the tongue—which is a single-pronged vajra born from *HŪṂ*—with his right hand holding an incense burner and sounding a vajra-bell with his left, [he says]:
"O Blessed One, Amuka-sadvajra, King of Vidyās, homage be to you!"
O Lord, whose nature is compassion, I desire to draw the maṇḍala.
Out of compassion for the disciples and for your own worship.
Therefore, O Blessed One, you ought to show favor to me, your devotee.
May the Buddhas, who bestow the purpose of the wheel of activity for the world, and the Bodhisattvas established in the fruit, as well as all other mantra-deities, attend to me.
The deities, the world-protectors, and the spirits who have been instructed in perfect awakening—
whatever beings there may be who delight in the teaching and possess the vajra-eye.
I, [Name], the Great Vajrin, shall draw the maṇḍala of [Name] for the purification of the world, according to my capacity and with proper ritual offerings.
Out of compassion for me and my disciples,
you all should together grant your presence within this mandala.
Thus, reciting three times while ensuring the meaning is understood, one should supplicate.

"Jagaccakrakriyārthadā" means those who grant benefit through their activities within the mandala for the sake of the world; these are sentient beings such as humans and so forth. "Vajracakṣuṣaḥ" means those with divine vision. This concludes the procedure for the consecration of the deities.
12. The Procedure for the Measuring Line (Sūtraṇavidhi).
12.1.1 Thereafter,
fearing a transgression of the samaya, one must by no means allow a non-disciple to enter.

Having spoken thus, one should seat the disciples—who are fit for the activities of a gate-teacher (*dvārācārya*) but have not yet received initiation—before the door in the east, having first performed the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsana*) according to the procedure for bestowing the two vows (*saṃvara*) that will be explained, or according to the procedure for preliminary consecration preceded by the bestowal of the master’s vow (*ācāryasaṃvara*). These should be four or three; if that is impossible, even a single person is accepted at the very least. It is stated in another tantra that a fifth person, distinct from these, who has been made a disciple in this manner, should be appointed as the Action-Vajra (*karmavajrin*);
however, in his absence, no other [person] may be used.

Having thus performed the mere ritual acceptance (*adhivāsana*) for the disciples, and having worshipped the deity-maṇḍala installed for the sake of that acceptance, one should mentally place [the deities] in the sky above the site of the maṇḍala for the purpose of the wisdom-thread (*jñānasūtra*) and so forth. Facing east, possessing the yoga of Vajradhara or the yoga of the Lord of the Maṇḍala, and having attained the signs (*nimitta*), [one prepares] five threads of five [each], spun by a virgin who has not been violated or purchased from a hero, placed in five vessels, and colored with fragrant pigments that are white, yellow, red, green, and black.

Having separately colored [the fingers] with powders of *siddhārtha* mixed with the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*), one should place them on the palm of the left hand, beginning from the tips of the fingers up to the base of the thumb.

Having visualized the wisdom threads (*jñānasūtra*), consisting of rays of light, produced from the syllables *brūṃ*, *āṃ*, *hrīḥ*, *khaṃ*, and *hūṃ*—or from *brūṃ*, *āṃ*, *jrīṃ*, *khaṃ*, and *hūṃ*—or from *oṃ*, *svā*, *āḥ*, *hā*, and *hūṃ*, or according to the specific tantra—arising within the hearts of the five Tathāgatas who have been generated and are gathered in their respective directions in the sky, one should request Vairocana with this: "Oṃ āḥ! O Śāśvata, grant me the vajra-thread for the purpose of laying out the great maṇḍala, hūṃ! One should likewise request Ratnasambhava and the others by substituting their respective names.

Having recited "Jaḥ! O you who have the nature of a yellow moon and sun produced from the syllable *jaḥ*, O blazing gaze, O goad! (*oṃ dīptadṛṣṭyaṅkuśi jaḥ*)," one should draw in those [deities] sent by Vairocana and the others with a blazing gaze—whose eyelashes move rapidly as they run forth—as if with a hook, and cause them to enter within their respective colors upon the threads held in the hands. For this very reason, they consist of the five wisdoms, such as the mirror-like wisdom and so forth.

Furthermore, because each of the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*) and the others is followed by four types of wisdom, they are divided into twenty-five. Moreover, because from each seed-syllable there is the radiation and reabsorption of the five Tathāgatas, each individual wisdom consists of a maṇḍala of twenty deities; thus, it is stated in some places that they are divided into one hundred.

Thereafter, either in the form of Vairocana or in the form of Amṛtakuṇḍalī and all other [deities] who accomplish all tasks, together with the disciple acting as the thread-holder, one should first wind each of the five sets of five threads. Thereafter, from those five [sets] thus wound, [one should make] a single thread. *Oṃ āḥ*, all phenomena follow one another; all phenomena have entered into one another; all phenomena have entered into one another completely. *Oṃ āḥ hūṃ*.

Reciting this, the preceptor, having inserted the four fingers—beginning with the index finger—of both his own left hand and that of the disciple into the middle of the coiled thread, and having led it out from the back and re-inserted it, while their hands remain in the vajra-fist gesture, he should fix it to the ground with the backs of the index fingers. Having adjusted the ends so as to remove any excess, the length should be double that of the mandala plus one-twentieth part; and the thickness should be the measure of a *yava* according to the preceptor’s standard, consisting of seven *yavas*.

According to the statement in the Abhidharma that "it is the joint of a finger," and because the description of the thickness as being one-twentieth of the door's eighth part refers specifically to a mandala of one cubit (hasta) consisting of twenty-four finger-breadths (aṅgula), it should be understood that this measurement is indicated by those same proportions even for mandalas of two cubits and so forth. Ānandagarbha and others maintain that for a mandala of six cubits, the smallest possible measure of the cord (sūtra) should be used, while in other cases it should be adjusted accordingly.

Immediately after the turning, one should place [the substance]—saturated with scented water, the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*), and the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), and containing the three syllables within—into a clean vessel made of gold or similar material that has been smeared with fragrance. Having worshipped it with perfumes, flowers, and incense, and having steadied it with the hand, one should protect it by reciting the *kuṇḍalī* mantra. Then, having beheld the sun and moon in the right and left eyes with the syllables *ma* and *ṭa*, one should perform the *vajra-dṛṣṭi* as before: *ma ṭ*.

Having thus stabilized [the site], one should sprinkle it with water consecrated by the *sarvakṛt* mantra, nectar, mustard seeds, and fragrant water, while touching it with the right hand holding a vajra. Reciting "Oṃ vajrasamaya sūtraṃ mātikrama hūṃ," and having recited this, one should perform the ritual consecration (*adhivāsana*) by reciting the three-syllable mantra one hundred and eight times.

Furthermore, having sprinkled the mandala ground with water from all the vases while reciting the mantra *oṃ sarvapāpaśodhani hūṃ phaṭ*, having smeared it with pure perfume, and having scattered flowers outside, one should rely upon the mandala to be drawn situated in the expanse of the sky, preceded by the offering of *argha*.

Having honored and bowed down [to the preceptor], being himself possessed of that yoga, he should visualize the *uttarasādhaka* as Vairocana or in the form of the all-creating Kuṇḍalī and so forth. Then, having meditated on the moon and sun—shining yellow and produced from the syllable *jaḥ*—in his own left and right eyes, and holding that thread with the left vajra-fist at his navel while standing in the vajra-step (*vajrapada*), he should dispatch that *uttarasādhaka*, who likewise holds the thread, by means of the three syllables *jaḥ* with the words "jaḥ jaḥ jaḥ. Regarding the *uttarasādhaka*:

Drawing [the thread] with three *jjaḥ* syllables—*jjaḥ*, *jjaḥ*, *jjaḥ*—and standing facing [the center] in that same manner, one situated in the west facing east, and one situated in the south facing north, should cast two Brahma-threads into the sky at the level of the navel. Taking the thread with the thumb and fingers of the right hand holding a vajra, one should produce the sound of snapping the fingers. During all the castings of the threads, one should recite: *oṃ vajrasamayasūtraṃ mātikrama hūṃ hūṃ oṃ svā āḥ hā*.

And by that sound of the *sūtra*, one should invoke the Tathāgatas who pervade all space; and they, having arrived, enter into the *sūtras*. For this sound, the conventional meaning is: "The time has come for you to act for the sake of sentient beings; therefore, please come here. Everywhere, the master and the assistant practitioner should proceed in a clockwise direction and resolve upon the equality of all directions.

Two Brahma-threads should be suspended equally upon the ground from the two ends of the Kha-thread, held by hands with the threads attached. However, first, on the hand-measured mandala, one should mark two points at the centers of the mandala-lines where the tips of the shadow of a *śaṅku*—one *vitasti* in length placed at the navel—enter and exit as it moves inward and outward. Holding a thread over those two points, which constitute the western and eastern limits, two mandalas are formed, resulting in a "fish" (*matsya*) figure.

Having placed a thread over the two dots made at the tips of the tail and the mouth on the south and north [sides], one should draw two circles. However, in a covered location, one should draw four circles above the four dots in the cardinal directions.

Then, having held a thread from the fish-heads and tails in the cardinal directions out to the edge of the circle of rays, [the master], having assumed the half-lotus posture with the left leg and placed the right foot on the ground, should—while the disciple sits in the opposite posture and takes the thread with the left vajra-fist and withdraws to the rear as appropriate—cast it down with the visualization of the thread in space. The same applies for the casting of the other threads.
If there are no auspicious signs, there will be no success; if the thread is broken, the preceptor’s life-force is diminished.
From deficiency or excess come diseases; from confusion regarding the directions comes the delusion of the disciple.
Having understood this and having made the necessary preparations,
if anyone should be unfit for the casting of the thread,
then one should oneself cast it by tying it to a peg, even without an assistant.

12.1.6 (p.150) One situated in the southeast corner [draws] the thread to the northwest corner, and one situated in the southwest corner [draws] the thread to the northeast corner. Each of these two [threads] measures seventeen doors. Then, one should erase the five mandalas. For the purpose of laying down the Brahma-thread itself, it is stated that the thread should be twice the length of the mandala.

Here, the "mandala" refers to the primary mandala together with its adjuncts, delimited by the altar of the universal vajra (*viśvavajra-vedikā*); from the outside of the primary thread, it extends as far as the eighth measure (*mātrā*), totaling forty-eight measures.

Outside of that, in successive order, by virtue of being twelve, two, two, two, four *mātrikās* respectively, there are twenty-four units—consisting of one archway (*toraṇa*), two wheels of Dharma (*dharmacakra*), two spikes (*śūka*), two lotus petals (*abjadala*), two vajra-garlands (*vajrāvalī*), and four rays (*raśmi*)—on one side, and likewise on the second side; thus it consists of forty-eight *mātrikās*. Therefore, the measuring line (*sūtra*) becomes ninety-six *mātrikās*.
And it is said:
"Having understood the division of the directions to be equal, [the line] should be twice as long as the mandala."
One should lay down the Brahma-sūtra according to the measurement of the length from east to west.
Thus it is said: another [line], double the length, is to be taken for the mandala ground;
here, from the mandala, one casts a thread that follows the measurement, long in the direction of Indra and Varuṇa.

Thus, if the needle and the ray were one or three *mātrās* long, or two or two *mātrās* long, the thread would be ninety-two *mātrās* long; in that case, the thread would be four *mātrās* longer than the circle at the end of the ray. To say that this [thread] is for the purpose of holding [the ray] is therefore inconsistent.
[This applies] starting from one cubit up to a thousand cubits.

According to this scriptural statement (*pravacana*), one *mātrā* would be thirty-one and a quarter cubits (*hastas*)—being a fourth part of a door that is an eighth part of a mandala with a thousand cubits at its base. By four of these, the cord (*sūtra*) becomes one hundred and twenty-five cubits longer. However, what is the use of that? Even if the petals and the vajra-garland were each one *mātrā*, there would still be an inconsistency. Therefore, learned scholars state that any other such position—where the archway (*toraṇa*) is three times the size of the door from above—is contrary to the scriptures (*āgama*).

In this case, the mandala is measured in cubits (*hasta*) and so forth, demarcated in the cardinal directions by four root-lines of that same measurement. Therefore, the preceptor (ācārya), standing in the southeast corner and facing north, should first lay down the eastern root-line according to the measurement of the mandala. Standing in the northwest corner and facing south, he lays down the western line; remaining in that same spot and facing east, he lays down the northern line. Again, standing in the southeast corner and facing west, he lays down the southern line. Thus it is said in the *Ḍākinīvajrapañjara*:
"First with the Brahma-line, second with the corner-lines, and with the third [line], one should lay down the four lines on the four sides."

Thus: one-eighth of that single *sūtra* is a door; one-fourth of a door is a single *mātrā*. Then, on both the right and left sides of the Brahma-line, together with the ground of the two root-lines of two *mātrās* each, that [space] becomes four *mātrās*. One should then divide the root-lines on both sides of the Brahma-line reaching that [area]; from there, the door [is formed] by means of the syllable *Hrīḥ*, Wrath, and the Gaze.

Thus, according to the teaching, with the resolve, "I shall destroy the obscuration that acts as a barrier to the gateway of liberation," one should generate the moon and sun in the left and right eyes by means of the syllable *hīḥ*. Then, gazing all around with a wrathful look while uttering the sound *hīḥ hīḥ*, one should destroy [the obscuration].
12.2.1 (p.154) % Drawing the Kūṭāgāra.

Then, outside the root-line, having omitted one, two, one, two, one, and one *mātrā* intervals respectively, six lines are drawn diagonally from the corner-lines. Among these, the first two belong to the ground of the colored powder (*rajoveḍī*) and the altar-ground (*bhuvaḥ*), joined by two lines of one *mātrā* each with their ends meeting one another; they remain at an interval of three *mātrās*, having bypassed the Brahma-line. The next three, however, belong to the ground of the jewel-hangings (*ratnahāra*) and the *bakulī*; they are at an interval of eight *mātrās*. The fourth, meanwhile, extends as far as the other corner-line.

From there, four lines emerge from the altar-lines; among them, one [line] runs transversely across the ground of the fringe and touches the ends of the three [other] lines. Beside that, at intervals of one *mātrikā* each, there are four dust-grounds (*rajobhūmi*) between the arch-pillars (*toraṇastambha*). Of these four, the first three are five *mātrikās* in length, and the fourth is four *mātrikās*. Here, the ground in the interval between the mandala and the arch is called the *andhapaṭṭikā*, the *andhakārapaṭṭī*, and the *pollī*.

Then, at a distance of two *mātrās* from the side of the *brahmasūtra*, a line extending two *mātrās* for the *niryūha* projects straight out from the root-line; it goes transversely for two *mātrās* to the cheek and then projects upward for two *mātrās* to the wing-line, forming one line with two bends. From its tip, a line extends transversely to the tip of the corresponding bend on the other side of the *brahmasūtra*, reaching a length of eight *mātrās*; this is the *śilī-sūcaka-sūtra*. Likewise, from the tip of that side-line to the tip of the other side-line, there is one line measuring ten *mātrās*.

The cord for the five-colored powders is [placed] upon the *śilpa* (artistic design) of the core which is provided with the *skandha*, *bhūmi*, and *śilī*. Outside of that, however, there is a single-measure (*ekamātrā*) band between the mandala and the archway (*toraṇa*).
By this, the following is also explained.
The gate is considered to be one-eighth of the wheel's diameter and is devoid of a railing;
the turrets and the deity-panels are equal in measure to the gate.

The altar (vedī) extends halfway across the door on all sides; likewise are the cheeks (kapola), the side-wings (pakṣaka), and the bands for the pearl-necklaces (hāra), half-necklaces (ardhahāra), the moon and sun, the cloth-strip (paṭṭa), the garland (sraj), and the ribbon-band (dāmapaṭṭikā).
The ground for the dust-marks is half of that, outside the ground for the root-line.

Thus [it is said]. The *devatāpaṭṭī* (deity-band) is inside the *mūlasūtra* (root-line). The *vedī* (altar), however, is called the *dhāraṇīpaṭṭī* (dhāraṇī-band) and the *nartanapaṭṭī* (dancing-band). Here, the claim that the side (*pakṣa*) extends horizontally and the cheek (*kapola*) extends upward is not based on tradition (*anāgamam*). And it has been stated: "The *niryūha* (turret) is equal to the door in height; the cheek extends horizontally for half the width of the door."
Thus:
above [the door], there is an intermediate panel five *mātrikās* in length, consisting of three doors.
Nāgabuddhipāda, however, does not accept the *antarālapaṭṭī* and the *skandhapaṭṭī*, intending that the *śilī* is simply the line situated between the two *pakṣasūtra*s. For he says:
"The door is one-eighth of the circumference of the wheel; likewise the *devatāpaṭṭī*kā, the *niryūha*, the *kapola*, and the *pakṣaka* are equal in measure to the door."
The altar (vedikā) should be half of that [the central area], and the colored floor (raṅgabhū) should be half of the altar.
The necklace (hāra) should be equal in measure to the altar, and the jeweled ground (ratnabhūmi) should be half of that.
Likewise, there is the *bakulī*, the *kramaśīrṣa*, and the decoration of the outer pillars and so forth.
Thus they have stated what is taught in other tantras.

However, regarding the description of a single line here in this system—which, for the sake of the reinforcement (*āsāra*) and the sake of the *kramaśīrṣa*, omits one unit of measure outside the lines contained within the two side-lines—that is not a syllable of the expressive mantra. Even if one were to conceive it oneself, it should be understood that this contradicts the statement by the Great Charioteers (the masters) made repeatedly: "The root mandala, together with its enclosure, is surrounded by a space of eight units of measure outside the root lines."

If it is argued that a *kramaśīrṣapaṭṭī* (ridge-course molding) is made above the *ratna* and *bakūlī* moldings for the sake of ornamentation, let it be so; what is our insistence on this point? These two [moldings] have been described by the Blessed One in other tantras as having measurements both equal and unequal to those of the *niryūha*, *kapola*, and *pakṣa*. However, in this case, the gabled chamber (*kūṭāgāra*) does not appear as beautiful with the eighth-part-measured *kramaśīrṣas* as it does without them—[otherwise] it would be like a head severed at the neck by the *bakūlīs*. Look at the great monasteries (*mahāvihāra*) and such places [for examples]. 12.2.4 (p. 159)

In this case, from the corner thread (*añcalasūtra*) up to the *kramaśīrṣa* [is drawn] on the written maṇḍala, whereas on the visualized (*bhāvya*) maṇḍala it extends up to the top of the wings. This is because of the statement in the *Vajramālā-tantra*: "The *kramaśīrṣa* is the winged one. Furthermore, although two pillars are not drawn on the surface of the stone slab, they are to be understood as present in the visualized maṇḍala. [It is] square, with four gates, and adorned with eight pillars.

This is according to the scripture (*āgama*). Furthermore, eight pillars for the inner mandala are not mentioned by this [text], for they do not exist in the Saṃvara and other mandalas. This characteristic—that it is adorned with eight pillars—is pervasive to all mandalas. As for the side pillars, however, they belong to the archways (*toraṇa*) themselves. For this very reason, those who imagine that the *niryūha* and so forth rise up into the sky above the base of the doors are simply ignorant of the meaning of the teaching (*pravacana*).

On the wall of dust, however, the jeweled necklaces (*ratnahāra*), half-necklaces (*ardhahāra*), and *bakūlī* garlands rise upward in succession, possessing great beauty; the *bakūlīs* should be understood as hanging down from their prepared edges. It is stated in some places that jewels should be painted on the seventh *bakūlī* measure.

However, he who does not desire the *kharvasūtra* in this manner should cast six lines outside the root line up to the diagonal corner line, omitting intervals of one, two, one, two, one, and one *mātrā* respectively. Seven lines emerge from the root line; on the right side of the Brahmā-line, one should omit two *mātrās* for the sixth line, and the others by one *mātrā* each. The same applies to the left side. One should erase those other than the *kharvita* lines mentioned in the previous sequence.
12.2.5 (p.161) [Drawing the *toraṇa*]

Above the pillar is a toraṇa measuring twelve *mātrikas*. There, extending outward from the top of the pillar, there are eleven lines. Regarding this, it is said: "The toraṇa is three times the width of the door, and it consists of eleven bands (*paṭṭikā*).

Accordingly, the intermediate bands are, in order, the bands of gold, *bakulī*, jewels, *khura*, darkness, *varaṇḍa*, darkness, *bakulī*, jewels, and *khura-śīrṣa*. Among these, each of the two "darkness" bands is one and a half *mātrikas* in height; the nine other bands are each one *mātrikā*. Some maintain that there is no gold band here, as it is merely a supporting band (*asāra-paṭṭī*).

Alternatively, there are bands for the *bakulīratnakhura*, the *svarṇamakara*, the *kāñcanakhura*, the *ratnakhura*, the *svarṇakramaśīrṣa*, and so forth. Of these, the first and second are one and a half *mātrās* each; the third is one *mātrā*; the fourth is half a *mātrā*; the fifth is one and a half *mātrās*; the sixth is half a *mātrā*; the seventh is one *mātrā*; the eighth is one and a half *mātrās*; the ninth is one *mātrā*; the tenth is half a *mātrā*; and the eleventh is one and a half *mātrās*. Now, the horizontal measurement of these aforementioned eleven bands is described.

There, to the right and left of Brahmā, at a distance of five and a half *mātrās*, is the first *paṭṭī* (fillet), measuring two and a half *mātrās*. Above that, the first *sūtra* (line) is three and a half *mātrās*; the second and third are three *mātrās* apart and measure three *mātrās* each; the fourth is four *mātrās* apart and measures five *mātrās*; the fifth is three and a half *mātrās* apart and measures four and a half *mātrās*; the sixth is three *mātrās* apart and measures five *mātrās*;
the four beginning with the seventh are seven *mātrās* each; and the eleventh measures five *mātrās*.

Here, the fifth band is three and a half *mātrās* wide across; the seventh on the upper part is three *mātrās*, while below and above it is six *mātrās*. For each of these bands, there is a single vertical line at the outer edge as appropriate, and at the inner edge, one rises after leaving half a *mātrā* from the first line. This appears as a single curved line connected to the other lines; however, it should be drawn according to what is aesthetically pleasing. Inside this, for the purpose of drawing jewels and so forth, one should leave half a *mātrā* and likewise draw a single curved line.

In the *āsārapaṭṭī* type, however, that [arch] consists of sixteen measures (*mātrā*). For those [arches], the king, the fault, the sun, the king, and the direction are three times [the measure]; the directions are the measures for the horizontal bands (*paṭṭī*) of the archway (*toraṇa*) in sequence.

Thus it is held; however, let it be examined how it is appropriate to say that "the Bakulī-paṭṭī is eighteen mātrās long" and so forth, given the absence of the Bakulī and other elements within those [measures] consisting of only the intermediate space.

The clusters of leaves and so forth issuing from the mouths of the upper makaras should be as beautiful as possible. Above the archway, at the Brahma-position, is the twelve-spoked Wheel of Dharma, measuring two mātrās.
The wheel is provided with eight spokes and has a rim consisting of five parts.
Thus it is said in some places. Her seat consists of a lotus and a moon on the eleventh beam of the archway.

On the left and right sides of the seat, upon the heads of deer situated in their respective order and facing the wheel, a male and female deer are to be drawn; they should be positioned half a mātrā away from the wheel, with their necks and faces raised one mātrā high, and their eyes fixed upon the tip of the wheel. For in the *Vimalaprabhā*, it is stated:
"On the right and left of the wheel are the male and female deer."
Thus it was said. Someone says: "There are no 'stairheads' (kramaśīrṣas); on that frieze there are only the deer and the doe. Regarding that opinion, the venerable Nāgabuddhipāda wrote:
"The architrave (toraṇa) is three times the width of the door; it stands above the pot-shaped pillar (kumbhastambha)."
It is joined with two *kramaśīrṣas* at the corners and resounds with the ringing of bells.

This contradicts the traditional scripture (*āgama*). For here, in this [scripture], two pairs of *kramaśīrṣa* are stated for the two wings, which have the tails of a male and female deer situated at the sides of the seat; therefore, in this system, the male and female deer do not reside in the *kramaśīrṣas*.
(Drawing the outer circles)

Outside the wheel, at two *mātrās*, the tips of the prongs of the universal vajra (*viśvavajra*) are visible even within the intervals between the spokes of the wheel. According to the view that the prongs consist of fourteen *mātrās*, the spokes—which occupy twelve parts of the universal vajra hub that serves as the basis for the mandala including its peripheral ornaments, and which extend in each direction as far as the center of the lotus—would not be able to occupy four door-portions. This view has already been examined previously [at 12.2.7, p. 167].

At the center of the mandala, one should visualize a ritual stake (*kīlaka*) made of *khadira* wood, having the form of a single-pointed vajra at its base and a five-pointed vajra at its top, born from the syllable *hūṃ*. Having recited the piercing mantra (*kīlanamantra*) one hundred and eight times, one should strike it with a vajra-hammer using the striking mantra. Then, with a cord twice as long as that [stake]—measuring ninety-six units—one should draw a circular line for the lotus filaments starting from the tip of the spike, beginning from the northeast and proceeding clockwise.

Outside of that, there is a circular thread for the circle of the row of lotus petals consisting of two measures (*dvimātra*), which indicates the portion of the *dharmodayā* attached to the tips of the petals; even in certain specific maṇḍalas such as the *Saṃvara*, where the *dharmodayā* is not visualized, some say that since it is contained within the *dharmadhātu*, that thread indicates the *dharmadhātu*. Others say it takes the form of the *cakravāḍa* (the mountain range surrounding the world).

Outside of that, a circular line consisting of two *mātrās* represents the form of the dense and solid Great Cakravāḍa mountain range. On the vajra-band, one should draw vajras with three or five prongs, or double-vajras (*viśvavajras*), according to the tradition. Outside of that, a circular line of four *mātrās* represents the ground of light-rays; this is for the purpose of ensuring the rays are of equal measure. Ānandagarbha states that one should draw a circular Cakravāḍa outside the halo of light (*prabhāmaṇḍala*). For this very reason, no colored powder (*guṇarajas*) is cast there.

On the upper edge of the *añcalapaṭṭī*, the spokes of the universal vajra (*viśvavajra*)—emerging from the mouths of sea-monsters (*makara*), extending slightly obliquely, and protruding outward—are three *mātrā*s in width and sixteen *mātrā*s in length at their center, positioned on the sides of the archways (*toraṇa*). However, in the case of a universal vajra with five spokes, other spokes are placed beside the [central] spokes.

The position that the archway pillars (*toraṇastambha*) emerge from the wall-lines at a distance of seven *mātrikās* is not tenable. Since the archway pillars are situated on square pedestals (*vedī*) each at a slight distance from the gabled chamber (*kūṭāgāra*), they appear as if attached to the pedestals because they stand on level ground; therefore, it is appropriate to draw these [pillars] outside the pedestals. Likewise, let it be understood that the claim that the upper intermediate band (*ūrdhvāntarālapaṭṭī*) consists of two door-widths minus one-quarter is erroneous. Thus, this first position has been stated. 12.3.1 (p.170) % Supplementary Remarks.

From the root mandala itself, which is delimited by the four root-sūtras, one should take a sūtra twice as long; with that, one should cast the Brahma-sūtra, measuring sixty-four mātrās. Thus it has been said:
"One should mark each side of the Brahma-sūtra with eight great portions (mahābhāga);
and each of these very great portions [should be marked] with four small portions (kṛśa)."
"On each side of Brahmā there are thirty-two *kṛśas*;
the door-measure is the *mahābhāga*, the fourth is the *kṛśa*, and the eighth is Śiva.
Thus it is stated elsewhere as well.
When a pure square has been made, exceeding twice the size of the mandala;
Then, having prepared a white thread, the practitioner himself, together with his superior, [should proceed].
One should moisten it with rice flour mixed with white sandalwood;
one should then apply a coating twice the size of the wheel.
Two pure Brahma-threads [should be used], and half of that [length] for the root-thread.
From the tip of the Brahma-line, there are the circles, threads, and [lines] of the lotus filaments, lotus petals, and vajra-rays. As it has been said:
The distance between the gates is sixteen [yojanas], as is the interval between the Cakravāḍa mountains.
Thus it is said. In that context, the *cakravāḍa* (the circular mountain range) is intended to begin from the line of filaments (*keśara*).

How so? For the *dharmodaya*, which has the nature of the filaments and petals, is not bound by a circle of vajras. Indeed, the *cakravāḍa* is called the "vajra enclosure" (*vajravalaya*) because it takes the form of a vajra-fence. And so it was stated by the venerable Nāgabuddhipāda:
"The archway has a vajra pinnacle, and outside of that is the *cakravāḍa*."
It is that which begins with the vajra-garland and the divine rays.
Thus it is said. For here it is clearly stated that the Cakravāḍa is indeed the Vajramālā, consisting of the *suraśmi* and so forth.
Alternatively, due to their similarity as circular enclosures (*valaya*), the *keśara* and other parts are also metaphorically designated as "Cakravāḍa," just like the [actual] Cakravāḍa.
And it is understood that such metaphorical usage (*upacāra*) is indeed accepted by them, as indicated by the statement "outside of that. If this is so, then it has been well said.

12.3.3 (p.172) On account of this very statement, some claim that the filaments and so forth do not exist; however, this is not tenable, because the universal vajra is situated upon a lotus. If it is argued that it is stated that the [vajra] exists in some cases even without the lotus and the *dharmodayā*, then in this context, it is appropriate to employ the metaphorical designation that it consists precisely of the lotus-petal. This is also the case in the *Piṇḍīkrama*:
"Having meditated on the void, which is of the nature of stable power..."
By this application of the ritual method, the stage of gnosis is empowered.
Situated in the middle of the space element, one should visualize the mandala of wind.
And so forth, up until the vajra-ground portion of the mandala where the four mandalas are withdrawn;
there, one should visualize a gabled palace produced from the syllable *bhrūṃ*.

Thus, in this context, the "ground of gnosis" (*jñānabhūmi*) is the element of space (*ākāśadhātu*), which is the source of phenomena (*dharmodayā*). Its center is the lotus; situated upon that, one produces the ground consisting of the four mandalas of wind, fire, water, and earth combined, in the form of a double vajra (*viśvavajra*). Above that, on a moon mandala, by means of the syllable *bhrūṃ*, the peaked pavilion (*kūṭāgāra*) is formed—this is the meaning. Therefore, to claim that there is a double vajra here without a lotus is a great error. 12.3.4 (p.174)

The Viśvavajra-nābhi [mandala], however, measures twelve door-widths; its spokes are each as long as two doors. Therein, the interior of the root-line measures eight doors, while the exterior measures two doors. In that space, there is no intervening fillet (paṭṭī) at all. The archway (toraṇa), extending to the end of its pillars, is three times the width of the door across.

Above that pillar is a single-door archway (*toraṇa*) with eleven horizontal bands (*paṭṭikā*) from top to bottom. Therein, in due order, are the finials (*śikhā*) and bands, which measure respectively one-eighth, one-eighth, one-twelfth, one-fourth, one-eighth, one-fourth, one-twelfth, one-eighth, one-twelfth, and one-fourth of the door-width. And it is said:
"The *bakūlī*, the jewel, the stationary, the golden, the sea-monster, then the golden, the stationary, [the golden], the sea-monster, and the golden."
Then there are Ratnā, Saṃsthānā, Svarṇā, and Kramaśīrṣakā.
The twelve parts of the door shall be the locations for the various forms of gold.

"The twenty-four parts of the door are the remaining [elements]; the eighth parts of the doors are the *śikhās* and *paṭṭīs*. Thus it is said. Now, their transverse measurement is described: on the right and left of the *brahman* line, at an interval of four and a half *mātrās*, the first *paṭṭī* is two and a half *mātrās*. Above that, the first cord is three and a half *mātrās*. At an interval of five *mātrās*, the second and third are three *mātrās* each. At an interval of four *mātrās*, the fourth is three *mātrās*. At an interval of three and a half *mātrās*, the fifth is three and a half *mātrās*. At an interval of three *mātrās*, the sixth is five *mātrās*.

The three lines beginning with the seventh consist of eight *mātrās* each; the tenth consists of seven *mātrās*; and the eleventh consists of six *mātrās*. For each of the bands (*paṭṭī*), there is one thread on the outside, inside, and above, and as appropriate, also on the inner side. However, the first thread rises after leaving half a *mātrā*. This thread, being connected to the other threads, appears as a single curved line. It should be made as it looks beautiful. Inside this, for the purpose of drawing jewels and so forth, one should leave half a *mātrā* and likewise draw a single curved thread. As for those which...
There, the jeweled plinth was four *mahābhāga* units wide;
it was likewise adorned with the marks of a horse’s hoof-prints.
Sārdhatraya, Mahābhāgā, Bakūlī, and likewise Kāñcanā; with these three Mahābhāgās, Makarā and Kramaśīrṣakā [are formed].

Thus they say. Now, let it be examined how, according to that view, it is appropriate to state that "the *bakūlī* [tuning] belonging to the *ṣoḍaśamātrikā* [scale] lacks *bakūlī* [notes] in the intermediate measures," and so forth, given the absence of *bakūlī* notes in those very intermediate measures.

Above the archway, within a Brahma-measure of one door-width, is a wheel of two measures; its seat is on the cornice of the successive steps, and on its two sides are a deer and a doe as before. On the next step beyond its tail, there is a white (or sometimes red) parasol with a handle of two and a half measures made of jewels topped by a jewel-vajra, and a circular panel of two measures adorned with *kamaruka* flowers, from which two strips of bark hang down. Above that, according to the measure of Śiva, is the staff and likewise the panel.

Thus says another. Some say the parasol is six *mātrās* [in height]. Above the top of the final tier (*kramaśīrṣa*), there are banners and flags (*dhvajapatākā*) one *mātrā* high; the *viśvavajra* spokes are two *mātrās* outside the circle, appearing in the intervals between the spokes of the wheel.
Beyond that, there are two rows of bands (*paṭṭikā*) measuring either one or two *mātrās*. The garland of light rays (*raśmimālā*) is two *mātrās* [in width].
And so it is said in the Vajraḍāka Tantra:
"Outside [the city], the halo of light is twice the measure of the ground of colored powder;
and outside that Cakravāḍa mountain range are the trees and the eight cremation grounds."

Thus, these cremation grounds belong only to the deities who dwell in the cremation grounds, and not to others. For them as well, they should not be drawn upon a dust-mandala when there is no assembly of worthy practitioners. Here, a radiating band (*kiraṇapaṭṭikā*) measuring four units is prescribed; however, some [place it] within the Saṃvara mandala.
One should also install the forms of Vajra, Padma, and Ari as the threefold enclosure wall.

By this [statement], he indicates that outside the vajra-fence there are lotus and wheel fences. For the purpose of marking the circle, however, the cord should be made one span or more longer; or else, the marking of the circle may be done with a single-fold cord. But by the statement regarding the length being twice that of the maṇḍala, the Blessed One has indicated that the maṇḍala to be drawn—extending as far as the edge of the universal vajra and its supporting lotus—is exactly the same both inside and outside the root maṇḍala; this is the second position.

Nāgabuddhipāda, however, has described only the first position; for he stated that the measurement of the *niryūha* and the *kapola* is equal, and that the *toraṇa*, situated above the *kumbha* and the pillar, is three times the size of the door.

And so it is said. For if that were the case, the archway (toraṇa) would not be three times the width of the door, but rather four times its width. Therefore, their intended meaning is that the threefold dimension is measured from the top [of the door].
The altar (vedī), the cheek (kapola), and the side-panel (pakṣaka) are all half the size of the door on every side.

Thus, based on the scriptural tradition (*āgama*), the Blessed One has also stated that the temple wall (*niryūha*) extends halfway up the cheek (*kapola*). We have thus described two positions: that the side-arches (*toraṇapakṣa*) extend horizontally three times the width of the door, and that there are two such side-arches. Regarding the second position, it is stated that the outer mandala is twice the size of the inner sanctum (*garbhamaṇḍala*), measured from inside the circular line of the lotus filaments (*padmakeśaravṛttasūtra*). However, as for the first position, it is rejected because the measurement of fourteen finger-breadths (*mātrikā*) beyond the arch-pillars and within the circular line of the lotus filaments does not fit either of these two positions.

12.4.1 (p.181) % Ornamentation: Here, at the junctions of the gates and the *niryūhas*, upon the *mātrikās*, there is a gem—red, yellow, dark green, or black—resting on a crescent moon; it is marked above either by a half-vajra or a complete vajra. Likewise, outside the colored ground, at the corners and the junctions of the gates and *niryūhas*.
It is illuminated on all sides by vajras, sprouts, jewels, and moons.
Thus it has been said. Furthermore, elsewhere, in the outer and inner corners of the altar, the skillful should draw them in the proper sequence:
on the moon and sun seats, there should be a single jewel marked with a vajra.
Thus, the pillars of the archways (toraṇa) stand upon jars placed on a square altar. And so it is said:
"The archway is three times the size of the door; from the mouths of the sea-monsters (makara), [the archway] extends."

It is stated: "The arch-pillars (*toraṇastambha*) emerge from the base of the altar-pitchers (*vedīkumbha*). At their base and at their summit there is a jeweled band (*maṇibandha*). In the middle, upon an elephant, stands a lion with its trunk raised. From the arch-structure (*toraṇasāra*), or in the absence of that [structure], from the *bakulī*-band, there hang clusters of jewel-leaves; and as is aesthetically pleasing, there are fringes of cloth in colors such as red or yellow, or variegated, as well as jeweled-handled fly-whisks (*cāmara*). However, some say: on the cloth-fringe above the elephant, there is a lion with a jeweled necklace hanging from its mouth, while in the middle of the pillar there is simply a mirror.
In the corner of the jeweled frieze, there are triangular, square, oblong, and circular *tilakas* in sequence, and jewel-enclosures (*ratnabandhas*) on each side of every pillar.

On the necklace-frieze (*hārapaṭṭikā*), there are four golden girdles; outside, pearl necklaces threaded with red thread are held in the mouths of sea-monsters (*makaras*). On both sides, above and below, are half-necklaces (*ardhahāras*) with rubies set in gold in their centers, and on the sides of the full necklaces, streams of jewel-garlands hang slightly lower; these have beautiful tips of large gems set in gold, and jeweled-handled fly-whisks (*cāmaras*) with bells at their ends hang down in some places.

However, some say that on both sides of the *ardhahāra* there hang garlands of flowers (*sumanaḥsraj*) and *ardhahāras*, and at their sides are *ardhahāras* of variegated cloth. Others say that garlands of flowers (*sumanaḥsraj*) and silken cloths (*aṃśukahāra*) are at the corners. Within the interior of the *hāra*, there is sometimes a lotus, a crescent moon, a half-vajra, a sprout, or a sun-maṇḍala; sometimes a jewel; and sometimes a vajra resting upon a lotus. 12.4.3 (p.184)

On the gradually tapering pinnacles situated upon lotus-petal bases, there are eight banners and flags in the cardinal directions, set within golden or jewel-encrusted jars; their tops are fixed with jeweled poles featuring crescent moons and jewel-vajras, and they are bound with bells and fine threads, their triple-jointed tips marked by lions, royal swans, serpents, leopards, and makaras. These flags, as well as the pennants, are resonant with hundreds of tinkling bells, adorned with yak-tail whisks, and move in a graceful triple-bend as they sway in the wind; however, the pennants are otherwise devoid of the lion and other such emblems.

In the four corners, upon the tops of the arches, are four parasols; on the gateways are variegated canopies, as well as necklaces and half-necklaces. Along the edges of the excellent railings are banners and flags, arranged for beauty. On the sides of the gateways, not too far away, are lions, tigers, swans, peacocks, kinnaras, and kinnarīs; and from the mouths of auspicious jars emerge wish-fulfilling trees (*kalpavṛkṣa*) accompanied by the seven jewels, such as elephants, with their forms emerging from clouds and holding garlands of flowers—such perfected beings (*siddhas*) appearing here and there.
Thus, this sequence for laying out the lines and drawing outside the root mandala is common to all mandalas.
12.5.1. *Mañjuvajramaṇḍala* (p. 186):

However, the specific details within [the interior] are now stated. Inside the root line, having set aside a space equal to the door-width consisting of the deity-pediment, one horizontal line is drawn extending as far as the two diagonal corner-lines. Within that, having set aside the measurement of a door for the purpose of placing Rūpavajrā and the others, one first draws a circular line marking the boundary of the inner mandala, holding the thread at the Brahma-line located at the navel or at the Īśāna-line.

Within that [space], between the lines of the vajra-enclosure, one should likewise draw a second circular line. From there, extending as far as the circular line in the western direction, two lines should be drawn on the right side of the Brahma-line: the first at an interval of two *mātrās*, and the second at an interval of the central pillar’s emblematic mark. The same applies to the left. Here, in the eastern direction, one standing to the south and facing north should draw the pillar-line; in the west, one standing to the north and facing south; in the north, one standing to the west and facing east; and in the south, one standing to the east and facing west.
In the *Vajraḍāka*, however, one circular line is prescribed with an interval of one *mātrikā* outside the first circular line for the purpose of the garland of rays (*marīcimālā*).

Then, by omitting the Brahma-line, nine squares are formed. The other Brahma-lines, as well as the lines from the central position of the leader (*nāyaka*) to the edge of the strips, are to be erased; whereas the diagonal lines and the lines of the deity-strips are to be retained and covered by the falling powder itself for the sake of distinguishing the powder at the locations of the deities.

In this case, if one exerts effort in laying out the lines otherwise than as described, then there is one line at a distance of two *mātrās* outside the Brahma-line; outside that, there are seven further lines, each at a distance of one *mātrā*, extending up to the peak-line (*kūṭāgāra-krama-śīrṣa-sūtra*) of the sixth [set]. Having laid out those seven mentioned lines exactly as prescribed, and having drawn three circular lines as before, one should leave the lines established at the points where the previous sequence of lines intersect and remove the others—this is the commentary on the Mañjuvajra-maṇḍala in both ways.
This also applies to the placement of other central deities.
With this,
one should delineate the outer maṇḍala as square, with four gates, adorned with four archways,
and provided with four boundary lines.
Inside that, there is a wheel resembling eight circles,
circular on all sides and half the size of the outer wheel.
It is auspicious, fashioned with a wheel, pillars, and so forth, and encircled by a garland of vajras.
Thus,
the ground for the lines of the wheel-pilasters and so forth is equal to that of the colored powder ground.
And thus it is divided.
12.5.2 The Maṇḍala Described in the Piṇḍīkrama:

This same procedure applies even to the maṇḍala described in the *Piṇḍīkrama*. The distinction, however, is that within the second circular line, a third circular line is drawn with a gap for the vajra-garland (*vajrāvalī*), and the garland of rays (*raśmimālā*) is placed within the first circular line, rather than a circular line being drawn outside the first circular line. As Nāgabuddhipāda said:
And the central wheel (garbhacakra) is half the size of the root sūtra in measurement.
And there, for Brahmā, it should be the size of the altar; the second [portion] half the size of the altar;
the third half the size of the altar plus a half-altar; and the other [portion] half the size of the altar.
One should make it radiant with a garland of vajras and adorned with five rays;
outside the inner wheel, one should draw four lines.
One should draw an eight-pillared [mandala], beautifully adorned and marked with vajras within the womb;
therein, there are nine compartments between each pair of vajra-pillars.
Thus:
12.5.3 The Vajrasattva Maṇḍala as described in the *Śrīsampuṭatantra*.

In the Vajrasattva maṇḍala taught in the *Śrīsampuṭatantra*, having set aside an interval of three *mātrikās* within the boundary line (*mūlasūtra*), there is an interval of half a *mātrikā* for the row of wheels situated between two circular lines. Within that, having abandoned an interval of three *mātrikās*, there is an interval of half a *mātrikā* for the row of lotuses situated between two circular lines. Within that, having left aside an interval of three *mātrikās*, there is an interval of half a *mātrikā* for the garland of rays.

Within that [space], between the two circular lines, there is an interval of half a *mātrikā* for the vajra-garland. Here, from the inner circular line to the circular line in the western direction, there are two lines on the right side of Brahmā: the first at an interval of one and a half *mātrikās*, and the second at an interval of half a *mātrikā* from the mark of the central pillar. The same applies to the left. The omission of Brahmā and the others is as before; this is the detailed instruction. 12.5.4 Jñānaḍākinī Maṇḍala (p.191)

In the Jñānaḍākinī maṇḍala, within the *mūlasūtra*, a circular thread is drawn at an interval of four *mātrikās*. Then, at an interval of one *mātrikā*, a second [thread] is the *garbharociḥ*. Then, at an interval of one *mātrikā*, a third is the *vajramālā*. Then, at an interval of six *mātrikās*, a single horizontal thread belonging to the Goddess (*devī*) is attached to the circular thread. Then, at an interval of one *mātrikā* for the sign of the Mistress of the Pillar (*stambhanāyikā*), a second [horizontal thread] is likewise drawn; such is the specific detail according to the *ṭippaṇī*. 12.5.5 Hevajramaṇḍala (p. 191).

In the mandala of the seventeen-fold Hevajra-catuṣṭaya, within the basic lines (mūlasūtra), there are only the Brahma-corner lines; no other line is to be laid down. Outside the Brahma-lines, there are four circular lines: therein, having set aside a space of two and a half mātrās plus one-eighth of a mātrā from the pericarp for the first [circle], having left a space of five and a quarter mātrās for the petals for the second, and having left one-eighth of a mātrā outside that, the third is at an interval of one mātrā for the vajra-enclosures;
the fourth is at an interval of one mātrā for the inner radiance.
12.5.6 The Maṇḍala of Nairātmyā (p. 192):
In the maṇḍalas of Nairātmyā, consisting of twenty-three deities, as well as of Kurukullā, consisting of fifteen deities, it is exactly the same.
12.5.7 The Maṇḍala of Vajrāmṛta (p. 192)

The same applies to the fourfold Vajrāmṛta. Regarding the nine-fold Hevajra maṇḍala (p. 192), the specific difference is that for the fourfold Hevajra, outside the Brahma-thread, one thread for the pericarp is drawn at an interval of five *mātrās*, and outside of that, one for the petals at an interval of ten *mātrās*. Some say that outside of that, there is a single *mātrā* for the vases and the vajra-fence (*vajrāvalī*).
12.5.9 Mahāmāyāmaṇḍala (p.193):
In the maṇḍala of the Blessed One in the form of Mahāmāyā, which consists of five aspects, it is exactly the same.
12.5.10 Buddhakapālamaṇḍala (p.193)
It is exactly the same in the mandala of the ninefold Lord Buddhakapāla.
12.5.11 Vajrahūṃkāramandala (p.193):

In the Vajrahūṃkāra-maṇḍala, at a distance of two and a half *mātrikās* from the Brahma-thread, the circular filament-thread (*keśara-sūtra*) is drawn. Outside of that, for the sake of the petals, a circular thread is drawn at a distance of five *mātrikās*. Then, at a distance of one *mātrikā*, there are eight lotuses in the cardinal and intermediate directions, each measuring seven and a half *mātrikās*. The specific instruction is that there is a lotus of three *mātrikās* outside the eastern lotus, and likewise from the western lotus.
12.5.12 *Saṃvaramaṇḍala* (p.194):

In the mandala of the Blessed One Śrī Saṃvara, as well as in the Vajravārāhī mandala, while the Brahma-lines remain within the lines of the primary grid (*mūlasūtra*), one should cast a single line from the Brahma-line outward, leaving an interval of two *mātrās*. From the primary lines, having left an interval of two *mātrās* on both the right and left sides of the corner lines, one should cast each [line] in length, measuring four door-widths on both sides of the navel.

Then, leaving a space of two *mātrās* outside the outer line from the corner-line of the *brahman* square, the first line is the measurement for the door above the *brahman* square, its corner-lines, and its side-lines;
since it is two *mātrās* wide on both sides horizontally. Outside of that, there are likewise five lines; the sixth line is also above the corner and its side-lines.

There, starting from the right side of the *brahman* line, the thread emerges at the end of the first square, goes to the front of the second, enters at the end of the third, goes to the front of the fourth, enters at the end of the fifth, goes to the front of the sixth, and finally enters at the end of the seventh; thus, this thread forms one curve. Leaving a space of half a measure within this, there is a second curve like this first one.
In this manner, there are two curved threads on the left side of the *brahman* line as well, and likewise on the left and right sides of the diagonal thread.

Then, having fixed a thread at the navel and taking the root-thread within, one should draw four circular threads through each of the intervals between the doors, following the thread held by Brahmā. As it has been said: "Taking the root-thread as a basis, one draws four circular threads."
Having rotated [the mandala] by the measure of the door of the triple wheel, it should be made consistent.
The remainder is an eight-petaled lotus; its measurement is not even slightly greater than this.
And the garlands of Vajra, Padma, and Ari are on the rims of the mind-wheel and the others.
Thus it is said.

Therein, for each of the first three [circles], there is one circular line at an interval of half a *mātrā* within; however, for the fourth—which indicates the center of the *cittacakra*—there is one circular line for the purpose of the pericarp (*karṇikā*), in the form of a circle of filaments (*keśara-valaya*), at an interval of two and a half *mātrās* from the outer petal, starting from a quarter-part of a *mātrā*.

Regarding the fourth [circle], some have stated that there is one circular line at a distance of half a *mātrā* for the purpose of the circle of the vajra-fence (*vajrāvalī*). Others say that one should encircle it with four extremely fierce vajras on both sides of the spokes (*arā*). Still another says that above the sides of the spokes, there should be garlands of vajras, lotuses, and wheels as appropriate. Here, the specific instruction in the *Ṭippaṇī* is that within the outer circular lines, the other circular lines and the spoke-lines should be preserved, while the rest should be erased. 12.5.13 The Buddhakapāla Maṇḍala (p. 197).

This is the specific procedure for the mandala of the twenty-five-deity Buddhakapāla: the first-mentioned fourth circular line and the filament (kesara) line must not be drawn. For within the sixth circular line, there is one circular line in the form of a filament, separated by a distance of five petals.
12.5.14 Yogāmbara-maṇḍala (p. 197)

In the mandala-circle of Yoga, having left a space of three and a half *mātrās* within the primary lines (*mūlasūtra*), there is a circle between two circular lines containing a vajra-garland with an interval of one *mātrā*. Then, at an interval of three and a half *mātrās*, there is another circle; this other *ṭipi* is like the mandala described in the *Piṇḍīkrama*. According to another [view], within the primary lines there are two gabled pavilions (*kūṭāgāra*) and a *ṭipi*, just like the Mañjuvajra mandala consisting of forty-three [deities] which will be described later.
Some say that the second gabled pavilion from the central gabled pavilion is circular; however, there is no gabled pavilion here.

"Another [teacher] says that the *vajrāvalī* is as before. (12.5.15) Regarding the *Yamārimaṇḍala*: in the mandala of the glorious *Yamāri*, which consists of thirteen deities, there are only the Brahma-line and corner-lines, and nothing else. Therein, having set aside the space between two doors from the Brahma-line, there is one horizontal line for the *viśvavajra* pedestal (*vedī*) extending to the corner-line. Inside that, having set aside a space of one *mātrikā*, there is one *vajrāvalī* line; from the pedestal-line to the door, there are five spokes. Following that, one should erase the Brahma and corner-lines—this is the specific instruction noted in the marginal gloss (*ṭippita*).
12.5.16 Vajratārāmaṇḍala (p.199):

While the Brahma-line cords remain in place within the maṇḍala of Vajratārā, one should draw a single circular cord at a distance of three *mātrās* outside the Brahma-line, and another circular cord at a distance of six *mātrās* outside of that; then, one should erase the Brahma-line cords.
12.5.17 Mārīcīmaṇḍala (p.199)
In the twenty-five-deity Maṇḍala of Mārīcī, there is a marginal note (*ṭippī*) regarding the Maṇḍala of Mañjuvajra.
12.5.8 *Pañcarakṣāmaṇḍala* (p. 199):

In the thirteen-deity Maṇḍala of the Five Protectresses (*Pañcarakṣā*), only the Brahma-line cords (*brahmakoṇasūtra*) are used, and nothing else. Regarding this, the specific marginal note states: "Outside the Brahma-lines, at a distance of four *mātrās* on all sides, one should place the central lotus; outside of that, at a distance of eight *mātrās*, one should erase the Brahma-line cords in the cardinal directions. This is the specific instruction.
12.5.19 Vajradhātumaṇḍala (p. 200):

In the Vajradhātumaṇḍala consisting of fifty-three deities, one should leave a space equal to two door-widths from the inner edge of the root-line (*mūlasūtra*) and draw a single horizontal line extending as far as the two diagonal corner-lines. This very [line] constitutes the root-line of the second inner maṇḍala, complete with doors, projections (*niryūha*), and so forth, up to the crest-line (*kramaśīrṣasūtra*), and including the archways (*toraṇa*) and other features.

Immediately within this root-line (mūlasūtra), first is the eastern circle-line; within that, second is [the line] with an interval of one *mātrā* from the vajra-garland; from there, up to the western circle-line, two lines are drawn on the right side of Brahmā—the first with an interval of two *mātrās*, and the second with an interval of one pillar (*stambha*)-unit. The same applies to the left. Then, by the removal of the Brahmā-corner lines, nine squares (*koṣṭha*) are formed.
The specific instruction (*ṭippikā*) is that the remaining Brahmā-lines and the internal lines ending at the position of the central deity (*nāyaka*) should be erased.
Regarding the phrase "the inner gabled chamber with an archway," this is stated specifically for the *Tattvasaṃgraha* Maṇḍala of Trailokyavijaya. As it is said:
"Upon the tops of the vajra-pillars, [it is] adorned with five maṇḍalas."

Thus, Ānandagarbha has explained that circular vajra-lines should be drawn in the positions of the five Tathāgatas, and within those lines, five moon-maṇḍalas should be drawn; however, that is inconsistent, for this tantric passage is not a description of circular vajra-lines.
(Mañjuvajramaṇḍala, p. 201)

In the Mañjuvajra maṇḍala consisting of forty-three [deities], within the root sūtra, between the two gates, there is one horizontal sūtra touching the two corner sūtras; that itself is the root sūtra of the second inner maṇḍala, provided with everything from the gate-niryūhas up to the sequence of the crest-sūtras, including the archways and so forth.

Within this [central area], a single horizontal line is drawn between the two of its own doors, touching the corner lines; this very line is the primary line (*mūlasūtra*) of the third inner *garbha*-maṇḍala, complete with doors, projections (*niryūha*), and so forth, including the archways (*toraṇa*) and other features. Immediately within this primary line, the third maṇḍala is to be constructed just as described for the *Vajradhātu-garbha-maṇḍala* starting with the words "the first," etc.—this is the specific point of the commentary.
12.5.21 Dharmadhātuvāgīśvara-maṇḍala (p. 202).

In the mandala of the Blessed One, the Lord of Speech of the Dharmadhātu, the procedure for laying out the outer mandala-line, which is common to all previously mentioned mandalas, should be understood. However, the specific distinction is that the seven lines, beginning with the root line, are circular. As it is said:
"Circular and auspicious on all sides."

Thus begins the description. Within this primary line (mūlasūtra) attached to the *niryūha* (projecting porch), one should leave a space between the two doors and draw a single horizontal line connected to the two corner lines (*koṇasūtra*). This very line constitutes the primary line of the second inner mandala, extending from the sequence of the doors and *niryūhas* to the end of the crest-line (*kramaśīrṣasūtra*), and it is appropriately devoid of an archway (*toraṇa*). Similarly, within this primary line, there is the primary line of the third mandala.
Within this root sūtra, the fourth maṇḍala is like the Vajradhātugarbha-maṇḍala described by the passage beginning with "svadvāradvaya" and so forth; this is the specific instruction (*ṭipi*).
12.5.22 *Durgatipariśodhana-maṇḍala* (p. 203):

Regarding the *Durgatipariśodhana-maṇḍala*, the instruction is similar to the maṇḍala described in the *Piṇḍīkrama*. However, the distinction is that it is inside the *Vajrāvalī*, devoid of the eight pillars and so forth, and is adorned solely by a yellow eight-spoked wheel.

12.5.23 *Bhūtaḍāmaramaṇḍala* (p. 203): Within the primary square line of the mandala of the Blessed One Bhūtaḍāmara, having set aside a space of four *mātrās*, one should draw three horizontal lines touching the two diagonal corner lines. Inside that, at a distance of four *mātrās*, another horizontal line is drawn in the same manner. Inside that again, at a distance of four *mātrās*, there is an inner chamber (*garbhapuṭa*) as described for the Mañjuvajra-maṇḍala; thus, it is composed of four chambers. 12.5.24 *Pañcaḍākamaṇḍala* (p. 204)

In the mandala of the five dākas, according to the measurement of the great mandala, one should leave a space of one and a half units within the primary lines; then, having divided another space of nine units into twelve equal parts and discarded two parts on each side, the four primary lines should be drawn with a measurement of eight such parts for the center. One-eighth of that part constitutes the door, and the six lines outside the primary lines and so forth should be executed as previously described.

Thus, there are four gabled chambers (kūṭāgāra) without archways in the cardinal directions, while the fifth gabled chamber at the center (nābhi) is likewise. Here too, the measurement of nine units (navamātrika) and so forth should be understood; however, the interval between this central gabled chamber and the four others is equal to one unit (ekamātrika), which is the measure of the great mandala.

Here, within the peaked pavilion (*kūṭāgāra*) of Hevajra, inside the root mandala, there is a semi-circular shape surrounded by a square vajra-garland situated on a single *mātrā* and positioned between two lines. For Śāśvata, it is circular, surrounded by a wheel-garland. For Vajrasūrya, it has the form of a nine-part jewel-garland, or an eight-part [garland] in the shape of a nine-part jewel. For Padmanarteśvara, it is a lotus-garland facing the doors with corners that are square, or it has the shape of a lotus.

A triangle is formed by a garland of swords for the supreme horse; this is a specific marginal note (*ṭippaṇī*). In all the peaked pavilions (*kūṭāgāra*), the measurement of the main lines and doors should be understood according to their respective proportions.
12.5.25 *Ṣaṭcakravartimaṇḍala* (p. 206).

In the mandala of the six universal monarchs (*ṣaṭcakravartin*), within the proportions of the great gabled pavilion (*mahākūṭāgāra*), one should divide into twelve parts the space that consists of a four-measure interval from the Brahma-thread together with another four-measure interval; then, on the front, back, left, and right sides, one should lay down the root-line (*mūlasūtra*) measuring eight parts within each pair of parts. The lines for the door-widths, the projections (*niryūha*), and so forth, should follow accordingly, up to the line for the top of the roof (*kramaśīrṣa*).

Then, outside that, leaving an interval of two *mātrās* from the extent of the great maṇḍala, one should hold the Brahma-thread and [draw] one circular thread for the sake of measurement. Having divided this into five equal parts, the Brahma-thread emerging from the center of each individual part should be eight *mātrās* in length according to the measure of the great maṇḍala; in its center, another Brahma-thread is likewise [to be drawn].

Having divided each of these two into twelve parts, one should perform the procedure just described, beginning with "for each of the two outer parts" and ending with "up to [the end]. In these six mandalas, the diagonal lines (koṇasūtra) must also be drawn. Outside the Brahma-line (brahmasūtra), one circular line is to be drawn at a distance of three units (mātrā) from the pericarp (karṇikā). Outside that, one circular line is to be drawn at a distance of six units from the petals. Outside that, there are eight lotuses, each measuring six units, located in the cardinal and intermediate directions.

Then, outside that, one should draw a circular line with an interval of one *mātrā*; thereafter, one should erase all the Brahma-line cords everywhere. Such is the specific instruction here in the *Ṭippaṇī*.
Furthermore, other specific types of maṇḍalas and kūṭāgāras consisting of seven layers and so forth should be inferred by the wise according to what has been taught and drawn with the cords.
12.6 Kālacakra Maṇḍala.

12.6.1 (p.207) Furthermore, regarding the Kālacakra maṇḍala, a different procedure has been taught here for the sake of disciplining those such as Sūryaratha, which differs from the rituals described in all other tantras. Therefore, for a practitioner of the completion stage (*niṣpannakrama*), it is accepted that even the performance of consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*) and other rites according to the procedures of other tantras is not contradictory, provided one possesses firm conviction that the Blessed Lord Śrī Vajradhara alone—through his various manifestations as the sovereign of all maṇḍalas—is capable of accomplishing every desired goal.

Regarding the statement "he accomplishes," having set aside the elaborate ritual procedure (*prakriyāprapañca*) of Kālacakra, only the laying out of the mandala lines and the mere scattering of colored powders (*rajaḥpāta*) are mentioned; the latter shall be explained in the upcoming section on the scattering of colored powders.

In this case, the hand of the preceptor consists of twenty-four finger-breadths (*aṅgula*), and the mandala is four hands [in width]. One should lay down two Brahma-threads eight hands in length, which is double that [width], as well as two diagonal threads (*koṇasūtra*). As for the thread, its thickness should be equal to the measure of a barley grain (*yava*) of the preceptor. In that mental mandala (*cittamaṇḍala*), the unit of measurement to be employed is half a finger-breadth, which is one-sixth of a door.

There, at the navel of the Brahma-thread, for the sake of the pericarp of the central lotus, one should cast a single circular thread by holding it two *mātrās* outside the Brahma-thread and over another Brahma-thread. Then, leaving a space of four *mātrās* for the petals, [cast] a thread. Then, a thread at an interval of one *mātrā* for the vajra-garland. Then, leaving a space of four *mātrās* for the deity's lotus, [cast] a thread. Then, a thread at an interval of one *mātrā* for the vajra-garland.
These four threads extend on both sides to the corner-threads. 12.6.3 (p.210)

Here, in the center of the four-measure deity [area], there is a lotus measuring four measures. On its two sides are two pillars, each one measure in width and four measures in length. Beside those are two vases, three measures in width and likewise in length. Beside those are two pillars in the same manner. Then, having set aside an interval of seven measures outside the final corner-line and the boundary line, [one draws] a line.

Then, having set aside a thread at a distance of four *mātrās* from the *devatā-paṭṭī*, one draws the *mūla-sūtra* by means of an interval of one *mātrā*, extending as far as the corner threads (*koṇa-sūtra*). Here, the *citta-maṇḍala* extends precisely to the limit of the *mūla-sūtra*. Likewise is the *vāk-maṇḍala*, and likewise the *kāya-maṇḍala*.

By omitting, as before, three *mātrās* each on the right and left of the *brahma-sūtra* of the *mūla-sūtra*, the door becomes six *mātrās* wide and one-eighth of the wheel (*cakra*). The *niryūha*, the *kapola*, and the *pakṣa*—these three—are equal in measure to the door.

Outside the base-line (mūlasūtra), at a distance of one and a half units (mātrā), the wall-line (bhitti-sūtra) emerges from the corner-lines (koṇasūtra) and follows the side-walls of the projections (niryūha-kapola-pakṣa), making three bends until it reaches the line of the stepped pediment (kramaśīrṣa). Beside that, at a distance of one and a half units from the pillar of the archway (toraṇastambha), there is a line whose tip is fixed to the line of the stepped pediment; its length inside is seven and a half units. Outside the line external to the base-line, leaving a space of three units for the altar-platform (vedī), there is another line.

Then, at an interval of one-and-a-half *mātrās*, there is a thread for the *ratnapaṭṭī*. Then, at an interval of three *mātrās*, there is a thread for the *hāra* and *ardhahāra* bands. Then, at an interval of one-and-a-half *mātrās*, there is a thread for the *bakulī* band. Then, at an interval of one-and-a-half *mātrās*, there is a thread for the *kramaśīrṣa*; this thread runs in length from one corner-thread to the other corner-thread. The four threads beginning with the *vedī* thread run as far as the other [central] thread. Here, a thread running from the top of one pillar to the top of another pillar indicates the *śilī* [pedestal]; however, the *kramaśīrṣas* are not to be drawn within it. 12.6.5 (p.212)

Above the pillar is the architrave (toraṇa), which is three times the height of the door. It consists of three tiers: the first is six mātras, the second is four and a half mātras, and the third is three and a half mātras. The frieze (harmyā) is two mātras, and above that, the pinnacle (kalaśa) is two mātras.
Therein, in the first tier, upon the pillar, there is a band (paṭṭī) one mātra in height and twenty-four mātras in length.

Above that is a single-mātrā band for the elephant-ornament (*mattavāraṇapaṭṭī*), sixteen mātrās in length. Above that is a four-mātrā square, in the center of which is the place for the worship-deity (*pūjādevī*); to its right and left are pillars one mātrā each. Beside those two are likewise places for worship-deities, and beside those again are pillars one mātrā each. On both sides of those, atop the arch-pillars (*toraṇastambha*), are two lions with upturned heads, treading upon lordly elephants.

Above the two heads and the four pillars, there is a *mātrikā* beam-strip eighteen *mātrās* in length. Above that is a *mātrikā* *mattavāraṇa* (elephant-head) beam-strip twelve *mātrās* in length. Above that is a beam-strip three *mātrās* [thick] and twelve *mātrās* in length. Upon it, there are four pillars each measuring three-quarters of a *mātrā*, and in the intervals between the pillars, there are three deity niches each measuring three *mātrās*. On both sides of the outer pillars are *śālabhañjikā* (carved female figures).

Above those two pillars and the [central] pillars, there is a frieze (*paṭṭī*) half a *mātrā* in height and fifteen *mātrās* in length. Above that is a *mātrikā* frieze known as the *mattavāraṇa*, eight *mātrās* in length. Above that is another frieze two *mātrās* in height and eight *mātrās* in length. Upon this [last frieze], there are four pillars each half a *mātrā* in height, and between the pillars, there are three locations for deities, each two *mātrās* in height. On both sides of the outer pillars are *śālabhañjikā* figures.

Above that is a fillet (*paṭṭī*) half a *mātrā* thick and twelve *mātrās* in length; above that is a cornice (*harmya*) eight *mātrās* in length; above that is a pitcher (*kalaśa*). To its left and right are the positions for the flagstaffs. Thus, at the tips of all the fillets are bells, chowries, mirrors, banners, and flags.

Here, outside the root line of the mind-maṇḍala (cittamaṇḍala) is the speech-maṇḍala (vāṅmaṇḍala). In each of its directions, there is a space of twelve units (mātrikās), pervaded by the bands (paṭṭīs) starting from the wall of the mind-maṇḍala and ending with the crest-line (kramaśīrṣa). Outside of that, leaving an interval of seven units, there is a line; then, omitting four units for the deity-band (devatāpaṭṭī), there is another line.

On this band, lotuses measuring four *mātrās* are to be drawn; however, those situated beneath the arches of the mind-maṇḍala and facing the cardinal directions should be drawn in the space of four *mātrās* belonging to the second enclosure, by shifting two pillars half a *mātrā* inward. Then, outside the line of the deities' band, the root-line is placed at an interval of one *mātrā*. These three lines extend in length as far as the corner-lines.
