In the root sūtra, however, by the elision of the six measures on the right and left of Brahmā as before, the gateway becomes twelve measures in length. Thereafter, the elements from the *niryūha* (corner pavilion) up to the *toraṇa* (arched gateway) are twice the measure of those from the *niryūha* and so forth of the mind-maṇḍala.

Outside the root-line of this speech-mandala (*vāṅmaṇḍala*) is the body-mandala (*kāyamaṇḍala*). In each of its directions, there are twenty-four cubit-spaces, pervaded by strips beginning with the wall of the speech-mandala and ending with the crest. Leaving a space of eleven cubits beyond that, one draws a line. Then, leaving twelve cubits for the deity-strip (*devatāpaṭṭī*), one draws a line. On this deity-strip, there are twelve lotuses, each measuring twelve cubits.
There, having divided the twelve-measure lotus into seven parts, there are four petals in the middle part—the pericarp—and in the right and left parts;

eight petals in the right and left parts of those; and sixteen petals in the right and left parts of those. Thus, with three circles, there are twenty-eight petals. Outside the line of the deities' pedestal, the root-line is at an interval of one measure. These three lines are as long as they extend to the corner-lines.

In the case of the *mūlasūtra*, which consists of twelve units (*mātrā*) on the right and left of the Brahmā-line, the gate becomes twenty-four units through the elision [of the central portion] as before. Thereafter, the elements from the *niryūha* (the projecting archway) up to the *toraṇa* (gate-arch) are double the measure of those from the *niryūha* etc. of the Speech-mandala (*vāṅmaṇḍala*), extending as far as half of the water-rim (*jalavalaya*). Outside the *toraṇas* of the Speech-mandala, within the gates of the Body-mandala (*kāyamaṇḍala*), there are chariots (*ratha*) measuring twelve units.
Then the earth-rim (*pṛthvīvalaya*) is twelve units; outside that, the water-rim is twenty-four units; and beyond that, the fire-rim (*agnivalaya*) is twenty-four units.

Beyond that is the wind-circle (*vāyu-valaya*), measuring twenty-four units. Outside the wind-circle is the space-circle (*ākāśa-valaya*), measuring twelve units. Outside that circle are the rays of light (*raśmi-jvālā*), measuring twenty-four units. For each of these six circles beginning with earth, there is one circular line at the beginning; however, for the circle of rays, there is also one at the end, making seven circular lines in total. Thus, this maṇḍala, whose essence consists of three circles and which has the Mind-Vajra as its leader, has a measuring-line (*sūtra*) of eight cubits extending from the beginning of the earth-circle [to the end]. This is the first position. 12.6.9 (p.219)

However, when the measurement of the door of the mental maṇḍala (cittamaṇḍala) is combined with the measurement of the door of the verbal maṇḍala (vāṅmaṇḍala), and the door is thus conceived as consisting of eighteen *mātrās*, then a sixth part of that is designated as a *mātrā*. In that case, by means of that *mātrā*, the count of *mātrās* should be made from the pericarp of the Leader’s lotus up to the edge of the circle of light.

Then, the second position is as follows: the maṇḍala of the Leader Cittavajra, consisting of three maṇḍalas, is twelve cubits; its cord is double that, twenty-four cubits, extending as far as the edge of the earth-circle.

When, however, the Lord Cittavajra occupies the place of Vāgvajra and Vāgvajra is the leader, the placement of the other deities and so forth is as in the first alternative. And when the inner maṇḍala is four cubits, the second is double that, and the third is double that again; then the speech-maṇḍala consists of three maṇḍalas and is sixteen cubits [in diameter]. The cord for it is double that, thirty-two cubits, extending as far as the edge of the ground-circle; this is the third alternative.

When, however, one combines the measurement of the door of the first-mentioned *cittamaṇḍala* with the measurement of the door of the first-mentioned *kāyamaṇḍala*, and having thus determined the door to be thirty units (*mātra*), the sixth part of that is designated as a "unit" (*mātrā*); then, by means of that unit, the count of units must be performed from the pericarp of the Leader up to the end of the circle of rays. Furthermore, the Blessed One *Cittavajra* is to be placed in the position of *Kāyavajra*, while *Kāyavajra* is the Leader; the placement of the other deities and so forth, however, is as in the first alternative.

Then, the leader of the Body-Vajra [is drawn] as a mandala consisting of the three circles, twenty cubits in size; the cord is double that, forty cubits, extending as far as the edge of the earth-circle—this is the fourth position.

And likewise, in the *Vimalaprabhā*, the sūtra states: "Eight hands" is the root [measurement]; "eight hands" is double the maṇḍala. Having explained this, it says therein regarding the *Ādibuddha*: "One should make the mind-maṇḍala twelve hands and the sūtra twenty-four hands; likewise, the speech-maṇḍala sixteen hands and the body-maṇḍala twenty hands"—this is the rule for the sūtra being double [the size of the maṇḍala]. Furthermore, for the purpose of initiation (*seka*), only a circular central maṇḍala is permitted. As it is said:
"Or the maṇḍala for the purpose of initiation may be according to the family, with the outer wheel omitted."
As for the fact that the *Trailokyavijaya-tantra* mentions a door consisting of nine parts of the circle,
and the *Mahāmaṇḍalavyūha-tantra* mentions one consisting of ten parts of the circle, these are not currently employed by the masters.
Thus have we refuted [the objection].
Furthermore, the measure of the mandala has been stated as it is well-known, yet it is not merely this much; for it was said by the Blessed One:
"Of the lords of Jambudvīpa, or of kings who are universal monarchs (cakravartin)..."
The outer mandala should be drawn extending for a distance of one yojana on all sides.
Having observed the minds of those to be trained, there is no fault whatsoever for the wise one to assume pride even by his own will.

Having drawn the entire maṇḍala at will upon the palm of their hand, they accomplish the purpose declared in the scriptures; what need is there to mention [drawing it] on the surface of the earth and so forth?
Thus, how many mandalas—divided into infinite varieties—could possibly be described or constructed? As the Blessed One said:
"Who is capable of fashioning mandalas according to their true nature?
The construction of mandalas is accomplished through union with one's own tutelary deity."
Thus ends [the section]. 12.7 Summary Verse of the Sūtras 12.7.1 (p. 222) ->
Here are the summary verses for the layout:

Having marked the points in the eastern and other directions and above with held threads, one should mark the Brahma-thread at the corners by means of four mandalas situated between the tails and mouths of the fish-shaped figures.
In the corner, the primary line for the layout consists of the hands (cubits) and so forth for the doors of those seven directions;
with the eighth part removed from the middle, that [line] is twice [the length], while the fourth part is the measure.
From the base, six lines are drawn outward at intervals of one, two, one, two, one, and one [units] respectively;
from the corners, they extend horizontally away from the Brahma-line in sequence.
With three measures [from the first sūtra], one attaches [the cord] to the tip of the second-measure sūtra;
with eight measures, one draws three straight lines from the altar-sūtra, making four in total.
The third [mark] is five mātrās, the fourth is four mātrās, and the first is likewise;
they are attached to the tips of the horizontal lines with an interval of one mātrā between each.
Three [threads] are at the tip of the fourth; the horizontal thread is ten units long.
The thread extending from the base to the tip is four units, and two units.
Horizontally and upwards, it extends eight *mātrās* with three bends;
from the top of the pillar, the threads are each separated by an interval of one *mātrā*.
In this [meter], the fifth and seventh [syllables] consist of one and a half mātrās each;
likewise, the third, seventh, or ninth [syllables] consist of one mātrā each.
The fourth, sixth, and tenth [syllables] consist of half-mātrās; five [syllables] consist of one and a half mātrās each;
and in those two groups, the intervening [syllables] consist of one mātrā each.
To the right and left of Brahmā, at an interval of one and a half mātrās,
there is a band (paṭṭī) of two and a half mātrās, and the thread (sūtra) is three and a half mātrās.
The second and third [notes] have a duration of three mātrās each, following a pause of six mātrās;
the fourth has a duration of four mātrās following a pause of four mātrās; and the fifth has a duration of five mātrās following a pause of three mātrās.
From one and a half [units], there are three and a half mātras; from three seasons, there are five mātras;
four times seven mātras make up the iṣumātra, which is the Rudra-thread.
The fifth horizontal row, however, is above the three-and-a-half-mātrā [space];
the seventh is below the three-mātrā [space] and above the six-mātrā [space], and then it proceeds upwards.
The thread that reaches to the end of the strips is at the edge together with those following it;
one [curve] from here is inward, and likewise another half-mātrā further.
Outside of that, at the end of the Veda-measures, there is a circle;
from there, two [more] circles, each separated by two measures, and the next separated by four measures.

12.7.3 (p.225) When the two side-pillars (*kapola*) are equal to the door-width, there is no blind-band (*andhapaṭṭikā*). However, when the width is three times the height of the archway (*toraṇa*), there is indeed no upward-extending [band].
Then, however, three straight lines are measured from the altar-line;
on the adjacent side, for the work of the Rudra-pattas and the arches.
Vasu, Vasu, Sūrya, Jina, Vasu, and Jina;
Ravi, Vasu, Sūrya, Jina, and Vasu—these are the [names] in sequence.
The measurement of these [door-frames] from top to bottom is as stated;
their width, however, is said to be one and a half *mātrās* to the right and left of the Brahmā-line.
The strip is two and a half finger-breadths wide, and the thread is three and a half finger-breadths; the second and third [threads] are three finger-breadths each, up to five finger-breadths.
From four mātrās, the fourth [foot] consists of three mātrās; from three and a half, the fifth is an iṣu (three mātrās);
from three and a half, the sixth is three [mātrās]; and from that, the seventh consists of five mātrās.
The eighth [square] is seven units, the seventh is one unit, and the last is six units;
outside that, at the end of the Veda-units, there is a circle of two units.
The *sūtra* consists of two morae; the *vṛtta* ends with four morae;
the last [type] is at the end of eight morae from the *brahman*; and the *vṛttaka* is at the end of seven morae. 12.7.4 (p.227)
From that [central] thread, two threads emerge toward the boundary of the western thread;
they extend outside the Brahma-thread at intervals of two and three *mātrās* respectively.
From the outer circle, a line for the outer circle is drawn at an interval of one *mātrā*; then, at an interval of three *mātrās*, a line is established from the corner lines.
One should erase the lines within the Brahma-cells and the fillets that extend everywhere,
slightly toward the interior of the mandala according to the distinction of the deities. 12.7.5 (p.227)
The measurement of the site is different, but that which pertains to the enclosure is said to be otherwise;
it does not extend beyond the Brahma-line from the lines situated at the corners of the Brahma-pada.
From the two points separated by two mātrās, a thread should be drawn from the base to the sides of the corners;
likewise, four doors should be made, with threads extending from the center of that [square] to its sides.
Four finger-breadths outside the navel, there is a cord of four finger-breadths;
then, transversely, on the Brahma-line and on the corner-threads, there are five [finger-breadths] from that point.
Likewise, those [lines] are at an interval of two and two mātrās; and the sixth [line] is at the corner.
To the right and left of Brahmā, as well as for the seven [deities] and the one at the corner, [the lines are likewise placed].
From the first [syllable] of the third [quarter] of the fifth [line], ending with one mātrā, it should emerge;
having gone to the front of its own second [syllable], it reaches the middle of the seventh.
There should be five crooked lines with a single thread; within that as well, there is an interval, and leaving another half-measure, there are likewise five circles.
From Brahmā, the king, and the Sun, there are three [groups] at intervals of one, two, and three mātrās respectively;
however, within Āditya, the triad is at intervals of half and half a mātrā.
And let those who would destroy the *Vṛttasūtra*—which is distinct from the *Vṛttārāsa-sūtras*—do so;
for another person, out of fear of prolixity, there is no inclusion of further particulars.
Thus [it is said].

12.7.6 (p.229) Then, at the conclusion of the marking-out, preceded by offerings and worship, one should release the wisdom-thread with "oṃ āḥ hūṃ vajra muḥ," place it within the hearts of the Tathāgatas residing in the sky, and set down the five-colored thread in its proper position; such is the procedure for the marking-out.
13. The Procedure for the Deposition of Dust (Rajaḥpātanavidhi) 13.1.1 (p. 299):

Then, having offered the sacrificial oblation (*bali*), one should [prepare] powders of white, yellow, red, green, and black colors, produced respectively from the seed-syllables *vaṃ*, *laṃ*, *raṃ*, *haṃ*, and *yaṃ*. These are derived from moonstone (*candrakānta*), karketana, ruby (*padmarāga*), emerald (*marakata*), and sapphire (*indranīla*), or alternatively, from pearl (*muktā*), gold (*kanaka*), coral (*pravāla*), and rājāvarta stone. Here, "mixed" refers to the mixture of these four, beginning with the pearl.

Having meditated upon [the materials], whether derived from minerals, rice, or flowers, as appropriate—refined with powdered baked bricks, charcoal, or the dust of moving creatures—as auspicious and having the nature of Vairocana and the other [Buddhas] produced from the syllables *vuṃ*, *āṃ*, *hrīḥ*, *khaṃ*, and *hūṃ*—and having brought them to a state of unity with the rays of gnosis produced from *vuṃ* and the others which have entered and merged with the hearts of all the Tathāgatas stationed in the sky, drawn in by the blazing gaze described in the *Sūtrasaṃskāra*, one consecrates them with *oṃ vuṃ* and so forth: *oṃ vajra-citra samaya hūṃ*.

One should consecrate [the powder] one hundred and eight times with this mantra. Likewise, while stimulating it with a blazing gaze, one should place the syllable *hīḥ* upon each [particle] and ignite it through the empowerment of truth (*satyādhiṣṭhāna*), saying: "By that truth through which sentient beings and the Blessed Buddhas are impassioned by passion for sentient beings, by that truth may the powder blaze! It blazes through the excellence of the practice of the deity.
Having worshipped it with incense, flowers, and so forth, one should place it in a new vessel.

Then, having generated the stake situated at the center of the mandala by means of the four *hūṃ* mantras to be described hereafter, and having mentally dissolved it into the vajra in one's own hand, one should fill the pit of the stake with five-colored powders and level it. Having dispelled any ill omens with the ringing of a bell and vajra songs, [one recites]:
"This is the pure realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), the liberator of the realm of sentient beings;
he himself is the King Vajradhara, the abode of all Tathāgatas."
Completely liberated from all defects, he is situated within the wheel.

Thus, having resolved upon the purity of the *dharmadhātu*, and standing within the inner mandala with the right hand marked by a vajra and the left in the vajra-fist, one should cast the colored powders (*raṅga*) while reciting either "Oṃ vajraraṅga samaya | Oṃ āḥ hūṃ" or "Oṃ vajracitra samaya hūṃ. Starting from the northeastern direction and facing east, standing within the mandala, one should cast the powders in a clockwise direction. Afterwards, the preceptor or the painter may do so as they please.
However, one should not cast a line that is too thick; it should be one-twentieth the size of the door.
Equal, level, and uninterrupted, they should be joined to one another as appropriate.
The space between them should be the measure of a barley grain from bottom to top, according to what is aesthetically pleasing;
if they are too thick, disease will arise, and by making them too thin, there will be loss of wealth.
If it is crooked, there is enmity; if it is broken, death occurs for both teacher and disciple;
and if it falls in a counter-clockwise direction, there will be the immobilization of the vital energies (rajas).

"Kīlana" (the act of pinning) is the absence of the basis for attaining spiritual accomplishment (*siddhi*). When [the substances] are mixed with one another, there occurs a severance of the lineage (*gotraccheda*).
However, for the sake of pacifying faults, the Blessed One has said:
"Whatever faults arise from the application of those whose intention is not directed toward reality when applying the colors."
For those who possess the yoga of the disposition toward the true reality of the teachings, no obstacles can ever prevail,
as long as they maintain the maṇḍalas according to their actual nature and conceptualization.
Thus, within the lines of dust, one should cultivate the conviction (*adhimoktavya*) that they consist of needles and other objects made of white and other precious gems,
due to the fear of entering or exiting them, or of stepping over or upon the threads and colors.

Having mentally cast up a line of the dust of gnosis (*jñānarajas*) from the sky by means of the "Vajra-impulse" (*vajrāvega*), while reciting *oṃ vajravegākrama hūṃ*, one may enter or exit the maṇḍala drawn within the root-thread.
234) In this regard, first, the sequence of colors for all the deity maṇḍalas is stated in general for both the outer and inner maṇḍalas.

The colors of the five wall-lines—from the outer line inward to the innermost line—corresponding to the directions east, south, west, north, and the center of the Tathāgata, follow the sequence of the colors of the deities and the Tathāgatas used for their placement and sealing. Some say that these five walls in the mandala to be visualized are composed of five-colored jewels and are separated by intervals the size of barley grains.
Others maintain that this is a single wall composed of five-colored jewels, arranged one above the other in successive layers.

Regarding this, in the first opinion, the ground of the jeweled bands (*ratnapaṭṭikā*) is red, while the ground of the necklaces and half-necklaces (*hārārdhahāra*) is black. In the second opinion, however, the jeweled band consists of various jewels placed upon the very portion made of the first-colored jewel; or else, the jeweled band is fashioned from jewels of a different color and set upon that [first-colored] portion. Likewise, the band of the various necklaces and half-necklaces consists of the very portion made of the fifth-colored jewel; or else, the band of necklaces and half-necklaces is fashioned from jewels of a different color and set upon that [fifth-colored] portion.

Above that, as stated in another section, is a jeweled band (*ratnapaṭṭī*) like a necklace-band (*hārapaṭṭī*). According to both views, the railing (*vedikā*) has a floor made of crystal, gold, ruby, or various other jewels, as is aesthetically pleasing.

The *bakulyas* and *kramaśīrṣas* are white; the ground between the *bakulī*, *kramaśīrṣa*, and their edges is blue because it has the appearance of the sky. For this very reason, the intermediate strips are called "darkness-strips" (*andhakārapaṭṭikā*). The *āsāra* is made of jewels as is fitting, adorned with clusters of leaves and so forth made of various gems.

The pillars of the archway are the color of the Tathāgatas of their respective directions; and within the curve, the moonlight and the ground below are likewise, for they are of the nature of space, adorned by the rays of the Tathāgatas’ own colors. The excellent hoof-rings are of beautiful colors, as is the *makara*-band. Some say the wheels are made of gold, while others say they are fashioned from various jewels. The deer and doe are made of gold, inlaid with various jewels.

The hub of the universal vajra is black and has the color of the presiding Tathāgata; in some cases, the spokes in the middle [of each direction] have the colors of the respective Tathāgatas of their own directions; the others [the outer spokes] have the colors of the Tathāgatas on both sides of those two. When there are five spokes, those in the middle of the other directions also have the colors of the Tathāgatas of their respective directions as appropriate. Furthermore, all spokes in a single direction may have the color of the Tathāgata of that direction. Alternatively, in the case where the Lord of the Wheel (Cakreśa) has four faces, they may have the colors corresponding to the faces of their own respective directions—this is another position.

The auspicious jars (*bhadraghaṭa*) are golden; the wish-fulfilling trees (*kalpataru*) resemble other excellent trees. The pericarp of the lotus is green, the filaments are yellow, and the petals are of various colors. Its ground is white with a brilliant hue. The lines of the *dharmodayā* are white; likewise, the lines of the circular rim (*cakravāḍa*) are white if it is made of crystal, or yellow if it is made of gold. The vajras are black, as are their lines; others say they are white or yellow.

The color of the vajra-ground should be visualized according to its beauty within the mandala, extending downward as far as the wind-mandala and upward as far as the Akaniṣṭha heaven, because the vajra-fence remains there. Furthermore, since the wind and other elements possess various colors as appropriate, the general rule is that the rays have the colors of the five Tathāgatas.
However, in the case of Mañjuvajra:
Because he possesses the wisdom-body of the Perfectly Awakened One, he is known as the eloquent one in the Vajra family;
in the complete purification of the self-nature of the Dharma-body, his mind-mandala [is established].
According to this principle:
white, yellow, red, green, and black are the colors of the wall-dust.
Thus it has been said: "But when white dharmas [arise] by nature, that is the 'whiteness' of Vāgīśa in this context."
Because of this statement, Vāgvajra is the central deity. At that time, there are dust-lines (*rajorekhā*) that are white, yellow, black, green, and white.

Although Vajrasattva, as taught in the *Sampuṭa*, is white, the inner wall is black in order to indicate his state of being of one flavor with Akṣobhya. Others, however, maintain that it is indeed white, just as in some cases where Vāgvajra, having become the central deity, is white.

Furthermore, within the mandala of the root-sūtra, the ground-areas demarcated by each pair of diagonal lines (koṇasūtra) in the four directions should be visualized as having the colors of the Tathāgatas of their respective directions; likewise, the panels in the four directions of the mandala, as well as the pillars, are marked with garlands of the emblems of the Tathāgatas of their respective squares. The ground of the central leader has the color of the leader. The southwest is green and black, while the northeast, southeast, and northwest are [black]. In the universal lotus, the petals in the cardinal directions are yellow, while those in the intermediate directions are red.
On the leader's path is a garland of the leader’s symbols; on the other lines, the colors of the qualities are according to their beauty.

13.2.5 (p.239) In the Saṃvara maṇḍala, however, the mind-wheel (*cittacakra*) is black, and the spaces between its spokes are red because it has the speech-wheel as its hub. The speech-wheel (*vākcakra*) is red, and the spaces between its spokes are white because it has the body-wheel as its hub. The body-wheel (*kāyacakra*) is brilliant white, and the spaces between its spokes in the directions of the east and so forth have the colors of the Tathāgatas Vairocana and the others. The three rims are respectively adorned with a row of black vajras, red lotuses, and white wheels.

From the exterior to the interior, there are five lines of green, white, red, yellow, and black colors; the grounds and the layers (*paṭala*) are white, green, red, yellow, and black in color, respectively, for the east, north, west, south, and center. According to another [tradition], the five lines and the grounds and layers are black, green, red, yellow, white, and mixed blue in color.

Thus, having thoroughly contemplated the sequence of letters from beginning to end, one should cast the colored powder (*rajas*). In that regard, if an actual union is not possible, the symbolic signs (*cihna*) and seals (*mudrā*) should be drawn according to the circumstances. However, if even the symbolic signs are impossible, the form of the deity should be depicted; it may be painted, cast, fashioned, or consecrated, and then installed. As it has been said by the venerable Nāgabuddhipāda:
"The placement of seed-syllables, or the sign, or indeed the form of the deity—whether cast, fashioned, or installed—in the mandala, according to one's capacity."
Thus, the drawing of mudrās is described in the Abhidhānottara Tantra:
"In case of inability, one should place a drawn mudrā and a symbolic mark."
As it has been said:
"Whether with colors or with variegated tufts of wool, it is beautifully adorned."
Thus, in the *Śrīsampuṭatantra*,
it is stated that the symbolic mudrās are also appropriate in the form of poured [liquids], fashioned [images], and so forth.
Thus: 13.3.1 Mañjuvajramaṇḍala (p. 241).
Therefore, in the Mañjuvajramaṇḍala, at the navel of the Blessed One Mañjuvajra, upon a moon disc, there is a dark-blue sword.

In the east, upon the moon of Vairocana, is a white eight-spoked wheel; in the south, upon the sun of Ratnasambhava, is a nine-faceted green jewel; in the west, upon the sun of Amitanātha, is a red eight-petalled lotus; and in the north, upon the sun of Amoghasiddhi, is a green sword.

In the southeast moon is the eye of Locanā, consisting of two eyes—one blue like a star and one white—situated within a cloud. In the southwest moon is the black five-pronged vajra of Māmakī, according to the reading in the Tantra. In the northwest moon is the blooming red lotus with its stalk and bulb for Pāṇḍarā. In the northeast moon is the blue-lotus (utpala) of Tārā, appearing yellowish-blue.

In the four corners starting from the southeast, and on the two sides of the eastern gate at a distance of two *mātrās* to the left and right of the center, upon moon discs, there are respectively the Vajras of Form, Sound, Smell, Taste, Touch, and the Dharmadhātu: a white mirror, a blue gandharva lute, a yellow conch of fragrance, a red vessel of taste, a multicolored cloth, and a white source of phenomena (*dharmodayā*).

Upon sun discs at the gates starting from the east, there are respectively the black vajra-mallet of Yamāntaka, the white staff marked with a vajra of Prajñāntaka, the red lotus of Padmāntaka, and the blue fierce vajra of Vighnāntaka.

Herein, there are nineteen moons and suns situated upon universal lotuses; all the symbols are radiant and have their heads turned toward their respective directions, while the head of the Lord of the Wheel (Cakreśa), however, is turned to the west. The same applies further on. When Vajrasattva is the Lord of the Wheel, some say there is a blue, gentle vajra in the center of the moon-lotus, and a crossed-vajra (viśvavajra).

The learned authorities maintain that the dust of the threads (*guṇarajas*) should not be removed from the *vṛtta-sūtra* (the circular thread). Having left a space of four *mātrās* outside the circular thread and alongside the *brahma-sūtra*, one places a four-*mātrā* vessel; thus there are eight vessels filled with nectar, made of gold—this is one position. Another [position] holds they are made of the jewels corresponding to the colors of the Tathāgatas of their respective directions. Here and later, when the internal symbols of the Tathāgatas are to be placed in the center, the central symbol should be drawn in that location. 13.3.2 The Maṇḍala as Described in the *Piṇḍīkrama* (p. 243)

In the maṇḍala described in the Piṇḍīkrama, in the center upon the sun of Akṣobhya is a five-pronged, gaping vajra with the luster of sapphire, as well as a garment; [these belong] to her who is devoid of touch.
For the twelve [deities] beginning with Vairocana, situated in the first and second enclosures, the hand-symbols are as previously stated.

On the third enclosure, on the frieze at the side of the door, by leaving a space of four *mātrās* from the Brahma-line, there is on the left the Naga-kesara flower with a wheel for Maitreya; on the right, an eight-spoked white wheel for Kṣitigarbha. Likewise, on the south [side] are the jewel, lotus, and vajra for Lokeśvara and Mañjughoṣa; and on the north [side], the sword and vajra for Sarvanivaraṇaviṣkambhin and Samantabhadra.

At the eastern and other gates, for Yamāri and the others, there are respectively a vajra-hammer, a white staff marked with a vajra, a red lotus, and a double-vajra (*viśvavajra*). In the corners beginning with the southeast, for Acala, Ṭakkirāja, Nīladaṇḍa, and Mahābala, there are a sword, a vajra, a blue staff marked with a vajra, and a black staff marked with a vajra. For Uṣṇīṣacakravartin, there is a blue vajra; another [teacher] says that outside the symbol of Yamāri is a yellow wheel. For Sumbharāja, there is a vajra outside the symbol of Padmāntaka.

The eight symbols of Maitreya and others are situated upon moons; the ten symbols of Yamāri and others are situated upon suns. Herein, thirty-one suns and moons are situated upon universal lotuses (*viśvapadma*); the drawing of the vases is as before.
13.3.3 Regarding the Vajrasattva Maṇḍala taught in the *Saṃpuṭa Tantra*:
in the center of the Vajrasattva maṇḍala taught in the *Saṃpuṭa Tantra*, there is a blue five-pronged vajra upon a moon for Vajrasattva.
On the eastern moon is the wheel of Śāśvata; on the southern sun is the jewel of Ratneśa; on the western sun is the arrow of Amitābha; and on the northern sun is the crossed-vajra of Amoghasiddhi.
For Locanā, it is a water-lily with eyes; for Māmakī, an arrow; for Pāṇḍarā, an arrow; and for Tārā, a red lotus.

In the second enclosure, in the eastern direction, there is an arrow for Raudrī; in the south, a vajra for Vajrabimbā; in the west, a sword for Rāgavajrā; in the north, a pestle for Vajrasaumyā; in the northeast, a white and yellow staff for Vajravaktrā; in the southeast, a yellow and red lotus for Vajraḍākinī; in the southwest, a spear for Śabdavajrā; and in the northwest, a green and white vase for Pṛthivīvajrā.

In the third enclosure, in the eastern direction is the vajra of Hāsyā; in the south, the vajra of Lāsyā; in the west, the bell-metal cymbal (kaṃsikā) of Gītā; in the north, the green three-pronged vajra of Nṛtyā; in the northeast, the flute of Vaṃśā; in the southeast, the lute (vīṇā) of Vīṇā; in the southwest, the mukunda drum of Mukundā; and in the northwest, the muraja drum of Murajā.

On the outer band: in the southeast is a flower garland for Puṣpā; in the southwest, an incense burner for Dhūpā; in the northwest, a lamp-stand for Dīpā; in the northeast, a scented conch for Gandhā; in the east, a mirror for Ādarśā; in the south, a vessel of flavors for Rasā; in the west, a multicolored cloth for Sparśā; and in the north, a white *dharmodayā* for Dharmā.

In the eastern and other gates, respectively, are Vajrāṅkuśī, Vajrapāśī, Vajrasphoṭā, and Vajraghaṇṭā; their symbols are a vajra-aṅkuśa, a vajra-pāśa, a vajra-mālā, a vajra-nigaḍa, and a vajra-ghaṇṭā, each situated upon a sun disk.

Here, the symbols other than those seven mentioned as having sun seats are seated upon moon disks. These thirty-seven [deities], both moon and sun, are situated within skull-cups upon double lotuses. The drawing of the vases is as before; however, the distinction is that it is outside the sixth circular line. 13.3.4 The Maṇḍala of Jñānaḍākinī (p. 248).

In the center of the mandala of Jñānaḍākinī, in the east, north, west, and south respectively, are the vajra-marked khaṭvāṅgas of Jñānaḍākinī, Vajraḍākinī, Ghorāḍākinī, Vettālī, and Caṇḍālī. In the northeast, southeast, southwest, and northwest are the vajra-hooks of Siṃhinī, Vyāghrī, Jambukī, and Ulūkī.

At the gates of the east, north, west, and south, those of Rājendrī, Dīpinī, Cūṣiṇī, and Kambojī have, respectively: two hands joined in añjali; the sampuṭa-añjali (hands hollowed together); an añjali filled with blood; and the vajra-añjali formed by joining the tips of the two thumbs while extending the two index fingers like needles.

Here, the signs and mudrās are situated upon a universal lotus and sun. Furthermore, the universal lotuses for Jñānaḍākinī and the others are, in their respective order, situated upon a lion, a white elephant, a heap of the seven jewels, a buffalo, the tail of a lordly eight-hooded serpent, and four dogs; these are to be visualized in the maṇḍala. At present, they are not drawn in the powder maṇḍala because of the lack of suitability for the assembly, and due to the donor's fear of effort and lack of interest. However, for the sake of inspiring faith in those who are suitable, they are drawn according to the donor's wish.
In this manner, it should be understood that in what follows, drawing and non-drawing occur as appropriate. The drawing of the vase is outside the circular line.
In the mandala of the seventeen-fold Hevajra—the triad of Hevajras—there is a blue wrathful vajra at the pericarp of the universal lotus.

In the petals starting from the southeast (southeast, south, etc., up to the northeast), in due order, are the [emblems] of Vajraraudrī, Vajrabimbā, Vajrarāgā, Vajrasaumyā, Vajrayakṣī, Vajraḍākinī, Śabdavajrā, and Pṛthvīvajrā: an arrow, a vajra, a sword, a hammer, a yellow staff, a yellow-red lotus, a spear, and a green-white vase. In the second enclosure, in the northeast, southeast, and so forth, are the flutes, lute, *mukunda* drum, and clay drum of Vaṃśā, Vīṇā, Mukundā, and Murajā: a flute, a lute, a *mukunda*, and a clay drum.
At the gates in the east and so forth are those of Vajrāṅkuśī, Vajrapāśī, Vajrasphoṭā, and Vajraghaṇṭā: a vajra-hook, a vajra-noose, a chain, and a vajra-bell.

These seventeen symbols are situated upon skulls and sun discs. For the eight [deities] beginning with Vaṃśa, there are double lotuses beneath the skulls; however, for those with two or four arms, there is no skull.
But for the sixteen-armed one in the maṇḍala, there is a blue fierce vajra upon the pericarp of a universal lotus.

In the petals starting from the east and ending with the northeast, in due order, are the emblems of Gaurī, Caurī, Vettālī, Ghasmarī, Pukkasī, Śavarī, Caṇḍālī, and Pramohā: an arrow, a vajra, a tortoise in a skull-cup filled with blood, a snake in a skull-cup full of fat, a lion in a skull-cup full of flesh, a mendicant in a skull-cup containing semen, a tiger in a skull-cup filled with blood, and a goblet.
In the corners of the second enclosure, the emblems of Vaṃśā and the others are as previously described.
At the gates in the east and other directions are the emblems of Hayāsyā, Sukarāsyā, Śvānāsyā, and Siṃhinī: a vajra-hook, a vajra-noose, a vajra-shackle, and a vajra-bell.

These seventeen signs are situated upon the sun. Beneath the suns of the eight [deities] beginning with Vaṃśā are double lotuses (*viśvapadma*); outside the central light-rays are vases as before. 13.3.6 *Nairātmyāmaṇḍala* (p. 252):

In the maṇḍala of Nairātmyā, on the pericarp of the double lotus and on the petals starting from the east, there are, in sequence, the vajras of Nairātmyā, Vajrā, Gaurī, Vārī, and Vajraḍākinī; and in the second enclosure, the vajras of the eight [goddesses] beginning with Gaurī as described in the sixteen-armed maṇḍala.

The symbols of Vaṃśā and the others are as before. For Hayāsyā and the others: outside Hayāsyā is the vajra of Khecarī; outside Śvānāsyā is the vajra of Bhūcarī. Here, the four flaying knives (*kartṛ*) rest upon the sun disk, while the other symbols rest upon the moon mandala. Among the eighteen external goddesses beginning with Gaurī, their symbols such as the moon rest upon a universal lotus (*viśvasaroja*).

In the absence of the eight [symbols] beginning with the flute, the remaining fifteen goddesses have the moon and the flaying knife. Outside Gaurī is the symbol of Khecarī; outside Vettālī is the symbol of Bhūcarī.
Thus, in the *Kurukullā* maṇḍala, upon the moon is an arrow consisting of a red utpala bud with its stalk. Indeed, all fifteen goddesses here are red in color, like Kurukullā herself.

In the *Vajrāmṛta* maṇḍala, in the first [circle], upon the pericarp of the variegated lotus and on the petals starting from the east and proceeding to the northeast and so forth, there is, in due order, the vajra of Vajrāmṛtā, Saumyā, Saumyavadanā, Cāndrī, Śaśinī, Śaśimaṇḍā, Śaśilekhā, Manojñā, and Manohrādanakarī. Following Śaśilekhā, there is a single digit of the moon (*candrakalā*).
In the second enclosure, starting from the northeast (aiśāna) and so forth, are the flower-basket, incense burner, lamp-stand, and perfume-conch for flowers, incense, lamps, and perfumes.
On the panels in the east and other directions are the four [instruments] beginning with the flute.
At the gates in the east and other directions are the vajra-hook, noose, chain, and bell for Bhṛkuṭītaraṅga, Bhayabhīṣaṇa, Hayarūpa, and Gaṇanāyaka.

These twenty-one emblems are situated upon the moon. Beneath the moon of the twelve [deities] beginning with Puṣpa are universal lotuses (*viśvāmbuja*). Alternatively, the source of phenomena (*dharmodayā*) should be drawn for all the mandala deities; according to others, this alone is what should be drawn. The emblems for the three mandalas of Aparavajrāmṛta are to be understood from the *Aparavajrāmṛtatantra*.
13.3.8 In the mandala of the ninefold Hevajra triad, there is a fierce blue vajra upon the sun at the pericarp of a universal lotus.

In the lunar discs on the petals starting from the east and ending with the northeast, there are, in order, the [emblems] of Gaurī, Caurī, Vettālī, Ghasmarī, Pukkasī, Śabarī, Caṇḍālī, and Ḍombī: a curved knife, a skull-bowl, a tortoise, a snake, a lion, an alms-bowl, a wheel, and a vajra.
For the sixteen-armed [deity], the specific difference is a white skull-cup marked with a double-vajra upon the solar disc. Outside the circle are the vases.
13.3.9 Mahāmāyāmaṇḍala (p. 256)

In the Mahāmāyā maṇḍala, at the center of a red lotus, is the lotus vessel of the Blessed One in the form of Mahāmāyā. On the moon-discs of the petals in the east and other directions, arranged clockwise, are the symbols of Vajraḍākinī, Ratnaḍākinī, Padmaḍākinī, and Viśvaḍākinī: a vajra, a radiating jewel, a double lotus, and a sword. As for Buddhakākinī, she remains embracing Vajrasattva; therefore, there is no separate placement of her symbol. 13.3.10 Buddhakapāla Maṇḍala (p. 257)
In the mandala of the ninefold Buddhakapāla, upon the sun at the pericarp of a universal lotus, there is a hand-drum (*ḍamaru*).

On the suns of the petals in the east, north, west, south, northeast, southeast, southwest, and northwest, there are curved knives (*karttikā*) belonging to Citrasenā, Kāminī, Pātālavāsinī, Saubhadrā, Sauṇḍinī, Bhūtinī, Caturbhujā, and Ākāśavāsinī.
13.3.11 Vajrahūṃkāramaṇḍala (p. 257).

In the center of the Vajrahūṃkāra maṇḍala is the vajra of Vajrahūṃkāra. In the directions starting from the east, arranged counter-clockwise, are the vajras of Vajradaṇḍa, Analārka, Uṣṇīṣa, and Vajrakuṇḍalī. In the southeast and other directions, arranged clockwise, are the vajras of Vajrayakṣa, Vajrakāla, Mahākāla, Vajrabhīṣaṇa, Uṣṇīṣa, and Vajrapātāla. [Their respective emblems are] the vajra-hammer, the vajra-staff, the red lotus, the double vajra (viśvavajra), the hook, the axe, the trident, the sword, the wheel, and the vajra-mortar. All these symbols rest upon a sun disk atop a double lotus.

Alternatively, in the directions starting from the east, arranged clockwise, are the symbols of Yamāntaka, Prajñāntaka, Padmāntaka, and Vighnāntaka: a vajra-hammer, a white staff marked with a vajra, a red lotus, and a double vajra (*viśvavajra*). In the intermediate directions starting from the southeast, are those of Acala, Ṭakkirāja, Nīladaṇḍa, and Mahābala: a sword, a vajra, a blue staff marked with a vajra, and a staff marked with a vajra. Outside the symbol of Yamāri is the vajra of Uṣṇīṣacakrin; outside the symbol of Padmāntaka is the vajra of Sumbha. These eleven symbols rest upon sun disks on universal lotuses (*viśvājasa*).

Alternatively, there is the formidable vajra of Vighnāri. In the [directions] beginning with the southeast, there are the goad, the blue-staff marked with a vajra, the trident, and the sword of Ṭakkirāja, Nīladaṇḍa, Mahābala, and Acala, respectively. For Uṣṇīṣacakrin, there is a yellow wheel. The rest is as before. Alternatively, for the four [deities] beginning with Yamārya, there are the vajra-goad, the vajra-shackle, and the vajra-bell. The rest is as before. 13.3.12 Saṃvaramaṇḍala (p. 259)

In the Saṃvara maṇḍala, upon the sun situated on the pericarp of a universal lotus, is the blue, fierce five-pronged vajra of Śrī Saṃvara; on the petals of the four cardinal directions are the flaying knives of Ḍākinī, Lāmā, Khaṇḍarohā, and Rūpiṇī; and on the petals of the intermediate corners are lotus bowls.

On the spokes of the first wheel of the twenty-four minds, there are the knives of Pracaṇḍā, Caṇḍākṣī, Prabhāvatī, Mahānāsā, Vīramatī, Kharvarī, Laṅkeśvarī, Drumacchāyā, Airāvatī, Mahābhairavā, Vāyuvegā, Surābhakṣī, Śyāmādevī, Subhadrā, Hayakarṇā, Khagānanā, Cakravegā, Khaṇḍarohā, Śauṇḍinī, Cakravarmiṇī, Suvīrā, Mahābalā, Cakravartinī, and Mahāvīryā. Because the heroes are subordinate, their emblems are not depicted.

At the gates are Kākāsyā, Ulūkāsyā, Śvānāsyā, and Sūkarāsyā; in the corners are Yamadāḍhī, Yamadūtī, Yamadaṃṣṭrī, and Yamamathanī. Upon the sun-mandorcas of the universal lotuses are the curved knives (*karttikā*). Here, the placement of the symbols is performed by moving counter-clockwise in the cardinal directions starting from the east, and clockwise in the intermediate directions starting from the southeast. Outside the circular line, one should draw the vases based on the corners. Regarding the symbols in other *Saṃvara* and *Vajravārāhī* maṇḍalas, they are described in the *Niṣpannayogāvalī*.
13.3.13 The Buddhakapāla Maṇḍala (p. 261)
In the center of the twenty-five-fold *Buddhakapāla* maṇḍala, upon a sun disk on a universal lotus, is a hand-drum (*ḍamaru*).

The twenty-four goddesses hold curved knives (*karttikā*). These are arranged counter-clockwise in the cardinal directions starting from the east, and clockwise in the intermediate directions starting from the southeast. Therein, above a black wheel, there are skull-cups in the cardinal petals for Sumālinī, Kapālinī, Bhīmā, and Sudurjayā, while in the intermediate petals there are skulls. Beyond that is a circle of blue vajras.

In the second enclosure, upon eight red lotuses situated on an eight-spoked wheel, there are [the goddesses] Śubhamekhalā, Rūpiṇī, Vijayā, and Kāriṇī in the cardinal directions, and Kālinī, Mahodadhi, Kāriṇī, and Māraṇī in the intermediate directions. Then follows a garland of red vajras. In the third enclosure, upon eight white lotuses situated on an eight-spoked wheel, there are Tāriṇī, Bhīmadarśanā, Sudarśanā, and Ajayā in the cardinal directions, and Śubhā, Astārakī, Kālarātrī, and Mahāyaśas in the intermediate directions. Then follows a garland of white vajras. In the lotuses at the gates are Sundarī, Vasundarā, Subhagā, and Priyadarśanā.
They maintain that there are twenty suns above the lotuses, each bearing a curved knife.
In the Yogāmbaramaṇḍala,
within the mandala, upon a moon disc atop a universal lotus, is the blue five-pronged vajra of the Lord of the Mandala.

In the compartments facing east, north, and west, there are skull-topped staffs (*khaṭvāṅga*) resting upon lotus-suns. In the compartments starting from the northeast (*īśāna*) and southeast (*āgneya*), there are skull-topped staffs, goads (*aṅkuśa*), ribbons (*parśu*), and clubs (*daṇḍa*). Outside the skull-topped staffs in the compartments starting from the east, there are, in order: two hands with palms joined and cast forward, a handful of blood (*rudhirāñjali*), and a mace (*muṣala*). These emblems, such as the skull-topped staff, rest upon lotus-suns.

Outside the circle of light rays, there are three skull-cups of nectar in the eastern direction; three skull-cups of lamps in the north; three skull-cups of offerings (*bali*) in the west; and three skull-cups of drinks in the south. In the northeast is a hand holding a *garva* [flower] and a perfume vessel; in the southeast, a lute and a flower basket; in the southwest, a hand making the threatening gesture (*tarjanī*) and an incense burner; and in the northwest, hands joined in *añjali* and a lamp.

Then, outside the circle of the vajra-fence, there are twenty-four *khaṭvāṅgas*—four on each of the plinths in the east and other directions, and eight at the corners of the gates. These, such as the skull-cups of nectar and so forth, rest upon lotuses and sun disks.
13.3.15 Yamārimaṇḍala (p.264):
In the Yamārimaṇḍala, in the center of the altar of the universal vajra (*viśvavajra*), is the dark blue, fierce five-pronged vajra of the Blessed Lord Yamāri.

At the roots of the spokes in the east, south, and so forth, are the white eight-spoked wheel, the nine-segmented green jewel, the red eight-petalled lotus, and the dark blue sword of Śāśvata, Ratneśa, Amitābha, and Amoghasiddhi, respectively.
In the corners starting from the southeast and southwest are the wheel, vajra, lotus, and sword of Vajracarcikā, Vajravārāhī, Sarasvatī, and Gaurī, who reside within the universal vajra.

Then there is a garland of vajras, and then five spokes of a double-vajra (*viśvavajra*) in each intermediate direction. At the gates in the east, south, and so forth, there are the mallet of Yamāntaka, the staff of Yamāntaka, the lotus of Padmāntaka, and the sword of Khaḍgāntaka; [their emblems are] a mallet marked with a twenty-spoked vajra, a white staff, a red lotus, and a sword.

Here, the symbols of Śāśvata and the goddesses are situated upon the moon, while those of the others are situated upon the sun. Upon the discs of the sun and moon are double-lotuses (*viśvapadma*). In the corners of the mandala are four skull-cups resting on lotuses. On the sides of the spokes are vases. 13.3.16 Vajratārāmaṇḍala (p. 265)
In the Vajratārā maṇḍala, upon a moon at the center of a variegated lotus, there is a nine-pronged golden vajra.

On the moon-discs of the petals starting from the east and south, there are a flower garland, an incense branch, a lamp branch, and a scent conch, belonging respectively to Puṣpatārā, Dhūpatārā, Dīpatārā, and Gandhatārā.
On the petals starting from the southeast, there are a wheel, a vajra, a lotus, and a sword, representing the purity of Śāśvata, Akṣobhya, Amitābha, and Amoghasiddhi.

In the eastern, southern, and other gates, upon universal lotuses and sun disks, are the goads and so forth of Vajrāṅkuśī, Vajrapāśī, Vajrasphoṭā, and Vajraghaṇṭā, as before. Outside Vajrāṅkuśī, on a universal lotus and sun disk, is the wheel of Uṣṇīṣavijayā. Outside Vajrasphoṭā, on a universal lotus and sun disk, is the serpent-noose of Sumbhā. In the lotuses of the fire and other corners, through the purification of Locanā, Māmakī, Pāṇḍarā, and Tārā, there are the bodhicitta jar, Mount Meru, the fire pit, and the great banner. Outside the lotuses are the vases. 13.3.17 Mārīcīmaṇḍala (p. 266)

In the Mārīcī maṇḍala, there is an arrow upon a moon or a sun disk at the center of a double-petaled lotus (*viśvājña*). For the goddess moves about by night when stationed on the moon, and by day when stationed on the sun, in the directions such as east and south. In the cardinal directions—east, south, west, and north—the symbols are, respectively: *arkam asi*, *markam asi*, *antardhānam asi*, and *tejom asi*; these correspond to the needle, the needle with its thread, the young *aśoka* leaf, and the arrow. In the intermediate directions—south-east, south-west, etc.—the symbols for *udayam asi*, *gulmam asi*, *vanam asi*, and *cīvaram asi* are, respectively, the same as the symbols for *arkam asi* and the others.

On the outer enclosure, on the frieze: in the east, for Mahācīvaramasi and Varāhamukhī, there are two vajra-hooks (vajrāṅkuśa); in the south, for Padākramasi and Varaledevī, there are two aśoka shoots; in the west, for Parākramasi and Vadaledevī, there are two arrows; in the north, for Ūrmamasi and Varālidevī, there are two needles. In the intermediate directions beginning with the southeast, for Vattāli, Vadāli, Varāli, and Varāhamukhī, there are a needle with thread, a needle, an aśoka shoot, and an arrow. At the eastern gate, for Ālodevī, there is a vajra-hook; at the southern [gate], for Tālodevī, there is a vajra-noose.
In the west is Vajrasphoṭa with the goddess Kālodevī; in the north is Vajrāveśa with the goddess Satsalosambamūrdhatidevī.
Here, the emblems of the female gatekeepers are upon lotus-suns, while those of the others are upon lotus-moons.
(Pañcarakṣāmaṇḍala, p. 268)

In the center of the maṇḍala of the Five Protectors (Pañcarakṣā), upon a moon on a double lotus (*viśvājja*), is the jewel-spray of Mahāpratisarā; upon a moon on a double lotus in the east, the wheel of Mahāsāhasrapramardanī; upon a sun on a double lotus in the south, the vajra of Mahāmantrānusāriṇī; upon a sun on a double lotus in the west, the lotus of Mahāśītavatī; and upon a moon on a double lotus in the north, the peacock feather of Mahāmāyūrī. In the second enclosure, in the corners starting from the southeast, are a conch, a banner marked with a vajra, an axe, and a trident. On the headbands of Kālī, Kālarātrī, Kālakarṇī, and Śvetā, there are vases.
At the eastern and other gates, upon the suns of the universal lotuses, are the four [implements] of Vajrāṅkuśī and the others, beginning with the vajra-hook.
13.3.19 Vajradhātumaṇḍala (p.269):
In the Vajradhātumaṇḍala, upon the moon at the pericarp of the universal lotus, is the white five-pronged vajra of the Blessed One Vajradhātu.

On the moon-discs at the cardinal and intermediate directions of the lotus petals, proceeding clockwise in order, are the five-pronged white and red vajra of Sattvavajrī; the five-pronged vajra with a crest-jewel of Ratnavajrī; the eight-petalled white and red lotus marked with a five-pronged vajra of Dharmavajrī; and the crossed-vajra (viśvavajra) in the colors of the five Tathāgatas of Karmavajrī. On the moon-mandalas at the pericarps of the lotuses in the east and other directions, in order, are the blue five-pronged vajra of Akṣobhya; the vajra-jewel of Ratnasambhava; the lotus of Amitābha; and the viśvavajra of Amoghasiddhi.

Upon the moon-disks at the petals of the eastern and other directions of Akṣobhya’s lotus are, in order, the five-pronged vajra, the vajra-hook, the arrow, and the vajra of Vajrasattva, Vajrarāja, Vajrarāga, and Vajrasādhu. Upon the lotus of Ratnasambhava are the blue five-pronged vajra marked with two [others], the jewel-garland, the sun, the wish-fulfilling jewel banner, and the vajra joined with a row of *dha* syllables, belonging to Vajraratna, Vajratejas, Vajraketu, and Vajrahāsa.

For Amitābha, Vajradharma, Vajratīkṣṇa, Vajrahetu, and Vajrabhāṣa, [the symbols are] a red lotus, a sword, an eight-spoked wheel, and a single-pronged vajra tongue. For Amoghasiddhi, Vajrakarma, Vajrarakṣa, Vajrayakṣa, and Vajrasandhi, [the symbols are] a crossed vajra (*viśvavajra*), a vajra armor, a vajra-marked fang, and a five-pronged thunderbolt (*kuliśa*). For Akṣobhya and the others, each third bodhisattva symbol should be drawn on the northern petal, while the fourth symbol should be drawn on the western petal.

In the moon disks at the centers of the lotuses starting from the southeast, there are [the hand-symbols] of Vajralāsyā, Vajramālā, Vajragītā, and Vajranṛtyā: a vajra, a jewel-garland, a lute, and a vajra.

Outside the womb-chamber (garbhakūṭāgāra), on the frieze (paṭṭikā): in the east, upon lotuses and moons, are five-pronged vajras for Maitreya, Amoghadarśin, Sarvāpāyañjaha, and Sarvaśokatamonirghātamati; in the south, upon lotuses and moons, are vajra-jewels for Gandhahastin, Śūraṅgama, Gaganagañja, and Jñānaketu; in the west, upon lotuses and moons, are vajra-lotuses for Amitaprabha, Candraprabha, Bhadrapāla, and Jālinīprabha.
In the north, upon lotus-moons, are the double-vajras (*viśvavajra*) of Vajragarbha, Akṣayamati, Pratibhānakūṭa, and Samantabhadra.
In the corners of the outer maṇḍala, beginning with the southeast, upon lotus-moons are the symbols of Vajradhūpā, Vajrapuṣpā, Vajrālokā, and Vajragandhā, as previously described.
On the moon-lotuses at the gates in the east and other directions are the symbols of Vajrāṅkuśa, Vajrapāśa, Vajrasphoṭa, and Vajrāveśa.
On the strips are the vases.

13.3.20 Mañjuvajramaṇḍala (p. 272): In the Mañjuvajramaṇḍala consisting of forty-three deities, the outer maṇḍala has five walls—blue, red, white, green, and yellow—and all the ground areas for the directions starting from the east and the center. In the second maṇḍala, there are three walls: blue, white, and yellow. In the third circle, there is one white wall.
There, upon a moon disc on a double lotus in the yellow middle square, is Mañjuśrī with a yellow fist and a sword.

On the sun discs in the eastern and other squares are the blue vajra, the jewel, the white lotus, and the sword of Akṣobhya, Ratnasambhava, Amitābha, and Amoghasiddhi, respectively. On the moon discs in the northeast and other squares are the yellow vajra, the blue vajra, the white vajra, and the green vajra of Locanā, Māmakī, Pāṇḍarā, and Tārā.

In the second enclosure circle, in the directions starting from the east, upon the moons are the emblems of Sattvavajrī, Ratnavajrī, Dharmavajrī, and Karmavajrī, which are like those of Akṣobhya and the others. In the moons of the corners starting from the northeast are the sword, the yellow jewel, the white vajra, and the green vajra-chain of Cundā, Ratnolkā, Bhṛkuṭī, and Vajraśṛṅkhalā, respectively.

In the third enclosure circle, on the eastern moons, [the emblems] of Maitreya, Mañjuśrī, Gandhahasti, and Jñānaketu are a sword with flowers, nāgakeśara blossoms, and sprouts; a vase containing an elephant’s trunk; and a yellow cintāmaṇi jewel. On the southern moons, [the emblems] of Bhadrapāla, Sāgaramati, Akṣayamati, and Pratibhānakūṭa are arrows that are red, white, yellow, and green.

In the western [direction], for Mahāsthāmaprāpta, Sarvāpāyañjaha, Sarvaśokatamonirghātamati, and Jālinīprabha, there are a white lotus, a white arrow, a yellow arrow, and a sun resting upon a red lotus. In the northern [direction], for Candraprabha, Amitaprabha, Gaganagañja, and Sarvanivaraṇaviṣkambhin, there are a moon resting upon a blue lotus, a red flask, a yellow arrow, and a blue arrow.
And here, in sequence, on the two sides of the doors starting from the east, there are two symbols each upon the frieze.

In the suns at the eastern and other gates are Yamāntaka, Aparājita, Hayagrīva, and Amṛtakuṇḍalī; their [symbols] are a black fist-sword, a yellow vajra, a red vajra-staff, and a blue fist-sword. In the suns of the corners beginning with the northeast are Acala, Ṭakkirāja, Nīladaṇḍa, and Mahābala; their [symbols] are a sword, a blue vajra, a blue vajra-staff, and a blue vajra-staff. Outside the symbol of Yamāntaka, on the sun, is the sword of Sumbha. Outside the symbol of Hayagrīva, on the sun, is the vajra-hook of Vajrapātāla.

Below all the suns and moons are universal lotuses; on the bands are vases. Some, however, say that outside the symbols of Yamāri and Āri there is the wheel of Uṣṇīṣacakrin upon the sun, and outside of that, the sword of Sumbha.
13.3.21 Dharmadhātuvāgīśvaramaṇḍala 13.3.21.1 (p. 276)
In the Dharmadhātuvāgīśvara maṇḍala, the inner wheel is to be filled with white colors; the rest is as before.
In the center of the middle maṇḍala, upon the pericarp of a double lotus, is Mañjughoṣa’s yellow fist-hilted sword.

On the petals of the east and so forth, starting from the northeast and proceeding clockwise, are the yellow wheels of the eight Uṣṇīṣas: Mahoṣṇīṣa, Tejorāśi, Sitātapatra, Vijayoṣṇīṣa, Vikiraṇa, Udgata, Mahodgata, and Jaya.

In the center of the eastern square, upon a double-lotus and sun disk, is the blue vajra of Akṣobhya. In the intermediate directions starting from the northeast, upon double-lotus and moon disks, are the vajras of Vajrasattva, Vajrarāja, Vajrarāga, and Vajrasādhu—namely, a vajra, a vajra-hook, an arrow, and a vajra.

In the center of the southern compartment is the yellow wish-fulfilling jewel banner (*cintāmaṇidhvaja*) of Ratnasambhava, upon a double-vajra marked with five śukas. In the intermediate directions starting from the northeast, upon double-lotuses and moons, are the [symbols] of Vajraratna, Vajrasūrya, Vajraketu, and Vajrahāsa: a jewel garland marked with two white double-vajras, a sun-maṇḍala, a wish-fulfilling jewel banner, and a double-vajra joined with rows of teeth.

In the center of the western cell, upon a sun disc on a *viśvābja*, is the red lotus of Amitābha. In the intermediate directions starting from the northeast, upon *viśvābja* moons, are the lotus, sword, Dharma-wheel, and single-pronged vajra-tongue of Vajradharma, Vajratīkṣṇa, Vajrahetu, and Vajrabhāṣa respectively. In the center of the northern cell, upon a sun disc on a *viśvābja*, is the sword of Amoghasiddhi. In the intermediate directions starting from the northeast, upon *viśvābja* moons, are the three-pronged vajra, vajra-armour, vajra-claw, and five-pronged thunderbolt of Vajrakarma, Vajrarakṣa, Vajrayakṣa, and Vajrasandhi respectively.

In the moon-discs upon the lotuses in the corner cells starting from the northeast, there are the emblems of Locanā, Māmakī, Pāṇḍarā, and Tārā, which are identical to the emblems of Mañjughoṣa, Akṣobhya, Amitābha, and Amoghasiddhi.

In the sun-discs upon the variegated lotuses at the gates starting from the east, there are the vajra-hook, vajra-noose, vajra-chain, and vajra-entry, which are the respective emblems of Vajrāṅkuśa and the others.

From this central maṇḍala, in the second maṇḍala in the eastern direction, upon universal lotuses and moons, there are, in clockwise order, the symbols for the twelve stages—*adhimukti-caryā*, *pramuditā*, *vimalā*, *prabhākarī*, *arciṣmatī*, *sudurjayā*, *abhimukhī*, *dūraṅgamā*, *acalā*, *sādhumatī*, *dharmameghā*, and *samantaprabhā*—namely: a red lotus, a wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*), a white lotus, a sun disc upon a universal lotus, a blue lotus (*utpala*), an emerald gem, and a book of the *Prajñāpāramitā* upon a lotus.

Above a universal lotus is a universal vajra; upon a moon disc on a lotus with its stalk stands a five-pronged red vajra. Above a blue lotus is a sword, a volume of the Prajñāpāramitā surrounded by the Dharmamegha clouds, and the image of a Perfectly Awakened One seated upon a lotus.

In the south, upon twelve lotuses and moons, for the twelve [Bodhisattvas] of the Ratna family—Ratnapadma-pāramitā, Dāna, Śīla, Kṣānti, Vīrya, Dhyāna, Prajñā, Upāya, Praṇidhāna, Bala, Jñāna, and Vajrakarma-pāramitā—the symbols are, respectively: a moon disc upon a lotus; a cluster of various grains and jewels with sprouts; an *aśoka* flower-cluster; a white lotus; a blue lotus (*utpala*); a white lotus; a book of the *Prajñāpāramitā* resting on a lotus; a vajra resting on a yellow lotus; a sword resting on an *utpala*; a book of the *Prajñāpāramitā*;
a vine of the Bodhi tree adorned with various jewels and fruits; and a double-vajra (*viśvavajra*) resting on an *utpala*.

In the west, upon a universal lotus and moon discs, for the twelve [Bodhisattvas]—[representing] mastery over life, mind, requisites, karma, rebirth, supernatural powers, resolve, vows, knowledge, and the Dharma, as well as suchness and the awakening of a Buddha—their respective symbols are: a Buddha image in the *samādhi-mudrā* resting on a ruby (*padmarāga*), a five-pronged red vajra, a wish-fulfilling jewel banner, a crossed vajra (*viśvavajra*), a creeper of various colors and species, a sun and moon disc resting on a lotus, a cluster of *priyaṅgu* flowers, a blue lotus (*nīlotpala*), and a sword resting on a lotus.
A *bhadraghaṭa* (auspicious jar) resting on a lotus, a white lotus, and a five-pronged vajra resting on a yellow lotus;

In the north, upon a universal lotus and moon, are the twelve *dhāraṇīs*: Vasumatī, Ratnolkā, Uṣṇīṣavijayā, Mārīcī, Parṇaśabarī, Jāṅgulī, Anantamukhā, Cundā, Prajñāvardhanī, Sarvakarmāvaraṇaviśodhanī, Akṣayajñānakaraṇḍā, and Sarvabuddhadharmakośavatī; [their respective emblems are] a cluster of grain, a wish-fulfilling jewel banner, a vase of moonstone, a needle with thread, a peacock-feather brush, a cluster of poisonous flowers, and a vase of inexhaustible great treasure upon a red lotus and human head.

[The central deities hold] a water-pot suspended from a cord, a sword upon a blue lotus, a white and red lotus marked with a three-pronged vajra, and a jewel casket; [and they hold] a chest of various jewels resting on a lotus. In the sun-discs upon the lotuses at the eastern and other gates are Vajrāṅkuśa, Ratnapāśa, Śṛṅkhalā marked with lotuses at both ends, and Ghaṇṭā marked with a three-pronged vajra—representing the analytical knowledges of phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*), meaning (*arthapratisaṃvid*), etymology (*niruktipratisaṃvid*), and eloquence (*pratibhānapratisaṃvid*). In the corners starting from the southeast are Lāsyā, Mālā, Gītā, and Nṛtyā, holding a vajra, a jewel garland, a lute, and a vajra-drum.

In the third maṇḍala, upon lotus-moons in the eastern direction, there is for Samantabhadra a sword resting on an *utpala* lily; for Akṣayamati, a sword; for Kṣitigarbha, a wish-fulfilling tree (*kalpavṛkṣa*) resting on a lotus; and for Ākāśagarbha, a jewel. In the south, for Gaganagañja, a wish-granting gem (*cintāmaṇi*); for Ratnapāṇi, a jewel; for Sāgaramati, a conch shell; and for Vajragarbha, a vajra. In the west, for Avalokiteśvara, a lotus; and for Mahāsthāmaprāpta, a sword.

Candraprabha’s [emblem] is a vajra-wheel; Jālinīprabha’s is a sword. In the north, upon lotuses and moons, are those of Amitaprabha, Pratibhānakūṭa, Sarvaśokatamonirghātamati, and Sarvanivaraṇaviṣkambhin: a double lotus, a sword resting on a lotus, a five-pronged vajra, and a sword.

In the suns upon the lotuses at the eastern and other gates are the goad, noose, chain, and bell of Yamāntaka, Prajñāntaka, Padmāntaka, and Vighnāntaka. In the suns upon the variegated lotuses in the corners beginning with the northeast are the sword, vajra, vajra, and double-vajra of Trailokyavijaya, Vajrajvālānalārka, Hetuvajra, and Paramāśva. Outside the symbol of Yamāntaka is the yellow wheel of Uṣṇīṣacakrin; outside the symbol of Padmāntaka is the vajra of Sumbha.

Outside the four symbols, such as Trailokyavijaya and the others, one should draw a line within the corners of the third maṇḍala itself. In the positions outside that [line], on the lotuses and moons situated on the right side of the corner-lines starting from the southeast, there should be a flower-basket for flowers, an incense burner for incense, a jeweled lamp-stick for lamps, and a conch for perfumes. On the lotuses and moons situated on the left side, there should be a mirror for Vajrarūpa, a vajra-lute for Vajraśabda, a vessel of nectar for Vajrarasa, and a multicolored cloth for Vajrasparśa.

In the outer Vajra-family maṇḍala, upon the lotuses in the cardinal directions starting from the east, are the vajra, the black staff, the snake-noose, and the goad, belonging respectively to Indra, Yama, Varuṇa, and Kubera. In the intermediate directions starting from the northeast, are the trident, the sacrificial ladle, the sword, and the wind-banner, belonging to Īśāna, Agni, Nairṛti, and Vāyu. Then, outside and near Īśāna, beginning from the northeastern direction, the emblems are to be drawn in sequence: there, the rosary of Brahmā, the discus of Viṣṇu, the trident of Maheśvara, and the spear of Kārtikeya.

The rosary of Brahmāṇī; the trident of Rudrāṇī; the discus of Vaiṣṇavī; the spear of Kaumāryā; the thunderbolt of Indrāṇī; the Rohita fish of Vārāhī; the knife of Cāmuṇḍā; the rosary of Bhṛṅgin; the axe of Gaṇapati; the trident of Mahākāla; and the drum of Nandikeśvara.

The [emblem] of Āditya is a solar disc resting upon a lotus; that of Candra is a lunar disc resting upon a white water-lily (kumuda); that of Maṅgala is a small knife (kaṭṭāra); that of Budha is an arrow; that of Bṛhaspati is a rosary; that of Śukra is a rosary; that of Śanaiścara is a black staff; that of Rāhu is the moon; that of Ketu is a serpent-noose; that of Balabhadra is a plow; that of Jayakara is a garland of flowers; that of Madhukara is a dolphin-banner (makaradhvaja); and that of Vasanta is an arrow.

There is also the gesture of the joined palms (*sampuṭāñjali*) for Ananta, Vāsuki, Takṣaka, Karkkoṭaka, Padma, Mahāpadma, Śaṅkhapāla, and Kulika; or else, their respective symbols are similar to those of their own fathers. In that regard, Ananta and Kulika are Brāhmaṇas, the sons of Agni; Vāsuki and Śaṅkhapāla are Kṣatriyas, the sons of Indra; Takṣaka and Mahāpadma are Vaiśyas, the sons of Vāyu; and Karkkoṭaka and Padma are Śūdras, the sons of Varuṇa.

The various weapons, such as swords and so forth, belong to the great lords of the asuras, beginning with Vemacitrin, Bali, Prahlāda, and Vairocana. The joined palms in the *sampuṭa* gesture belong to Garuḍendra. The lute belongs to Druma, the lord of the kinnaras; the lute belongs to Pañcaśikha, the lord of the gandharvas; and the flower garland belongs to Sarvārthasiddha, the lord of the vidyādharas. The *bījapūra* fruits belong to the yakṣas, headed by Pūrṇabhadra, Māṇibhadra, Dhanada, Vaiśravaṇa, Civikuṇḍalin, Kelimālin, Mukhendra, and Carendra. And the two *jaḍī* fruits belong to Hārītī.

The *samputāñjali* hand-gestures correspond to Aśvinī, Bharaṇī, Kṛttikā, Rohiṇī, Mṛgaśirā, Ārdrā, Punarvasu, Puṣyā, Aśleṣā, Maghā, Pūrvaphālgunī, Uttaraphālgunī, Hastā, Citrā, Svātī, Viśākhā, Anurādhā, Jyeṣṭhā, Mūlā, Pūrvāṣāḍhā, Uttarāṣāḍhā, Śravaṇā, Dhaniṣṭhā, Śatabhiṣā, Pūrvabhādrapadā, Uttarabhādrapadā, Revatī, and Abhijit.
Here too, at the gates, there are the Vajrāṅkuśa and other [mudrās]. The vases are in the fourth maṇḍala.
13.3.22 *Durgatipariśodhana-maṇḍala* (p. 288).

In the *Durgatipariśodhana* maṇḍala, within a circle of blue vajras, upon the altar of a yellow eight-spoked wheel is the yellow mudrā of the Wheel of Dharma (*dharmacakra*). On the spokes starting from the east are the white Earth-touching mudrā (*bhūsparśa*), the blue Varada mudrā, the red Dhyāna mudrā, and the green Abhaya mudrā. On the spokes starting from the southeast are the sun, the wish-fulfilling jewel banner (*cintāmaṇidhvaja*), the sword, and the parasol.

Outside the *vajrāvalī*, in the corners starting from the southeast, are the symbols of Lāsyā and the others; on the friezes starting from the east, there are two symbols to the left of each door and two to the right. Among them, [the symbols are]: a *nāgakeśara* flower, a lotus with an eye, a goad, a staff, a conch, a sword, a Dharma-treasury upon a lotus, a wish-fulfilling jewel banner, an ambrosia flask, the lunar disc upon a lotus, a jewel, a vajra-fence, a blue lotus with a vajra, an ambrosia jar, a jewel upon a lotus, and a cluster of jewels. In the corners starting from the southeast are the symbols of Puṣpā and the others. At the doors are the vajra-goad and so forth.

The thirty-seven marks are also situated upon the moon on a universal lotus; however, the marks such as the blue-throated one (*nīlakaṇṭha*) and so forth are not even drawn. 13.3.23 *Bhūtaḍāmaramaṇḍala* (p. 290):

In the *Bhūtaḍāmara* maṇḍala, there are five walls—white, yellow, red, green, and black—and the grounds starting from the east likewise. There are three lines for the cords (*sūtra*), colored white, red, and black; one cord-line is black, as are the lines for the vajra-rings. In the central square of the inner enclosure (*garbhapuṭa*), upon a moon on a universal lotus, is the five-pronged blue vajra of the Blessed One Bhūtaḍāmara.

In the east, on the sun of Maheśvara, is a trident; in the south, on the sun of Viṣṇu, is a discus; in the west, on the moon of Brahmā, is a rosary; in the north, on the sun of Kārttikeya, is a spear; in the northeast, on the moon of Gaṇapati, is an axe; in the southeast, on the sun of Ravi, is a solar disc situated upon a lotus; in the southwest, on the sun of Rāhu, is a lunar disc; and in the northwest, on the moon of Nandikeśvara, is a hand-drum.

In the second enclosure, in the directions starting from the east, [the deities] Śrītilottamā, Śaśī, and Umā rest upon moon disks; their attributes are, respectively, a white lotus, an incense burner, and a lamp-stick with hands in the *bhoga* (enjoyment) mudrā. In the southeast and other directions, Ratnaśrī, Sarasvatī, Surasundarī, and Ābhūtī likewise rest upon moon disks; their attributes are, in order, a scent-conch, a lute, a jewel garland, and a three-pronged vajra.

In the third enclosure, in the directions starting from the east, are Indra, Yama, Varuṇa, and Kubera; their emblems are a vajra on a moon, a staff marked with a skull on a sun, a nāga-noose on a moon, and a mace on a moon. In the intermediate directions starting from the southeast, are Agni, Nairṛti, Vāyu, and Candra; their emblems are a rosary on a sun, a sword on a sun, a wind-banner on a moon, and a moon-maṇḍala on a white water-lily within a moon. Near the moon-mark of Īśāna is a trident on a sun.

In the fourth enclosure, in the directions starting from the east, upon the moons of Siṃhadhvajadhāriṇī, Vibhūtī, Mahāpadmavatī, and Surahāriṇī, are the symbols: the lion-banner, the goad, the arrow, and the wish-fulfilling gem. In the [directions] starting from the northeast, upon the moons of Varahārī, Ratneśvarī, Bhūṣaṇī, and Jagatpālanī, are the symbols: the flower-basket, the incense burner, the perfume conch, and the lamp-staff.
Here, all the suns and moons are situated upon universal lotuses. The vases are in the fourth enclosure. 13.3.24 *Pañcaḍākamaṇḍala* (p. 292).

In the center of the maṇḍala of the five ḍākinīs, within the central peaked pavilion, are the curved knife and skull-cup of Hevajra with Prajñā. On the spokes in the east and other directions are the vajra-hook, noose, chain, and bell of Gaurī, Caurī, Vettālī, and Ghasmarī. In the corners starting from the northeast are the vessel of bodhicitta, Mount Meru, the fire-pit, and the great banner and flag of Pukkasī, Śabarī, Caṇḍālī, and Ḍombī.

Therefore, in the center of the eastern gabled hall (kūṭāgāra) is the peacock of Śāśvata holding a skull-cup (kapāla). At the gates in the east and other directions are those holding a pair of tongs (saṃdaṃśa), a noose (pāśa), a snare (vāgurā), and a goad (aṅkuśa); [the deities themselves] hold a pair of tongs, a noose, a snare, and a goad. In the northeast and other corners are those of Flower, Incense, Lamp, and Perfume, holding a flower-basket (puṣpakaraṇḍa), an incense burner (dhūpakaṭacchu), a lamp-stand (dīpayaṣṭi), and a conch filled with yellow perfume.

In the center of the southern gabled chamber is the bird kāraṇḍava, situated within the skull-cup of Vajrasūrya. At the eastern and other doors are Sūryahastā, Dīpā, Ratnolkā, and Taḍitkarā, whose emblems are a sun disc, a lamp-stick, a jewel, and a flash of lightning. In the northeast and other directions are Lāsyā, Mālā, Gītā, and Nṛtyā, whose emblems are a vajra, a jewel garland, a cymbal, and a vajra. In the center of the western gabled chamber is a black bear, situated within the skull-cup of Padmanarteśvara.

In the eastern and other gates are Padmā, Dharmodayā, Sphoṭā, and Svāśleṣā; their respective symbols are the lotus, the source of phenomena (dharmodayā), the sphoṭa, and the vajra. In the northeast and other directions are Vaṃśā, Vīṇā, Mukundā, and Murajā, each holding her own musical instrument. In the center of the northern maṇḍala is Paramāśva, with Mercury (Budha) situated in his skull-cup. In the eastern and other gates are Tālā, Kuñcī, Kapāṭā, and Paṭadhāriṇī; their symbols are the clapper, the key, the door-panel, and the curtain. In the northeast and other directions are Locanā, Māmakī, Pāṇḍarā, and Tārā; their symbols are the wheel, the vajra, the lotus, and the blue lotus.

At the gates of the outer great maṇḍala are the symbols of Gaurī and the others; in the [directions] beginning with the northeast are the symbols of Pukkasī and the others. All these symbols rest upon a double-lotus and a sun disk. That of Śāśvata alone rests upon a moon seat. In each subsidiary maṇḍala are vases of nectar; some say they are in the great maṇḍala itself. 13.3.25 The Maṇḍala of the Six Universal Monarchs (p. 295).

In the maṇḍala of the six universal monarchs, upon the viśvapadmas, the symbols of the Buddha-ḍākas are situated on the sun, while that of the [central] Buddha is situated on the moon; furthermore, in the corners of all six gabled pavilions, there are skull-cups resting on viśvapadmas.

Therein, in the center of the womb-maṇḍala, upon a lotus, is the vajra of Vajrasattva. On the intermediate lotuses are the hand-drums (ḍamaru) of Ḍākinī, Lāmā, Khaṇḍarohā, and Rūpiṇī. The sequence of placement here is as follows: in the doors starting from the east, proceeding counter-clockwise, and in the intermediate directions starting from the southeast, proceeding clockwise. On the lotuses at the doors are the four vajras of Khaṇḍakapāla and Pracaṇḍā, Mahākaṅkāla and Caṇḍākṣī, Kaṅkāla and Prabhāvatī, and Vikaṭadaṃṣṭrin and Mahānāsā. In the middle of the enclosure is a garland of vajras.

In the mandala of Buddhadaṅka, there is a wheel in the central lotus; in the lotuses at the gates, there are wheels for Surāvairin and Vīramatī, Amitābha and Kharvarī, Vajraprabha and Laṅkeśvarī, and Vajradeha and Drumacchāyā. In the middle of the enclosure is a circle of wheels. In the mandala of Ratnadaṅka, there is a jewel in the center; in the lotuses at the gates, there are jewels for Aṅgulika and Airāvatī, Vajrajaṭila and Mahābhairava, Mahāvīra and Vāyuvegā, and Vajrahūṃkāra and Surābhakṣī. In the middle of the enclosure is a circle of jewels.

In the center of the Padmaḍāka maṇḍala is a lotus; in the lotuses at the gates are lotuses for Subhadra and Śyāmādevī, Vajrabhadra and Subhadra, Mahābhairava and Hayakarṇa, and Virūpākṣa and Khagānanā. Within the enclosure is a garland of lotuses. In the center of the Vajraḍāka maṇḍala is a vajra; in the lotuses at the gates are vajras for Mahābala and Cakravega, Ratnavajra and Khaṇḍarohā, Hayagrīva and Śauṇḍinī, and Ākāśagarbha and Cakravarmiṇī. Within the enclosure is a garland of vajras.

In the center of the mandala of Viśvaḍāka is a double-vajra (viśvavajra). In the lotuses at the gates are double-vajras for Heruka and Suvīra, Padmanarteśvara and Mahābala, Vairocana and Cakravartinī, and Vajrasattva and Mahāvīrya. In the middle of the enclosure is a garland of double-vajras.

At the doors of the great gabled pavilion (*mahākūṭāgāra*) are the [deities] with the faces of a crow, an owl, a dog, and a pig, holding a vajra-hook, a noose, a chain, and a bell. In the corners are Yamadāḍhī, Yamadūtī, Yamadaṃṣṭrī, and Yamamathanī, with mirrors, lutes, incense burners, conch shells, vessels for flavors, and vases, as appropriate.

Thus, having been described according to their essential nature, the application of colored powders (*rajaḥpātanam*) within the other mandalas should also be understood accordingly; however, it has not been set forth here for fear of excessive prolixity.
13.3.27 Kalācakramaṇḍala 13.3.27.1 (p.299):
Regarding the Kalācakramaṇḍala, however, a sequence of powder colors is described that is for the most part dissimilar to the sequence of powder colors mentioned previously.

The entire inner ground of the mind-maṇḍala, extending as far as the second vajra-fence, is black. Of the maṇḍalas of mind, speech, and body, the eastern ground is entirely black; the southern is red; the western is yellow; and the northern is white. The altar-platform (vedī) is white; the jeweled band (ratnapaṭṭī) is red, and upon it is a variegated jeweled knot. The ground for the necklaces and half-necklaces is black; upon it, the necklaces and half-necklaces are white. On the black ground, the *bakulī* (architrave) is white. On the black ground, the stepped pediments (*kramaśīrṣa*) are white. The pillars of the archways (*toraṇa*) are yellow.

In the mind-mandala, however, the leader’s lotus is green; in rites such as pacification and the others, it becomes white and so forth. The vajra-fence and the sixteen pillars are black. They are joined with black swords in the east, red jewels in the south, yellow wheels in the west, and white lotuses in the north. The eight vases are white, resting upon lotuses, and their mouths are adorned with lotuses. In every case, the pericarp of the seat-lotus is one-third [of its size].

The second *vajrāvalī* (row of vajras) is green; the panel for the deities (*devatāpaṭṭī*) is white. There are three wall-lines starting from the inner sanctum (*garbha*), which are white, red, and black in color. Their ground consists of nine parts; there, having set aside one part, each of the two remaining parts is inlaid with lines of vajras and jewels at the junctions of the door-frames (*niryūha*). The arches (*toraṇa*) are twelve and of various colors.

In the speech-maṇḍala (*vāṅmaṇḍala*), the deity-band is white; upon it are eight lotuses devoid of moon and sun. Those in the cardinal directions are red, and those in the intermediate corners are white. From the center outward, there are five lines of green, black, red, white, and yellow. Their ground consists of fifteen parts, and upon them are lines as previously described.
In the body-maṇḍala (*kāyamaṇḍala*), the deity-band is white; upon it are lotuses devoid of moon and sun. The five lines are like those in the speech-maṇḍala. 13.3.27.2 (p. 301)

Beneath the pillars of the archways, at the locations of the altars, are the seats of the hooded serpents (*phaṇin*), each measuring twelve *mātrās*. There, in the eastern direction, are two black circles with banners above them; in the southern direction, two red triangles marked with swastikas; in the western direction, two yellow squares marked with thunderbolts (*vajra*); and in the northern direction, two white semicircles marked with lotuses.
