In the east, on the left side of the circular [mandala], is the jar of nectar belonging to the Naga king named Jaya; in the west, on the left side of the square [mandala], is the jar of nectar belonging to the one named Vijaya.

On the eastern archway of the first city, upon the *mattavāraṇa* (elephant-railing) in the central square, there is a black *dharmacakra*; to its right and left are a black male deer and female deer. To the south is a red *bhadraghaṭa* (auspicious jar); to its right and left are a red conch and a red lotus. To the west is a yellow *bodhivṛkṣa* (bodhi tree); to its right and left are a yellow *kinnara* and *kinnarī*. To the north is a white *dundubhi* (celestial drum); to its right and left are a white staff and a mallet.

Between the Kramaśīrṣa and the earth-circle, the ground is black; upon it, one should draw the articles of worship as they appear beautiful. The earth-circle is yellow; within it, in the northeast intermediate direction, is the rising full moon mandala, twelve units in size. In the southwest, the setting sun is twelve units in size. The water-circle is white. The fire-circle is red. The wind-circle is black. Between those two, the fire and wind circles, there are eight cremation-wheel spokes, each measuring twelve units.

In the cardinal directions they are red, and in the intermediate directions they are white. Outside the eastern wheel is a circle of emptiness (*śūnyamaṇḍala*), and outside the western wheel is a circle of emptiness. The drawing of these two circles of emptiness is according to the method taught in the *Sādhanapaṭala*. In all ten [directions], a severed flaying-knife (*karttikā*) is drawn. On the wind-circle (*vāyuvalaya*), various symbols are drawn; there is no arbitrary choice here. The space-circle (*ākāśavalaya*) is black. Having made its two sides three finger-widths (*mātra*) each, one should place two gnaw-marks (*ghūṇa*) there, and in the middle, at six finger-widths, a green vajra-garland (*vajrāvalī*) should be made. The flames of the rays are five-colored. 13.3.27.3 (p. 304)

Furthermore, the elevation in the center of the mandala is one-quarter of a barleycorn for the black dust in the eastern direction; two for the red in the south; four for the yellow in the west; and three for the white in the north.

The height of the wall-lines and the diamond-garlands (*vajrāvalī*) is three times the yellow powder; other lines are twice the yellow powder. The lotuses are twice the size of the bands (*paṭṭikā*); the moon and sun are twice the size of the lotus-lines. Thus, compared to the aforementioned heights, the heights in the speech-mandala (*vāṅmaṇḍala*) are double, and those in the body-mandala (*kāyamaṇḍala*) are double those. From the top of the steps to the outer worship-ground, there is one barleycorn (*yava*). In the circles of earth and so forth, as well as in the two *ghūṇa* measures, the height is according to the measurement of the wall-lines of the body-mandala.
The descent of the other dust is equal everywhere across all the levels by way of a twofold division. The triple-layered measurement of the vajra-walls is threefold.

Therein, upon the central pericarp of the leader, above mandalas that are equal to the pericarp—white, red, black, and red, representing the moon, sun, Rāhu, and the fire of time—is the blue three-pronged vajra of the Blessed One Kālacakra.

On the eastern petal is a black incense burner; on the southern, a red lamp; on the western, a yellow conch; and on the northern, a white offering. In the southeast and other intermediate directions are fly-whisks that are black, red, white, and yellow respectively. Outside of those, in the northeast is a white Dharma-conch; in the southeast, a black wish-fulfilling gem (cintāmaṇi); in the southwest, a red Dharma-gong; and in the northwest, a yellow wish-granting tree (kalpavṛkṣa).

In the second enclosure: on a white lotus and sun in the east is a black sword; on a red lotus and moon in the southeast is a blue lotus; on a white lotus and sun in the south is a nine-faceted red jewel; on a red lotus and moon in the southwest is a red lotus; on a white lotus and sun in the west is a yellow wheel; on a red lotus and moon in the northwest is a yellow wheel; on a white lotus and sun in the north is a white lotus; and on a red lotus and moon in the northeast is a white water-lily.

In the third enclosure, on the frieze, there are eight lotuses—two on each side at every door. Among these, six contain sun discs. On the left of the western and northern doors are two moon discs; in the four corner lotuses are four moon discs. Starting from the northeast (Īśāna), [the objects] are: a mirror, a vajra, a sword, a garment, a vajra-jewel, a vessel of nectar, the source of phenomena (dharmodayā), a wheel, a fragrant conch, and a lute and a lotus. Their colors are white, black, black, black, green, red, red, green, yellow, yellow, blue, and white.
At the eastern gate, on a lotus and sun disk, is a black sword; at the southern, a red staff; at the western, a yellow lotus; and at the northern, a white mallet.
Here, the sun disks are situated upon white lotuses, and the moon disks are situated upon red lotuses.

On the eastern altar, to the left of the base of the archway pillar, is a black conch; to the right, a garland of blue flowers. On the southern [altar], a red incense burner and a lamp. On the western [altar], a yellow crown and a yellow necklace. On the northern [altar], a white fruit and a white vessel filled with nectar (*pīyūṣa*). On all the altars, however, are various goddesses of offerings (*dhāraṇī-pūjā-devīs*). At the position of the offering goddess on the eastern archway, there is a cloth in the center; on the southern, a lotus; on the western, a drum (*paṭaha*); and on the northern, a vajra. 13.3.27.5 (p. 308)

In the mandala of speech, however, there are black flaying knives upon the pericarp and petals of the eastern lotus; black wheels in the southeast; red staffs in the south; red spears in the southwest; yellow vajras in the west; yellow Brahma-staffs and suns in the northwest; white tridents in the north; and white lotuses in the northeast.

On the band of the body-maṇḍala, there are emblems upon the petals of the lotus pericarp. There, to the right of the eastern gate, are swords; in the southeast, wish-fulfilling trees (kalpavṛkṣas). To the left of the southern gate, are staffs marked with vajras; to the right, are spears (śaktis). In the southwest, there are spears or javelins (kuntas). To the left of the western gate, are jewels or maces (gadās); to the right, are vajras. In the northwest, are needles. To the left of the northern gate, are tridents (triśūlas); to the right, are nooses (pāśas). In the northeast, are axes; to the left of the eastern gate, are wheels (cakras).
At the eastern gate is a staff; outside of that, a blue trident. At the northern gate is a white mace. These symbols, such as the staff and the rest, are situated upon lotus-suns.

In the cardinal directions of the speech and body maṇḍalas, the lotuses are red, while the corner lotuses are white. Here, on the altar of the speech maṇḍala, to the right of the eastern door, there are black blue lotuses, a cloth, a knife, a wheel, and a khaṭvāṅga; to the left, there are black knives, swords, and small knives. To the right of the southern door, there are red lotuses, a vessel of nectar, a staff, a spear, and lotuses; to the left, there are red arrows, ribs, and small knives.

To the right of the western door are yellow [symbols]: a wheel, fragrance, a conch, a vajra, a needle, and wheels. To the left are green *dharmodayās*, wheels, and curved knives, all yellow. To the right of the northern door are white [symbols]: an utpala lotus, a mirror, a trident, and a lotus-utpala. To the left are blue lutes, mallets, and curved knives, all white. Thus, these thirty-six symbols are also placed upon the altars of the body-maṇḍala. 13.4 (p.310)

Then, having recognized that the drawn mandala of Mañjuvajra or any other [deity] has become perfectly clear in all its aspects, one should smear the area outside the mandala with water scented with the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) over which the *hūṃ*-syllable and the *kuṇḍalinī* have been recited. Having sprinkled the wheel (*cakra*) with that same consecrated water, one should release the remaining colored powders (*rajas*) with the mantra "Oṃ āḥ hūṃ vajra muḥ," thereby dismissing the gnosis-powders (*jñānarajas*), and place the powder-vessels in a secluded spot. This is the procedure for the deposition of the powders.
14. The Procedure for the Deposition of the Vases (Kalaśanyāsavidhi) 14.1 (p. 311)

Thereafter, one should place the previously consecrated vases in a clockwise direction. Among them, having caused the *vijaya* vase of the Lord of the Mandala to circumambulate the mandala circle, one should place it slightly to the south in the position facing the eastern gate of the mandala, outside the perimeter of the vajra-fence, the circular rim, and the garland of flames of the earth. On the left side, in order and clockwise, are the vases of Vairocana, Locanā, and Sārvakarmika; on the right are those of Rūpavajrā, Dharmadhātuvajrā, and Yamāri. To the left of the southern [gate] are those of Ratnasambhava and Māmakī.

In the right [corner] are Śabdavajrā and Prajñāntaka; in the left of the western [corner] are Amitābha and Pāṇḍarā; in the right [corner] are Gandhavajrā and Padmāntaka; in the left of the northern [corner] are Amoghasiddhi and Tārā; and in the right [corner] are Rasavajrā, Sparśavajrā, and Vighnāri.

Some say that the Yamās and so forth are in the corners starting from the southeast; others say that immediately after the Tathāgatas, the Krodhas and the Mothers of the families are in the right sides of the doors. Following this, the placement in other positions may be inferred. There is also another opinion—what is the use of it? Thus is the placement in the Mañjuvajra Maṇḍala. 14.2 (p. 312)

In the Piṇḍīkrama maṇḍala, immediately after the Kula [deities] on the left, and first on the right, are the eight Bodhisattvas; in the corners are the Corner-Krodhas, following Yamāri, then Uṣṇīṣacakrin, and following Padmāntaka, Sumbha—this is the distinction. Following this method, the placement of the vases (ghaṭanyāsa) in other maṇḍalas is easy to understand and thus has not been elaborated upon. In the four corner vases, there are four stalks with wings; they are to be placed with the mantra: *oṃ vajrayakṣa hūṃ*.

Furthermore, outside the Kālacakra dust mandala, there are four vases in the directions starting from the east; in the east, there is also a fifth, the Jaya vase. Above that is the Vijaya vase, and the conch is the sixth—this is according to the system of five jars. According to the system of ten jars, however, there are eight jars in the eight directions. Outside the western jar, at a distance of two finger-breadths, is the Vijaya vase.

Outside the eastern jar, at a distance of two finger-breadths, is the *jayakalaśa*; above that is the *mahāvijayakalaśa*, and the conch is the eleventh. Thus, even among the hundred-thousand jars, there is the *mahāvijayaśaṅkha*. This is the procedure for the placement of the jars for pacification (*śānti*), nourishment (*puṣṭi*), and all ritual sequences (*sarvakarma*).
15. The Procedure for Accomplishing the Mandala with its Retinue, 15.1 (p. 314)

Then, outside the mandala in the four directions, the fourfold collection of the true Dharma, beginning with the Noble Prajñāpāramitā, should be recited. Eight incense burners should be placed there, filled with camphor, agallochum, frankincense, and so forth. Having placed one thousand pieces of variegated cloth—or one for each deity, or according to one's capacity—into baskets and the like, and having consecrated the parasols, banners, and flags with the *hūṃ* syllable and the presiding mantra, one should offer them with the mantra *oṃ vajra sphara khaṃ* and arrange them in their respective places.
[He should prepare] archways with fine cloths, along with bells and chowries, full vases, and plantain pillars with leaves.

Having bathed, his body anointed with fragrance, wearing an upper garment, a turban, and ornaments, he should sprinkle the mandala with water consecrated by the *kuṇḍalī* mantra and protect it with the three-syllable mantra and the *kuṇḍalī* mantra. Holding a vajra and a vajra-bell, he sits near the eastern gate facing west; being the very essence of the Lord of the Mandala (*cakreśa*), he instantly perceives the drawn mandala as having the nature of the mandala to be meditated upon—following emptiness and surrounded by the ritual procedures for the protection wheel, the pinning of obstacles, and so forth.
Having obtained a sixteen-year-old woman of radiant beauty,
and having covered her with perfumes and flowers, one should desire her in the midst of that [mandala].
Having empowered that girdle of Māmakī’s qualities, the wise one should create the gentle state of Buddhahood, adorned by the realm of space.

Thus, according to the teaching: having brought forth the *jñānacakra* by means of the union with an external *mudrā* as previously established, or in its absence, by means of the union with a *jñānamudrā*, and having caused it to enter within oneself preceded by the offering of water for the feet (*pādya*) and the guest-offering (*argha*) through the sound of the rising melody of passion; and having contemplated that it has dissolved into a state of great passion (*mahārāga*), emerged via the path of the *vajra*, and having pervaded the lotus in the form of the circle of wisdom-deities (*jñānadevatācakra*), it has entered the *samayacakra* in its respective places—thereafter, following the consecration of the eyes, body, and so forth.

Having been consecrated by the Tathāgatas and goddesses drawn forth by the rays of light from the seed-syllable in one’s own heart, one should seal [the deity] according to the appropriate application; however, for those whose family is unknown, one should seal them with Akṣobhya or Vajrasattva.

Thereafter, having performed worship with a mental offering (*manomayapūjā*) by means of the emanated goddesses, one should present a pair of garments from Śīlalikā, a canopy with hanging cloths, offerings such as food, drink, what is licked, what is sucked, and what is swallowed consecrated with the three syllables, and [images of] a golden maiden, elephants, horses, and cattle; then, having worshipped with their respective offerings by means of the sixteen, eight, or four external yoginīs in the form of Rūpavajrā and the others, while ringing the bell, one should praise [the deities] with "Akṣobhyavajra... and so forth, for oneself and for one's consort (*prajñā*).

Having cast the *bodhicitta* together with flowers into a lotus vessel, having consecrated it as nectar (*amṛta*), and having offered it, one should satisfy [the deities] with the taste of that nectar, resolve upon the state consisting of great bliss (*mahāsukha*), and recite the mantra of the Lord of the Mandala one hundred and eight times, the mantras of the other maṇḍala-deities twenty-one times, and the hundred-syllable mantra.

One should offer the *sārvabhautika* (all-beings) bali according to the procedure to be described. If possible, having established the assistant (*uttarasādhaka*) within the mandala and having gone outside, one should offer the bali to one's own chosen deities, such as Indra and others, in the directions starting with the east, according to the procedure for the *sārvabhautika* bali to be described.

Then, having turned the right hand palm upward, one should hold the middle and ring fingers slightly bent and directed forward. Placing the hands with their tips between the knees while sitting in the *utkuṭuka* posture, one should silently rub the face many times with the hollow of the palms. Then, twice or thrice, one should touch the openings of the ears, the eyes, the mouth, the arms, the navel, and the head; thus one should perform the ritual of ritual sipping (*upasparśana*).

If that occurs, one should perform a *śāntika* (pacifying) and *pauṣṭika* (prosperity-bestowing) fire offering (*homa*) to pacify defects such as deficiencies and to master the mandala; then, being endowed with the Trailokyavijaya yoga, one takes a garland of flowers and recites: *oṃ sumbha nisumbha hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ / oṃ gṛhṇa gṛhṇa hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ / oṃ gṛhnāpaya gṛhnāpaya hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ / oṃ ānaya ho bhagavan vidyārāja hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*.

Thus, reciting the Trailokyavijaya mantra as taught in the *Śrīsampuṭa*, one should enter the maṇḍala with vajra-speed, brandishing the vajra, ringing the bell, and likewise [treading] with the vajra-step while reciting: *oṃ hūṃ phaṭ*; *oṃ hūṃ āḥ phaṭ*; *oṃ hūṃ āḥ āḥ āḥ phaṭ*.

Reciting the four mantras in sequence—*oṃ hūṃ hana māraya duṣṭān ghāṭaya ghāṭaya aḥ aḥ hūṃ hrīṃ phaṭ*—the preceptors at the eastern, southern, and other doors should circumambulate [the maṇḍala] three times clockwise. To pacify defects of deficiency or excess, they should gaze upon the *cakra*, offer the garland to the Blessed One, and then, standing in the four directions starting from the western door, recite for each of the four doors beginning with the east: *oṃ vajrodghāṭaya samaya praveśaya hūṃ*.

Having visualized that [the door] has been opened by means of the mantra, and having said, "Oṃ, I enter the pledge (*samaya*)," one should again take up the garland while dancing, bind it upon one's own head, bow to the wheel (*cakra*), and request, "Grant all accomplishments (*siddhi*) to all sentient beings. Thus one should meditate and recite.

Regarding this, Prajñāpālita states that outside the mandala house, in the directions of Indra and so forth, one should offer eight banners—white, pale-red (*pāṭala*), black, smoky-grey, red, variegated, yellow, and green—to the deities of the mandala and raise them in the east and other directions in their proper order.
And by the Blessed One in the Buddhakapāla Tantra:
"It is four-cornered, with four doors, and adorned with eight banners."

Thus it has been said: one should place the banners of Vairocana and the deities of his family in the southeast; those of Ratneśa and his family members in the southwest; those born of the family of Amitābha in the northwest; and those of Amoghasiddhi and his family deities in the northeast. Some say that the banner of the Lord of the Wheel (Cakreśa) should be in the east, while those of his family deities are in their respective directions. The banner of yellow Indra is black; that of Viṣṇu is black; that of white Indra is red; that of the Sun is red; that of Pitāmaha (Brahmā) in the direction of Indra is yellow; that of Vahni (Agni) is red; and that of Yama is black.

Smoke-colored [flags] belong to Nairṛti; each is in its own respective direction. In the west, the white flag belongs to Varuṇa; the yellow, to Pṛthivī; the black, to Vemacitrin; in the northwest, the dark-gray, to Vāyu; in the north, the yellow, to Kubera; and the white, to Gaṇapati. In the northeast, the white flag belongs to Īśāna—these fifteen flags are for the satisfaction of the lords of the directions. However, if it is impossible, one should offer flags according to one's capacity. This is the procedure for the ritual of accomplishing the maṇḍala with its retinue. *Vajrāvalī*, the Maṇḍalopāyikā, Vol. 2: Consecration.
16. The Ritual for the Invoking of the Deities (Devatādhivāsanavidhi) 16.1 (p. 325):

Thereafter, in that [place], whether it be a mandala of colored powders, a mandala on a cloth, or a mentally visualized mandala, one should perform the consecration of the images and so forth—preceded by the aforementioned offerings and other rites—just as one performs the consecration of the disciples.

Therein, within the mandala, having first performed the consecration and placement of the vases according to the previously mentioned procedure, one should visualize the image and so forth as the form of the *samayasattva*—either produced from seed-syllables following emptiness or appearing instantaneously—and contemplate the seed-syllable in one's own heart. Having covered it with fresh red or other colored cloth and provided it with flowers, the patron, taking the flower garland for it, should enter along with the image and others into any one of the mandalas, such as the *rajo-maṇḍala*, like a disciple.
The preceptor, however, should cause the flower to be placed upon the sign of the presiding deity of the image or upon the sign of the Lord of that family.

Alternatively, entry may occur simply by beholding the maṇḍala of the images and so forth, even without the casting of flowers. Then, outside the maṇḍala hall, in the eastern direction—or if there is no space there, in the northeast, not too far away—in a pleasant spot, one should prepare a bathing altar four cubits square and two cubits high; or else eight cubits in length and half that height.

Alternatively, having caused to be constructed on an auspicious day a [mound] twelve cubits in length and half that in height—made of clay, brick, or whatever material is available in their absence, or even the ground as it naturally lies, adorned with plaster and the like, marked with a sacrificial altar (vedikā), with eight jars placed in the cardinal and intermediate directions, cleansed with earth, smeared with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and nectar, and made beautiful according to one's means with canopies, white umbrellas, banners, flags, full vases, flowers, dancing, singing, instrumental music, and so forth; and having done so... in a pure place.

On an auspicious lunar day, weekday, asterism, and moment, having performed his ablutions and wearing ornaments such as necklaces, anklets, armlets, earrings, bracelets, and rings—or whatever ornaments he has obtained—the Preceptor, who is the embodiment of Vajrasattva together with his consort, should draw a *viśvapadma* in the center of that altar, surrounded by a square enclosure with a single line on its western gate, using colored powders or by means of anointing and other methods.

Alternatively, it may be located in the center of a square lacking an archway at its western gate; or it may be a square measuring half the size of the inner maṇḍala, with four gates, two enclosures, and no archways. On the eastern and other side-pieces, there are the [emblems] of the wheel, jewel, lotus, and sword; in the corners, the symbols of the four Mothers; and in the center, a universal eight-petaled lotus. Thus, according to the divisions of concise, intermediate, and extensive, the bathing maṇḍala is threefold. 16.3 (p.328)

Upon that, on a pedestal featuring an eight-petaled lotus inscribed above it, or on a lion throne covered with a cloth depicting a moon mandala and so forth, one should sit by means of the meditative resolve (*adhimokṣa*) of sitting upon the pericarp of the bathing mandala lotus; or, in the absence of a bathing mandala, one should likewise place the image, cloth painting, manuscript, stūpa, or other object—having visualized that very mandala upon a seat or similar surface—facing east or facing another direction.

However, regarding those objects such as monasteries, caityas, perfumed chambers, and images that are not suitable for being moved to another location—one should resolve upon the vision of the mandala of that very object, which has been visualized in the form of the Samayasattva as previously described; in that case, there is no need for a bathing altar.

In either case, at the time of dusk, one should place the image and so forth before oneself, face it directly, and perform the *nīrājana* rite preceded by the offering of water for the feet (*pādya*), the guest-offering (*argha*), and so on—or even without the offering of the *argha* and other items.

There, having recited seven times the Kuṇḍalin mantra, *oṃ āḥ vighnāntakṛt hūṃ*, and the syllable *hūṃ*, one should take white mustard seeds (*siddhārtha*) with the left and right fists respectively. Reciting *oṃ sarvapāpadahanavajrāya vajrasattvasya sarvapāpaṃ daha svāhā*, one should sprinkle them twice each time while moving counter-clockwise, and then cast the mustard seeds into the fire. Likewise, one should do so clockwise from the left and the right, and similarly with water.

Likewise, with white earthen bowls, with balls of cow dung mixed with dūrvā grass sprouts, with balls of cooked rice, and with the *śītalikā* rite; however, the bowls and other such items must not be thrown into the fire.

Then, with both hands, one should touch the image and so forth. With the mantra of the Lord of the Wheel (*cakreśa*), one should perform, as appropriate for the image and other objects—whether directly or via their reflection in a mirror—the anointing of the heart with perfume, the binding of the head with a garland of flowers, and the offering of the *argha* water before it. Having whirled a lamp, one should fumigate it with incense made of resin and ghee over which the *kuṇḍalī* *hūṃ*-syllable has been recited seven times. This is the sequence for the *nīrājana* rite.

Thereafter, one should smear the image or other object suitable for bathing with the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*)—consisting of curd, milk, ghee, honey, and sugar-candy—placed in a copper vessel and mixed with a bundle of *dūrvā* grass over which the *Kuṇḍalī* mantra has been recited; then, with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*)—curd, milk, ghee, cow dung, and cow urine—one should anoint it with the mantra: *oṃ hūṃ trāṃ hrīḥ aḥ*. However, in the case of images painted on cloth, in books, or made of clay, one should perform the rite upon their reflection in a mirror.

Then, having bathed [the image] with fragrant and pure water consecrated by the *kuṇḍali* mantra, and having rubbed it dry with a paste made from the five barks of the five milk-trees—namely the *nyagrodha*, *udumbara*, *plakṣa*, *pippala*, and *gandhamuṇḍa*—while reciting the mantra "Oṃ sarvatathāgatakāyaviśodhane svāhā" or "Oṃ hūṃ trāṃ hrīḥ khaṃ khaḥ," one should anoint it with fragrant oil kept in a bronze vessel, rub it dry, and likewise smear it with *āmalaka* fruit kept in a bronze vessel.

Having bathed [the image], having smeared it with turmeric held in a bronze vessel, and having bathed it again, one should anoint it with *śrīkhaṇḍa*, red sandalwood, saffron, and *granthika-aguru*, or as available, with saffron, agallochum, musk, camphor, and so forth. While reciting the verse beginning with "Just as [the Bodhisattva] immediately upon birth... and so on, which will be cited below, one should visualize the image being bathed by Tathāgatas and goddesses summoned by the rays of the heart-seed syllable (*hṛdbīja*), using water from the victory-vase (*vijayakalaśa*) and others collected in a conch shell or elsewhere, accompanied by auspicious songs and various musical instruments.
One should bathe [the image]. Having wiped away the water clinging to it with a soft cloth, one should adorn it with garments and other offerings according to one's ability.

Then, by means of the light rays of the heart-mantra, one should summon the *jñānasattva* to be installed and the deities such as the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas into the sky before oneself. Preceded by the offering of water for the feet (*pādya*), water for rinsing the mouth (*ācamana*), and the respectful offering (*argha*), one should drop the right knee to the ground, ring the bell with the left hand, and offer incense with the right hand, while the tongue is transformed into a vajra by the syllable *HŪṂ*.
O Blessed One, Amuka Sadvajra, King of Vidyās, homage be to you!
O Compassionate Lord, I wish to perform your consecration.
For the sake of compassion for the disciples, for your own worship,
for the increase of the merit of sentient beings, and for the arising of the thought of awakening.
Therefore, O Blessed One, you ought to grant your grace to me, your devotee;
may the Buddhas, who bestow the purpose of the wheel of activity for the world, attend to me.
Bodhisattvas established in the fruit, as well as other mantra-deities,
deities, world-protectors, and spirits who have been instructed in perfect enlightenment.
"Those beings who delight in the teaching, and others who possess the divine eye— [I], such-and-such a Great Vajrin, shall perform the consecration for such-and-such [a person]."
Therefore, I shall do so; you ought to grant me your presence.
Thus one should recite three times.

In this manner, having requested the consecration (*adhivāsana*) for the purpose of installation by means of the section ending with "you are worthy" (*arhasi*), and having requested the presence (*sannidhāna*) by means of the remainder; then, having fully worshipped, prostrated to, and praised the circle of deities situated in the sky, one should dismiss them with: *oṃ vajra punar āgamanāya muḥ*.

For an image or similar object that has been bathed, one should apply [fragrant substances] to its heart, head, throat, arms, and crown, worship it, touch it three times with the hand holding the *vajra* while reciting the *Kuṇḍalī-mantra*, and then mutter either the respective mantra or the *Kuṇḍalī-mantra*; furthermore, one should offer the directional oblations (*digbalī*).

16.6 However, for one who possesses firm resolve (*adhimokṣa*) such that the consecration (*pratiṣṭhāpana*) of a deity can be performed even without the preliminary invocation (*adhivāsana*), he may perform all the procedures—the previously mentioned purpose of the invocation as well as those to be described—on a single day, without having performed the invocation at all. Nevertheless, rites such as the lustration (*nīrājana*) and others of a similar nature must be performed only once. Furthermore, if the patron (*dānapati*) has the capacity, he should indeed perform the invocation for the sake of accumulating merit; this is the ritual procedure for the invocation of the deity.
17. The Ritual for the Consecration of Images and Other Objects.

Thereafter, at dawn, having caused a beautiful bathing altar to be prepared, the preceptor—adorned with ornaments at an auspicious moment and assuming the form of Vajradhara together with his consort—should sit down. Having first performed the offering of bali and worship, he should once again manifest the image and so forth, as well as the monastery and other structures as they stand, in the form of the *samayasattva*.

In that regard, concerning the *tantras*, *abhisamayās*, *sādhanas*, and so forth, one who knows the sequence of the arising of a particular deity should meditate on the image of that specific deity—either sequentially or instantaneously—following emptiness, as having the form of the *samayasattva*.

However, in the case of a book, one should contemplate that following the emptiness of the collection of syllables, upon a red lotus and sun disk, Amitābha arises from a red syllable *hrīḥ* embraced by Pāṇḍaravāsinī who arises from a red syllable *hrīḥ*; he then transforms into the form of the *samayasattva*, appearing as a reflection of Amitābha with the collective form of the syllables.

Following the emptiness of Dīpaṃkara, his monastery, and so forth, [the seed-syllable] *bhrūṃ* arises upon a white lotus and moon. From the transformation of the white *bhrūṃ*, the eight-spoked wheel, and the *bhrūṃ*, Vairocana appears embraced by Locanā. Having transformed into the form of Dīpaṃkara, he takes the form of a monastery, a perfumed chamber (*gandhakūṭī*), or a reliquary (*caitya*). However, as for the monastery, it is the Samayasattva, consisting of the reflected image of Vairocana together with Prajñā. One should meditate thus on the perfumed chamber and the reliquary.

Having thus accomplished the Samayasattva, one should perform the *nīrājana* ceremony as before, preceded by the offering of water for the feet (*pādya*), the respectful oblation (*argha*), and so forth.

Then, having performed the anointing with the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) and so forth according to the procedure just described—extending up to the application of saffron and other unguents, the bathing, and the removal of clinging water—one should bring [the image] into the maṇḍala house and place it facing the maṇḍala in the northeast direction or another nearby spot. Whether it be a statue or the like, which should remain motionless, or a temple and so forth, which remains in its own place, one should first perform the meditation on the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of its heart-seed syllable, eyes, and so forth, as well as its body and limbs, by means of the rays from the seed-syllable in one's own heart.

Having performed the aforementioned rites, such as the invitation of the respective *jñānasattvas* and so forth, one should recite the passage beginning with "O Blessed One" and ending with "you are worthy" three times. Then, having drawn in the deities by means of light rays from the heart according to the circumstances, one should cause the *jñānasattva* to enter its respective *samayasattva*, unify them into a single flavor, and bring [the deity] under control. Alternatively, another method is to generate the *samaya-maṇḍala* within the heart of the image and perform the entry of the *jñāna-maṇḍala* and so forth right there.

Then, having worshipped the Tathāgatas drawn from the ten directions into the sky before him by means of the rays from the seed-syllable in his own heart, as well as the goddesses Locanā and the others, for the sake of consecrating the image and so forth:
"Just as the Buddha-consecration, which is a mine of virtues, was bestowed by the Vajrī for the protection of the world, so indeed do you bestow it upon this [image]."

Thus one should entreat with this verse. Then those Tathāgatas, having entered into meditative absorption on wisdom (*prajñā*), melt through great passion; entering through one's own *vairocana* gate, they emerge via the *vajra* path. With those fluids, they consecrate the image and so forth by causing them to enter the mouth of the Goddess’s lotus. Then, emerging from the lotus in the form of [deities] with arms, faces, and so forth, they remain filling the external sky, accompanied by the vidyās such as Locanā and the others.

With white jars filled with the nectar of the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*), their sprout-like handles adorned by showers of parasols, banners, dance, song, instrumental music, flowers, saffron, and so forth, and emerging from the lotus outside that image and the rest, while it is being consecrated by Rūpavajrā and the others—
may that auspiciousness which belongs to the Lord of all Families, who dwells in the hearts of all beings, who is the self of all,
and who is the Great Bliss that gives birth to all sentient beings without exception, be yours today at this excellent consecration.

Thus, while auspiciousness is being brought forth by this auspicious song and the songs to be recited hereafter, one should—either singing it oneself or [having others] sing them—perform the consecration with water from the victory-pitchers (vijayakalaśa) and so forth. This water may be collected together in a single conch shell or used individually; in either case, it should be held in the hand by one grasping a vajra along with sprouts, or it should drip from the tip of the vajra held with sprouts. Taking on the form of the nectar of *bodhicitta*, one should say:
"Just as all the Tathāgatas were bathed immediately upon their birth, so shall I bathe [the deity] with pure, divine water."

"Oṃ āḥ, for the glory of the pledge of the empowerment of all Tathāgatas, hūṃ svāhā! and "Oṃ, empower with the vajra-water, hūṃ! Reciting these, the Blessed One Vajrasattva himself, the supreme guru in the form of the lord of the maṇḍala, empowers and consecrates [the disciple]. With firm conviction, one should thus perform the empowerment; this is the water empowerment. 17.4 (p.343)

The crown consists of garments, jewels, and so forth, empowered by the five Tathāgatas. Reciting either "Oṃ āḥ vajrābhiṣiñca hūṃ," or "Oṃ vajraratna āṃ," or "Oṃ hūṃ trāṃ hrīḥ aḥ," the Guru—who is indeed Vajradhara, the embodiment of the Lord of the Maṇḍala—places it upon the head of the deity in the image with firm conviction. This is the crown consecration (*mukuṭābhiṣeka*). For a hero (*vīra*), however, one should also bind a cloth (*paṭa*) to the forehead with the mantra "Oṃ hūṃ trāṃ hrīḥ aḥ.
"Today you have been consecrated by the Buddhas through the vajra consecration."
Take this, which is the state of all Buddhas, as a vajra for the sake of perfect accomplishment.

Reciting thus, one should present the vajra with the conviction that Vajrasattva himself is presenting it; and through the resolve that it has been accepted by the deity of the image and so forth, this is the vajra consecration. Reciting "Oṃ, I consecrate you as the Lord of the Vajra; abide, O Vajra, you are the Samaya," one should present the bell with the same conviction; and through the resolve that it has been accepted by the deity of the image and so forth, this is the bell consecration.

"Oṃ, Vajrasattva, I consecrate you with the vajra-name consecration. Oṃ, you are [Name]vajra. Reciting thus, while resolving that Vajrasattva himself assumes the name of the respective deity of the image and so forth, one should utter it; this is the name-consecration.

Having visualized the deity of the image and so forth performing the gesture of embracing with the knowledge-mudrā (jñānamudrā), with hands holding a vajra and a vajra-bell, and having consecrated them according to the procedure for water-consecration mentioned immediately above, one should seal their head with the Lord of their respective family. However, for those whose family is unknown, one should seal it with Akṣobhya or Vajrasattva. Other Tathāgatas, Bodhisattvas, and Goddesses should be made to enter into that very form of the Knowledge-Being (jñānasattva), and one should empower them with the mantra: *oṃ supratiṣṭhita vajre svāhā*.

With the mantra *oṃ hūṃ hrīḥ bhrūṃ khaṃ vajrībhava dṛḍhaṃ tiṣṭha bhrūṃ khaṃ*, one consecrates a monastery, a *caitya*, and a book; and with the two mantras *oṃ supratiṣṭhita vajre svāhā* and *oṃ hūṃ hrīḥ tvaṃ*, this is the *ācāryābhiṣeka*.

Thereafter, one should contemplate as follows: Vajrasattva, in the form of the Lord of the Mandala (Cakreśa), having caused a host of Tathāgatas such as Vairocana together with their consorts to arrive via rays of light from the seed-syllable in his own heart, enters through the door of Vairocana; having experienced the state of melting into great bliss (*mahāsukha*), he emits the form of bodhicitta through the vajra and lotus and causes it to enter the mouth of the deity of the image and so forth—this is the secret initiation (*guhyābhiṣeka*).

Then, one should resolve that the deity of the image and so forth, who has entered into union with the goddess presented by that Vajrasattva, consists of innate joy (*sahajānanda*)—this is the initiation of the knowledge of wisdom (*prajñājñānābhiṣeka*).

Thereafter, one should resolve with conviction that the deity of the image and so forth—whose nature as the fourth consecration was imparted by that Holder of the Vajra—is of a single flavor with emptiness and compassion consisting of great bliss, in which all obscurations along with their habitual tendencies have been abandoned; this is the fourth consecration.
As it is said in the *Sārdhatriśatikā* (Tanemura ed.): [17.7] (p.347) "That which was stated..."
Having properly drawn the wheel, this is the procedure for the initial consecration;
however, for images, books, and the like, it extends up to the *pauruṣa* rite following the sprinkling.
The water-crown initiation is indeed the outflow (*niḥṣyanda*); the ripening [initiation] is called the Lord of Vajras;
here, the initiation of the Victor is the heroic one, and purity arises from the secret yoga.
Regarding the *Guhyasamājamaṇḍalavidhi*:

therein, the "human" (*pauruṣa*) refers to the master initiation (*ācāryābhiṣeka*). Since this [initiation] is the goal (*upeya*) of that human means (*upāya*), it is also called "human" (*pauruṣa*); the meaning is that the "human-final" (*pauruṣānta*) initiation procedure consists of the final stages—the stainless initiation (*vaimalyaseka*) comprising the secret, wisdom, and fourth initiations—and thus it is termed "human-final. The expression "human-final" is used with the intention (*ākūtena*) that the other three fruits manifest solely from human effort (*puruṣakāra*), which consists of an excellence of virtuous enthusiasm.

In this context, "yoga" is intended as both conventional wisdom (*sāṃvṛta-prajñā*) and ultimate wisdom (*pāramārthika-prajñā*); thus, purity consists of these three aspects. Furthermore, through the master’s initiation (*ācārya-abhiṣeka*), the purification of the body alone is effected for the deity manifested in the form of a statue and so forth. For the sake of purifying speech and mind, the secret [initiation] and the others must indeed be bestowed.
For even to the great Bodhisattvas, these are bestowed.
As it has been said:
"In order to bestow the consecration upon Vajragarbha, Tilottamā was summoned."
Thus, as it is said in *Hevajratantra* II.v.42cd:

"When the Blessed One Siddhārtha had reached the seat of enlightenment, the perfectly awakened ones dwelling in the sky removed the mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) of the *āsphānaka-samādhi* from him; then, at midnight, having bestowed upon him unsurpassed wisdom (*prajñā*), they granted him the wisdom-consecration and the fourth consecration. Intending this very point, the Great Charioteers (*mahāratha*) have refuted, without distinction, the consecration of images and so forth by comparing it to the consecration of a disciple.

Then, one should offer garments and other items to the deities of the images and so forth with their respective heart-mantras; or alternatively, with these mantras: Oṃ āḥ vajravāsase hūṃ svāhā / Oṃ āḥ vajrapuṣpe hūṃ svāhā / Oṃ āḥ vajradhūpe hūṃ svāhā / Oṃ āḥ vajradīpe hūṃ svāhā / Oṃ āḥ vajranivedye hūṃ svāhā / Oṃ āḥ vajragandhe hūṃ svāhā / Oṃ sarvābharaṇavibhūṣaṇe svāhā / And with this mantra: Oṃ āḥ sarvaśodhani hūṃ phaṭ.

The mantra for sprinkling various items such as fruits and flowers is: *oṃ jaṃ svāhā*. This is the mantra for offering fruit. Having presented the pledge-substance (*samayadravya*) and yellow pigment (*rocanā*), one should show the mirror with the mantra: *oṃ vajrasattva āḥ*. 17.9 (p.350)

Immediately after that—or, if a fire offering (*homa*) is possible, after nourishing [the image] by means of the *homa*—one should, according to the form of the image and in accordance with the disposition of the donor, desire for the donor and others the welfare beginning with pacification (*śānti*) and ending with Buddhahood. Reciting "Oṃ cakṣuś cakṣuḥ samantacakṣur viśodhane svāhā," while applying collyrium with a gold rod no smaller than a *māṣaka* that has been smeared with ghee and honey placed in a silver *mallikā* vessel, one should open the eyes.

Furthermore, for a deity in the form of a statue, a book, or the like, one should resolve upon that presiding deity—which has been visualized as a reflection in a mirror—as being intent on observing the donor and others for the sake of pacification and other rites.

Thereafter, having poured milk, sugar-candy, rice, ghee, honey, and sugar into the fire of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) using a vessel and a ladle—or in their absence, using a leaf of the *pippala* tree—one should prepare the milk-rice (*pāyasa*) with grand ceremony in a vessel placed upon the tripod, while reciting the mantra of one's own tutelary deity (*svādhipamantra*). However, in the absence of a sacrificial pit, that milk-rice should be prepared in another fire with the mantra: *Oṃ divyānne samādhidhyānaprīṇane svāhā*.

Having thus consecrated [the offerings] while reciting [the mantra], one should cause the deity—whose reflected image has been meditated upon within the statue, book, or other support—to partake of them; one should then offer water for rinsing the mouth (*ācamana*), sandalwood paste and the like, and betel. Thereafter, one should cause [the deity] to hear the pledge (*samaya*) with the mantra: *oṃ hūṃ trāṃ hrīḥ aḥ*.

Then, one should contemplate that Amitābha, together with Prajñā, enters into the letters within the book and takes on the form of those letters; and that Vairocana, together with Vidyā, enters into the monastery or the *caitya* and takes on the form of the monastery or the *caitya*. One should visualize it as the support for all the Buddhas, their Dharmas, Bodhisattvas, Śrāvakas, and so forth, as a dwelling place for various meditative absorptions (*samādhi*), and as a *caitya* that, for the sake of benefiting the world, remains until the end of *saṃsāra*, empowered by Vajrasattva and the others.
Then, having offered flowers and other gifts with palms joined in reverence:
"Just as all the Buddhas are currently established in Tuṣita..."
Just as [the Bodhisattva] remained in the womb of Queen Māyā, so let them remain here in this form.
Remaining here constantly as the Protector, accept these offerings and so forth for the sake of [the disciple named] so-and-so, for the purpose of increasing the spirit of awakening (bodhicitta).

Having thus entreated [the deity] for the sake of long-lasting stability, and while reciting the Kuṇḍali-mantra, one should encircle the lower, middle, and upper parts of the image and so forth three times with the vajra moved and drawn upward by the right hand, thereby making it firm:
"O Akṣobhyavajra, Great Wisdom, Vajradhātu, Great Sage;
O Triple Mandala, Supreme of the Three Vajras, Vajra of Sound, homage be to you!"
Vairocana, great purity, vajra-peace, great delight; O Vajra of the teaching, supreme among the supremely luminous by nature—homage be to you!
O King of Jewels, most profound, vajra-like sky, stainless,
pure by nature, untainted— homage be to you, Vajra Body!
O Vajrāmita, Great King, non-conceptual space, wielder of the vajra;
you who have attained the perfection of passion, O Bhāṣavajra, homage be to you!
O Amoghavajra, perfectly awakened one, fulfiller of all hopes,
arisen from the nature of purity, Vajrasattva— homage be to you!

Having praised with these verses, in order to pacify any deficiencies in the ritual procedure, one should recite three times the hundred-syllable mantra: *Oṃ vajrasattva samayam anupālaya | vajrasattvatvenopatiṣṭha | dṛḍho me bhava | sutoṣyo me bhava | supoṣyo me bhava | anurakto me bhava | sarvasiddhiṃ me prayaccha | sarvakarmasu ca me cittaṃ śreyaḥ kuru | hūṃ ha ha ha ha hoḥ | bhagavan sarvatathāgatavajra mā me muñca | vajrībhava mahāsamayasattva āḥ.* [Then one says: "O Compassionate One, [this was done] through non-attainment, lack of understanding, and incapacity."
Whatever has been done deficiently or otherwise, you ought to forgive all of that.
Having thus asked for forgiveness:

"May the perfectly awakened Buddhas, the goddesses, and their sons, as well as the deities beginning with Brahmā and the nāgas, forgive whatever deficiency in the ritual procedures or other such errors may have occurred."
May Agni, Bhū, Vāri, and Marut protect the images for a long time;
may they bring peace, prosperity, and well-being in every way to the lord of the donors.
May his sons, his disciples, and we ourselves go from there with joy to the domain of the Buddha, in order to return here once again.

Having thus requested three times, he should offer the offerings to the directions (*digbalī*) and the offering to all beings (*sārvabhautikabali*). The patron of the gift (*dānapati*), for his part, having performed circumambulation, worship, and salutation toward the image and so forth, should fully satisfy the preceptor (*ācārya*) with appropriate sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*).

In this case, a book should be consecrated in a maṇḍala where Amitābha is the presiding deity; however, in one where Vairocana is the presiding deity, a monastery or similar structure should be consecrated. In a maṇḍala where Akṣobhya or Vajrasattva is the presiding deity, all types of images may be consecrated; even those whose family (kula) is unknown should be installed. Alternatively, whichever family of a particular image-deity is known, that image should be placed in a maṇḍala where the Tathāgata of that family is the presiding deity.
In some instances, however, an image should indeed be installed in the maṇḍala of the tantra in which it is established.
That mandala of his should be constructed, or else that of his own tutelary deity.
Whatever belongs to the teacher, one should treat that as distinct, viewing it with a sense of separation.

Thus [the source remains] to be identified. Here, "of that" refers to the *bimba* (the reflected image) by virtue of its being the presiding deity of the mandala. "His own tutelary deity" means the Tathāgata who is the lord of the family (*kula*) of that *bimba*; for him, this mandala is to be performed. Alternatively, the mandala belonging to the preceptor himself—his own personal mandala—is to be performed. For whatever he meditates upon, that indeed belongs to him. Thus three positions have been stated. By this, it is established that even when a mandala of this kind is taught in one tantra, the consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*) of deities taught in other tantras is appropriate within it.
This is because the maṇḍalas of those families are subsumed by the aforementioned maṇḍalas of the leaders.

Regarding the abbreviated consecration (*saṃkṣiptapratiṣṭhā*), however, immediately after the emptiness (*śūnyatā*) of the image and so forth, one should instantaneously (*jhaṭiti*) produce that respective *samayasattva*, empowered by the eyes, body, and so on. Within that, one should internalize the *jñānasattva* brought by rays from the seed-syllable in one's own heart; then, having been consecrated by oneself with the water from the flask along with the Tathāgatas and others brought by the rays from the seed-syllable in one's own heart, and having performed worship, one should recite its mantra one hundred and eight times. In this way, the image and so forth become consecrated.

17.13 (p.359) However, when a special honor for the *tathāgatadhātu* is desired, then at the very time of assembly, one should have a cavity made in the head or the pedestal of the image, or within the interior of the *caitya*. Upon its completion, [one should write] on birch bark with saffron and *gorocanā*: *Namo bhagavate śākyamunaye tathāgatāyārhate samyaksambuddhāya | oṃ mune mune mahāmunaye svāhā |* *Ye dharmā hetuprabhavā hetuṃ teṣāṃ tathāgato hy avadat |*
And the Great Śramaṇa is one who teaches the cessation of these very things.

Having thus written down this specific dhāraṇī and wrapped the relics that have been bathed with it, one should recite "Oṃ, to the one whose womb contains the mantra-relics, svāhā! and cast it into the cavity. Thereafter, while muttering "Oṃ, to the one whose womb contains the vajra-relics, svāhā!", one should seal the opening of the cavity with adamantine cement (*vajralepa*) and perform its consecration as before.

Others, however, maintain that even for an image of Saṃvara, Hevajra, or the like, there must indeed be consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*) through the entry into the gnosis-maṇḍala and the initiation following the generation of the *samayasattva* of the *Samāja*; for the *Samāja* is unsurpassed. Immediately thereafter, the Lord of the *Samāja* Gnosis-maṇḍala should manifest in the form of Saṃvara and so forth. Since the image of that deity is likewise of that very form, they ask: where is the contradiction? (17.15, p. 361)

In the consecration of the vidyā, the preceptor—having the form of Vajradhara or the form of the Lord of Vidyās—should meditate upon the vidyā and the entry of the Jñānasattva therein according to the ritual procedure.

In the same way, according to the circumstances, one should likewise know the specific object to be accomplished (*sādhya*). Having incorporated the name of the object to be accomplished into the mantra of the Lord of Knowledge (*vidyādhipa*), one should cause the Knowledge-Goddess (*vidyā*) to enter through the upper aperture or the mouth; having caused her to exit via the path of the *vajra* and enter the lotus of the deity, she is consecrated by the Tathāgatas summoned by the rays from the seed-syllable in the heart who have likewise entered. One should then consecrate her with the water from the flask as she exits and is being consecrated. Having performed worship, one should recite the heart-mantra of the Lord of Knowledge one hundred and eight times.

Regarding specific types of knowledge (*vidyā*), a particular meditation (*bhāvanā*) that is somewhat brief should be understood from the *Āmnāyamañjarī*; this constitutes the "establishment of knowledge" (*vidyāpratiṣṭhā*).

The preceptor, visualizing himself instantaneously as the form of Vajradhara, should contemplate his right hand with the fingers instantly formed into the shape of a five-pointed vajra, upon which is a sun disk born from the syllable *ĀḤ* and presided over by the syllable *ĀḤ*. In his left hand, he should contemplate the fingers instantly in the shape of lotus petals, upon which is a moon disk born from the syllable *A* and presided over by that same syllable. Between these two hands, he should visualize the central thread of the held rosary as having the nature of Vajrasattva, while the eight threads extending to the cardinal and intermediate directions [have the nature of the eight Bodhisattvas].

One should instantly resolve that the pills consist of Padmapāṇi, Maitreya, Gaganagañja, Samantabhadra, Vajrapāṇi, Mañjuśrī, Sarvanivaraṇaviṣkambhin, and Kṣitigarbha, whose nature is the Tathāgatas such as Vairocana; and that the upper pill is the stūpa of the qualities such as the powers (*bala*) and fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*). Then, having summoned Vajrasattva and the others by means of rays from the seed-syllable in the heart, one causes them to enter each according to its own [deity], reciting: *akkyarukāraṇaru asohi amanta visāru gaṇi a asaṃkhu alikku sihya itatta visāru*.

"Oṃ pade pade mahājñānaṃ sarvabuddham ahaṃ bhave hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ ho ho ho aḥ khaṃ svāhā. With this mantra, one should consecrate [the rosary]. One should sprinkle it with water from the ritual flask and worship it; such is the consecration of the rosary (*akṣasūtra*). In brief, however, regarding the rosary: having visualized Vāgvajra and unified him with the Jñānasattva, one should contemplate that he transforms into the form of the rosary. Having sprinkled it with water from the ritual flask and worshipped it, one should recite the heart-mantra of Vāgvajra one hundred and eight times; such is the consecration of the rosary. This concludes the procedure for the consecration of images and so forth.
18. The Ritual for the Consecration of Lotuses, Ponds, and Wells 18.1 (p.

364): When the patron possesses the necessary capacity, one should draw the Vairocana-led maṇḍala; then, standing on the bank and possessing the yoga of the Lord of the Wheel (Cakreśa), having cast offerings into the various directions of the lotus pond and so forth, one should contemplate the water as having become empty.

Having visualized the *samayasattva*—who is born from the syllable *Bhrūṃ*, arisen from the wheel of *Bhrūṃ*, and through the transformation of Vairocana absorbed into Locanā—as white Vajravaruṇa with a human face and seven hoods, gracefully embracing his consort with his left hand holding a snake-noose while she is absorbed into him, and holding a blue lotus in his right hand, his body being like a serpent from the navel downwards; then, having invited Vairocana by means of light rays from the seed-syllable in one's own heart, preceded by the offering of water for the feet, water for rinsing the mouth, and the *argha* offering.

Having said, "Oṃ, you are the vajra-samaya," and having caused [the disciple] to enter, consecrated, and worshipped with flowers and so forth, one should cause waves to arise all around—extending down to the netherworld (rasātala), the abode of the eight families of nāgas—consisting of the nectar of gnosis transformed from that [water], endowed with a reflection, and possessing the eight qualities of water because it is fragrant, sweet, light, clear, soft, and cool, and does not afflict the throat or the stomach.

And there, upon the surface of the water, one should instantly establish eight fashioned *nāgas* in the form of *samayasattvas*, non-different from the *jñānasattvas* summoned by rays from the seed-syllable in the heart. This should be done either in the middle of a lotus pond—measuring twice as wide as it is deep, or equal in height—or near a sacrificial post (*yūpa*) erected in the center of a pool containing both types of beings (and possessing a head adorned with an image of Varuṇa), or even in the center of a body of water that lacks a sacrificial post. Therein, in the east is Ananta, made of gold; in the south is Padma, made of copper.

In the west is Takṣaka, made of copper; in the north is Vāsuki, made of pure silver; in the northeast is Mahāpadma, fashioned from various pigments; in the southeast is Śaṅkhapāla, made of lead; in the southwest is Karkoṭaka (Karkoṭaka, according to the Sakurai edition), made of brass; and in the northwest is Kulika, made of iron. However, in the absence of a staff, there is Vajravaruṇa in the center, made of crystal. 18.3 (p. 367)

Then, having poured the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*), milk, camphor, and so forth into [the vessels] for Varuṇa and the others, and having worshipped them with flowers and other offerings, one should perform a fire-oblation (*homa*) for the sake of nourishment if possible. Then, sitting on a bank smeared with cow dung and having drawn a mandala with white sandalwood paste, one should summon [the deities] by means of rays from the seed-syllable in one's own heart. One should place Vajra-Varuṇa upon the pericarp of the lotus situated in the mandala; Ananta on the eastern petal; Padma on the southern; Takṣaka on the western; Vāsuki on the northern; Mahāpadma on the northeast; Śaṅkhapāla on the southeast; and [Kulika] on the southwest.

Having visualized Karkkoṭaka in the northwest and Kulika [in the northeast], and all the nāgas outside on every side, one should worship them with white flowers using mantras interspersed with their respective names: *oṃ āḥ vajravaruṇāya hūṃ svāhā* and *oṃ āḥ anantāya hūṃ svāhā*. Then, making the gesture of a hood with the left hand, one extends the right hand.

Oṃ! Ananta, Vāsuki, Takṣaka, Karkkoṭa, Padma, Mahāpadma, Śaṅkhapāla, Kulika, Pāla, Devati, Mahādevati, Somaśikhi, Mahāśikhi, Daṇḍadhara, Mahādaṇḍadhara, Apalālahuluṇḍa, Nanda and Upananda, Sāgara, Mahāsāgara, Tapta, Mahātapta, Śrīkānti, Mahākānti, Ratnakānti, Surūpa, Mahāsurūpa, Bhadrāhika, Mahodara, Śili, and Mahāśili—Oṃ! Eat! Come, come, O Great Lord of Nagas!

Reciting the *nāgabali* mantra: “*sarva bhūr bhuvaḥ phuṃ phuṃ svāhā*,” one should consecrate the milk offering. Then, having requested [the deities] to remain for a long time, recited the hundred-syllable mantra (*śatākṣara*), and asked for forgiveness, one should have that consecrated milk offering placed in eight shallow bowls in the eight directions. One should also cast it outside. And one should satisfy young maidens. This is the procedure for the consecration of lotus ponds, tanks, and wells.
19. The Procedure for the Consecration of Groves and so forth (p. 370)

In the consecration of mango groves, gardens, and so forth, one should offer the directional bali offerings. Then, identifying oneself as Vairocana, one should contemplate the principal tree as the form of Vairocana immediately following the meditation on emptiness. Having caused the Jñānasattva Vairocana to enter it preceded by the offering of water for the feet and other honors, and having consecrated it with a vase, one should resolve that the principal tree has been transformed into that [deity], and likewise that the other trees have been transformed into it. One should then worship that principal tree and its presiding deity with flowers and so forth, and the others with fruits and so forth.

The ritual procedure for the consecration of gardens and the like is as follows: one who is undergoing the *upakurvāṇa* stage of life should request the deities of the directions to remain long in the garden and so forth, and then offer the oblations to the directions (*digbalis*). This is the rule for the consecration of gardens and similar structures.

Regarding all these aforementioned procedures, there is a general injunction (*paribhāṣā*): in whatever rite a mantra has not been specified, one should recite the "all-purpose" mantra (*sārvakarmika-mantra*).
20. The Ritual Procedure for the Consecration of the Disciple (*śiṣyādhivāsana-vidhi*).

20.1 (p.371) Then, in the dust-mandala or within another mandala, having first performed the preliminary rites— the consecration of the vases, the ritual placement (*nyāsa*), the fivefold offerings, and so forth— according to the previously stated procedure, one should also consecrate other well-examined disciples who are free from defects such as pride, who have been prepared through the lay practitioner’s vows (*upāsaka*) and extensive study, who are devoted, and who are fit to receive the *vajrasattva* vows (*saṃvara*). Even those lacking noble lineage, virtues, or beauty may be consecrated, provided that they possess faith, are intensely intent upon the *vajrasattva* vows, and have no other teacher than the Vajrayāna.
This was stated by the Blessed One in the *Sārdhatriśatikā*:
"One should tolerate those who are deformed, devoid of qualities, or even inferior;
the ritual procedure in the mandala is authorized for all four types of assemblies."
For those who are engaged in their own trainings and whose minds delight in the Mahāyāna.
(1) Thus it is said.

"Of the four assemblies" refers to the monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen. "The procedure" refers to the entry and so forth. "Of those who are disciplined" means those devoted to that [practice]. By the phrase "of those whose souls delight in the Mahāyāna," he demonstrates that mental action (*manaskarma*) is the primary factor in this vehicle, for the sake of showing non-contradiction. For even in an action that is inherently transgressive (*prakṛtisāvadya*), the Blessed One has frequently declared and we have explained in works such as the *Āmnāyamañjarī* that there is no offense due to a particularity in the motivation (*samutthāna*).
This is also stated elsewhere.
There is no offense for one whose mind is virtuous, nor for one who acts out of affection and compassion.
Thus,
even that which is prohibited is permitted for the compassionate one who perceives the welfare [of others].

And thus: Furthermore, for one who has accumulated merit, extensive learning, and so forth, and who possesses a very firm conviction that all phenomena are like illusions and dreams, having the single flavor of emptiness—for such a person, where even a scent of contradiction could there be between the vows of a monk and those of a Vajradhara? For this very reason, it was said by the Blessed One:
"One should make a monk a Vajradhara."

Thus it must necessarily be accepted. Otherwise, how could one reconcile the fact that, as established in the Vinaya (the rule), a monk who experiences a dream due to the simultaneous awakening of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of both [parties], even while experiencing the pleasure of the two organs with an external woman who is likewise dreaming and experiencing the pleasure of union, remains free from transgression? This must be properly understood.

If, however, the location should be a domain frequented by wicked people, then even for such a person the secret and wisdom-knowledge empowerments should be bestowed by means of the knowledge-seal (*jñānamudrā*). But in the absence of wicked people, they should be bestowed by the action-seal (*karmamudrā*) alone. For a monk who lacks firm conviction in reality—even if he is faithful—the reception of the external wisdom empowerment is forbidden; otherwise, due to the loss of his previous vows, great harm would ensue.

If, however, the guru is one whose meditation is stable, then when the *jñānamudrā* is offered by him, the *prajñā-abhiṣeka* should also be conferred; and for the recipient, there is not even the slightest suspicion of non-celibacy, because of the absence of physical action. For him, however, the distinctions of *ānanda* and so forth are to be demonstrated through the recollection of the bliss previously experienced during his state as a householder. Furthermore, regarding the guru, if he is a monk (*bhikṣu*), all that has been said concerning the conferral of the secret initiation (*guhyābhiṣeka*) and the others should be applied accordingly. Enough of this digression; the subject at hand shall now be discussed. 20.4 (p.375)

Therein, one, two, or many disciples—having had the mandala prepared, having knelt upon the ground, and holding handfuls of flowers—should be made to enter the mandala for the sake of attaining the perfection of the three bodies of the Tathāgata, rather than merely for the sake of prosperity in this world or even for prosperity in the next world.

Having thus informed him that "in this way, the two types of exaltation (*abhyudaya*) will be accomplished," [the master] causes [the disciple] to enter his own mouth and exit from the *vajra*. Having visualized that he has been consecrated by the Tathāgatas together with their Prajñās—who have entered through the mouth, drawn in by the rays from the heart-seed syllable, and are situated upon the lotus of the Prajñā, having become liquefied—he should seat him at the eastern gate of the mandala and have him request entrance:
"O Great Passion (*mahārata*), you alone are my teacher, the sole deliverer from the ocean of existence, which is terrifying due to death, birth, old age, sickness, and other such calamities. (2)

I desire, O Great Lord, this firm path of great awakening; grant me the commitment (*samaya*) and the reality (*tattva*), and grant me the spirit of awakening (*bodhicitta*). (3) Grant me the Three Refuges: the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.

"O Lord, lead me into the supreme city of great liberation. Thus he recites. "Mahārata" refers to one who is equal to the Holder of the Vajra. *Naya* means the path; *samaya* refers to mantra, tantra, mudrā, and so forth. Some say that [the disciples] have first been made to undertake the *poṣadha* vows.

Thereafter, having designated one disciple as the principal, [the teacher says]: "Come, child! I shall correctly teach you the method of the Mahāyāna mantra practice; you are a worthy vessel for the Great Vehicle."

The Buddhas, arisen throughout the three times, who possess the vajra of body, speech, and mind, have attained incomparable gnosis through the cultivation of vajra-mantras. By means of this incomparable application of mantra, the one of great power was defeated. (6)
The most formidable army of Māra was [conquered] by the excellent ones, such as the Lion of the Śākyas;
having conformed to worldly convention and set the wheel of Dharma in motion, they have attained nirvāṇa.
Therefore, my child, apply this mind toward the attainment of omniscience. (7–8)
One should cause [the disciple] to undertake this by reciting the text: "This [teaching]," which is devoted to the method of mantra;
"therefore, the Three Jewels are my refuge; I confess all my misdeeds."
I rejoice in the merit of the world; I fix my mind upon the awakening of a Buddha.
(9) Thus one should recite three times.
20.6 (p.378) Thus, in order to cause him who possesses the common vow to receive the vow of a master:
"O Lord, having bestowed the irreversible empowerment upon the wheel, please speak to me."
The reality of the wheel and the deity, and the preparation of the preceptor;
(10) the commitment of all Buddhas, the supreme secret vow:
"May I always be a preceptor for the sake of accomplishing the welfare of all sentient beings. (11)

Having thus caused [the disciple] to make this specific request, one should cause them to generate the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*): "May all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas attend to me! I, named so-and-so, from this moment until I sit at the seat of awakening (*bodhimaṇḍa*), shall generate the supreme, unsurpassed thought of awakening, just as the Protectors of the three times have made their resolve for perfect awakening. (12)

I firmly undertake the threefold training in ethical discipline, the gathering of wholesome qualities, and the ethical discipline of acting for the benefit of sentient beings. [I take refuge in] the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, the supreme and unsurpassed Triple Gem.
From this day forward, I shall undertake the vow born of the yoga of the Buddha.
I shall truly accept the vajra, the bell, and the mudrā;
and I shall accept the master within the exalted assembly of the Great Vajra Family.
I shall bestow the fourfold gift six times every day,
within the worthy and delightful assembly of the Great Jewel Family.
I accept the True Dharma— outer, secret, and pertaining to the three vehicles.

In the pure Mahāpadma family, which arises from great awakening, I accept the vow associated with all [families] in its entirety. I perform the rite of worship according to my ability within the exalted Mahākarma family. (17–18)
Having generated the supreme, unsurpassed mind of awakening,
and having undertaken the complete vow for the sake of all sentient beings,
I shall cause those who have not crossed over to cross, and I shall liberate those who are not yet liberated. (19)

"I shall cause all beings who have not yet found rest to find rest; I shall establish them in nirvāṇa. Reciting this three times, [it is said]: "This has been explained in the *Āmnāyamañjarī*, 20.7 (p. 381)."

Then, having protected them with the *Amṛtakuṇḍalī* mantra, one should visualize the syllables *HŪṂ*, *ĀḤ*, and *OṂ*—black, red, and white respectively—situated upon a sun, a lotus, and a wheel at their heart, throat, and head; or [alternatively] situated upon a sun, a sun, and a moon. Reciting those [syllables], one should touch the heart, throat, and head with the right fist joined with a *vajra* and scented water. Then, one should offer a flower on the head, incense and a lamp before [the face], and again scent at the heart.

Thereafter, facing north, he should give to the disciples a tooth-stick made of *aśvattha* or other such wood, twelve finger-breadths long, straight, unblemished, unsplit, free of wounds, washed with fragrant water, and with a flower tied to its tip. They, facing either east or north within a four-cubit square mandala smeared with cow dung and the like, recite "Oṃ vajrahāsa haṃ," chew the tooth-stick from the tip, and then, looking upward and without regard for the remains, they cast it away facing forward.

One should declare the future success for them according to the direction in which their tooth-stick falls: if it falls facing east, north, west, south, upward, or downward, there will be success in pacification (*śānti*), enrichment (*pauṣṭika*), subjugation (*vaśya*), malevolent rites (*abhicāra*), the state of a *vidyādhara*, or the underworld (*pātāla*), respectively.
But if one falls outside the mandala, there is no accomplishment.

Thereafter, having given water consecrated with the *vaṃ*-syllable and recited over it for rinsing the mouth, he should cause [the disciple] to drink three handfuls of scented water recited seven times with the *kuṇḍalī* mantra, while reciting: "Oṃ hrīḥ! O Pure Dharma, purify all the sins of this person; remove all conceptual constructions, hūṃ! Thus he should cause him to drink.

Then, having seated them outside, one should spread many *kuśa* grasses with unbroken tips—produced from the syllable *hūṃ*, consecrated by its recitation, or consecrated by the *Kuṇḍalī* mantra—for the purpose of a bed; likewise, for the purpose of a pillow, one should give a single *kuśa* blade produced from the syllable *dhīḥ* and consecrated by that same *Kuṇḍalī* mantra, with the mantra: *oṃ vajratīkṣṇa dhaṃ*.

Thereafter, taking a red thread equal in length to the disciple's body, tripled [in thickness], and consecrated seven times with the *hūṃ*-born *kuṇḍalinī* mantra, he should tie it with three or six knots according to the teachings of other tantras—either on their right arm or left hand—and while reciting: "Oṃ buddha maitrī rakṣa rakṣa sarvān svāhā," he himself should bind it, properly protect [the disciple], and encourage them, saying:
"Whatever evil was committed in the past over many millions of eons, all of that indeed goes to destruction upon seeing such a maṇḍala. (21)
The miserable states, which are the source of all suffering,
are cut off for those whose minds are utterly pure regarding this supreme conduct. (22) O noble beings, today you have obtained incomparable gains.
Because you have all been embraced here in this teaching by all the Victors together with their Sons,
those great-souled ones at the very moment of your birth,
therefore you shall indeed be well-born in the Mahāyāna. (23–24)
"This is the glorious, supreme path, the great arising of the Mahāyāna,
by which you, proceeding along it, shall become Tathāgatas.
(25) Having thus caused them to hear this— "being born" refers to the entry into the maṇḍala— the Mahāyāna itself is "great" because its arising occurs through a succession of successive excellences.

386) Thereafter, having protected them with the Kuṇḍalī mantra and having taught the Kuṇḍalī mantra for the purpose of its recitation, one should say, "In the morning you will tell us your dream," and then have them sleep on a lion’s bed either inside the peaked pavilion, at the edge of the maṇḍala ground, behind a curtain or similar screen, or elsewhere. Having entered the maṇḍala house oneself, one should recite the Kuṇḍalī mantra for the sake of protection.

In this context, that vow which is bestowed even without making someone an *ācārya* is the "common" one, characterized merely by taking refuge and generating the bodhicitta. However, that which is bestowed for the purpose of making someone an *ācārya* is the "ācārya-vow," which is comprised of the five families. Therefore, this is the procedure for the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsana*) of the disciple, preceded by the bestowing of these two vows.
21. The Procedure for Entering as an *Ācārya*.

Thereafter, at dawn, the Guru, having offered the *bali* and emerged from the maṇḍala house, asks the disciples about their dreams. If an inauspicious dream is indicated by such signs as falling from a mountain, he protects them with the Kuṇḍalī mantra. At the time of entering the maṇḍala house, [the Guru recites] with the disciples: "Oṃ, enter, O Blessed One, into the city of liberation of great bliss, which bestows the bliss of all accomplishments; O supreme one of ultimate bliss, attain success! Jaḥ hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ, may you be fully accomplished!"

Thus encouraged, having entered and circumambulated [the mandala], one stands at the western and other doors as the form of Cakreśvara and opens the eastern and other doors of the mandala while reciting: *oṃ vajrodghāṭaya samaya praveśaya hūṃ*. Having thus opened [the doors], one offers a flower garland while reciting: *oṃ paramasukhāśayasulalitavilāsanamitair namāmi bhagavantaṃ jaḥ hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ hi hi hi hi hrīḥ pratīccha kusumāñjaliṃ nātha hoḥ*.

Having cast [the garland] into the maṇḍala with this mantra, and having taken it up again and bound it upon one’s own head with the intention of the garland-consecration (*mālābhiṣeka*), one should visualize the Guru as the Lord of the Mandala appearing before one’s eyes. Having received from him the garland-consecration and all the other consecrations to be described hereafter according to the ritual, as well as the permissions for all the activities of a master, one should, for the sake of admitting the disciple, aspire for the accomplishment of the maṇḍala preceded by a praise of reality consisting of wisdom and means in the nature of great bliss (*mahāsukha*). One should also perform the empowerment through truth (*satyādhiṣṭhāna*).
Because he is the sign of the arising of space, the supreme one is without beginning or end;
O Sattva composed of the great vajra, Akṣobhyavajra and the rest, grant me accomplishment! (1)
O supreme among all, the great accomplishment, the presiding deity of sovereignty, the King who holds all vajras, may you, the supreme syllable, grant me success! // 2 //
You are faultless and eternal, the one who inspires passion for all passions; O Blessed One, as the Great Passion and the Great Joy, be realized for me in reality. // 3 //
The Tathāgata, the ultimate purity, the supreme dharma, the crown of the beginning, Samantabhadra, the soul of all—may you, O Bodhisattva, grant me success! 4.

O supreme among all, through the mudrā of great accomplishment and the pinnacle of sovereignty, may you grant me success; O Vajra, through this great extraction, may I attain the state of Vajragarvāpati! 5.
Pervading the minds of all sentient beings, abiding in the hearts of all sentient beings,
he is indeed the father of all sentient beings, the supreme object of desire for those who hold the samaya.
By that truth through which perception is the maṇḍala consisting of wisdom and skillful means, by that truth, O Protector, may you fulfill my desires. (7)
All phenomena are like reflections; they are transparent, pure, and unclouded.
They are ungraspable and inexpressible, yet they arise from causes and karma. // 8 //
"By this truth—that [the mandala] has emerged from the reality of suchness—may all the disciples, free from stain, clearly behold the reflection of the mandala. (9)

Reciting thus: "He for whom space is the sign and the example regarding arising is such [a being]; because of that reality, he is Vajrasattva, consisting of emptiness and compassion. All "vajras" refers to the Body-vajra and the others. "By all passions" means by all desires, he is one who causes beings to feel affection. "Great passion" is non-referential great compassion. "Primordially crowned" means that, through natural purity, he is the self of all; as the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), he is a being whose essence is awakening (*bodhi*). He is both "desirable" (*kāma*)—because he is desired—and "supreme" (*agra*).

"Of those who hold the supreme pledge" means those possessing correct knowledge (*samyagjñāna*). The five terms beginning with "pure" (*accha*) refer to being free from the obscurations of afflictions (*kleśa*), objects of knowledge (*jñeya*), and meditative absorption (*samāpatti*), as well as being devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*) and being beyond the scope of words (*śabdāviṣayatva*). They are "stainless" (*akalmaṣāḥ*) due to the empowerment of truth (*satyādhiṣṭhāna*) and the empowerment of the Blessed One (*bhagavadadhiṣṭhāna*). Thus concludes the procedure for the entrance of the master.
22. Procedure for the Entrance of the Disciple 22.1 Procedure for Bestowing the Water of the Pledge (*samayodaka*)
