Then, if the door-keepers (dvārācāryas) are unwilling, but others are willing, [the master] should bathe another disciple who has been consecrated and observes the two vows; having purified him with fragrant substances and the like, he should clothe him in red garments consecrated by the Kuṇḍali-mantra, or otherwise [in white], and have him stand outside the curtain (kāṇḍapaṭa) in the form of Vairocana or in the form of the Lord of the Mandala (cakrādhipa). Having performed the donning [of the garment] with: *oṃ sarvatathāgatānuttarabodhyalaṃkāravastrapūjāmeghasamudraspharaṇasamaye hūṃ*, [he recites]: *oṃ vajrarakṣa haṃ*.

Thus, the upper garment is donned. *Oṃ vajroṣṇīṣa hūṃ phaṭ*; thus the uṣṇīṣa is donned. With a cloth that is red or yellow, consecrated by the recitation of the *Amṛtakuṇḍalin* mantra, one binds the blindfold with the mantra: *Oṃ cakṣurbandhaṃ varam ānaya hūṃ*. *Āḥ khaṃ vīra hūṃ*.

Having recited this, [the disciple]—who holds a flower garland, has offered the ritual fee (*dakṣiṇā*), and has been sprinkled with water from the *sārvakarmika* vase—should be addressed by the Karma-vajrin for entry into the mandala after being established at the eastern gate. His body is made radiant by the rays of light from the black *HŪṂ*, red *ĀḤ*, and white *OṂ* syllables placed upon sun, moon, and sun disks, which are situated atop a vajra-fist, lotus, and wheel at his heart, throat, and head. Having uttered "HŪṂ," [the officiant] should question him.

"Who are you, O beloved of pleasure? He should reply: "I am Subhaga, the Great Bliss. Then, having caused him to generate the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*) while reciting: "Oṃ, I generate the mind of all yoga," and having placed the flower-adorned vajra at his heart while reciting: "Oṃ, in the great pleasure (*surata*), you are the pledge (*samaya*); Hoḥ! Accomplish, O Vajra, as is fitting!"—[the teacher says]: "Today you shall be empowered by all the Tathāgatas."

And you must not speak of this mandala of the supreme secret of all the Tathāgatas to anyone who has not entered a mandala, nor should it be believed by one lacking faith. Having said this, [he recited]: *oṃ yamāntakṛt hūṃ*.

Reciting thus, he draws [the disciple] in. With the mantra *Āḥ khaṃ vīra hūṃ*, he causes him to enter within the curtain. Reciting *Mahārata sudṛḍha suṭoṣya susukho vajrasattvādya sidhya mām* (O Great Joy, firm one, well-pleased, most blissful Vajrasattva, grant me success now!), he makes him circumambulate the maṇḍala with palms joined at the eastern gate. He says: *Oṃ, I offer myself for the service of worship to all the Tathāgatas; O Vajrasattva of all the Tathāgatas, empower me! Oṃ, I offer myself for the service of worship to all the Buddhas.*

"O all Tathāgatas, Vairocana, empower me! [Thus he says. To the south: "Oṃ, I offer myself for the consecration of the worship of all Tathāgatas; O all Tathāgatas, consecrate me with the vajra-jewel! To the west: "Oṃ, I offer myself for the performance of the worship of all Tathāgatas; O all Tathāgatas, set me in motion with the vajra-dharma! To the north: "Oṃ, I offer myself for the activity of the worship of all Tathāgatas; O all Tathāgatas, perform the vajra-activity for me!"

Thus, having prostrated to the Tathāgatas, Akṣobhya and the others, situated in the maṇḍala, by means of these five mantras in their proper order, one should again recite at the eastern gate: “Oṃ, I offer myself for the service of the Guru’s feet; Oṃ, I offer myself for the sake of protecting all sentient beings. One should cause this to be recited while preceded by an understanding of its meaning. Regarding this, some have stated that there is another placement (*nyāsa*) of the Great Bliss (*mahāsukha*) entered into the heart and so forth; however, this should not be visualized at this juncture, for that belongs to a different ritual procedure. 22.1.3 (p. 397)

"Therefore, today you have entered the family of all the Tathāgatas; thus, I shall generate in you the vajra-knowledge by which you will attain even the accomplishments (*siddhi*) of all the Tathāgatas, let alone other accomplishments. You must not speak of this before anyone who has not seen the maṇḍala, lest your *samaya* be violated. Having said this, he places the vajra on the [disciple's] head and, sounding the bell, makes him hear: "This is your *samaya*-vajra; it would shatter your head if you were to speak of this to anyone. Then, placing the vajra at his heart:
"Oṃ! Vajrasattva himself is now established within your heart;
should you speak of this method, he would depart at that very instant, having pierced through [your body].
Having thus commanded, [the preceptor] places water from atop the victory flask (*vijayakalaśa*) into the disciple's mouth by means of a vessel held with the ring finger and thumb.
This water of yours is hellish; it shall burn you for transgressing the pledge.
Through the preservation of the pledge, there is accomplishment; drink this vajra-amṛta water!
Oṃ pañcāmṛtodaka ṭhaḥ.

Having recited this and caused [the disciple] to drink from the vessel, he should say: "From this day forward, I, Vajrapāṇi, am your master. Whatever I tell you to do, that must be performed by you. You must not disregard me; lest, by failing to avoid calamity, you bring about your own death and fall into hell. Here, *te* means "you"; *nāraka* means "like the waters of the Vaitaraṇī river"; and *vajrāmṛtodaka* means "water that is a vajra in its suppression and nectar in its favor. This is the procedure for the offering of the water of the pledge (*samaya*). 22.2 The Procedure for the Descent [of the Deity] (*āveśavidhi*) (p. 400)

Thereafter, prior to the time of the actual practice, for the sake of ascertaining success and so forth, one should cause the deity to descend into a worthy disciple. In this regard, first, having performed the preparatory rites (*puraścaraṇa*) in a place favorable to the mind such as a mountain and possessing a steady mind, one should firmly rely upon the yoga of Vajrasattva. Having attained the power of possession (*āveśa*), one should consecrate (*adhivāsya*) a disciple endowed with all the auspicious marks and, placing him before oneself, instantly—immediately following the realization of emptiness—generate him in the form of Amitābha born from the syllable *ĀḤ*, and [pray]: "May all the Tathāgatas empower [him]!"

Having caused him to recite, "May Vajrasattva enter me," one should visualize a blue *hūṃ* upon a sun disk within a yellow, four-cornered earth-maṇḍala marked with a vajra born from *laṃ* at his heart; a white syllable *haḥ* upon a moon disk within a white, circular water-maṇḍala marked with a vase born from *vaṃ* at his head; and a red syllable *āḥ* upon a moon disk within a dark-blue wind-maṇḍala, shaped like a bow and marked with two fluttering banners born from *yaṃ*, at his throat.

Having summoned the Vajras of Mind, Body, and Speech by means of the light rays from the seed-syllable in one’s own heart, one should cause them to be absorbed respectively into the syllables *hūṃ*, *haḥ*, and *āḥ*, which constitute their essential nature. Then, visualizing the disciple being lifted up by the red syllable *jhaiḥ* situated upon a triangular fire-maṇḍala—which radiates beams of light and is produced from the letter *ra* transformed from the syllable *raṃ* ignited by the wind-maṇḍala beneath the feet—one should meditate on his entire body being filled by the mass of light rays from the syllable *jhaiḥ* entering through the pores of the feet and by the light rays from the syllable *hūṃ* and the others.

Preceded by the raising of incense and while ringing a bell, one should cause [the deity] to enter [the disciple], saying: "Enter! Paralyze! Ra ra ra ra! Move! Move! Hūṃ haḥ āḥ jhaiḥ! Reciting this mantra a hundred times while intent on meditation, one should effect the descent. If, once possessed, [the disciple] leaps far upward, then one should visualize a Mount Meru made of vajra above him, above that the maṇḍala of Mahendra, above that a yellow five-pronged vajra, above that the syllable *yaḥ*, and above that Vairocana; having visualized this, one should bring him back down. 22.2.2 (p.402)

When such possession has occurred, one should visualize the speech-vajra, which consists of the seed-syllable, being impelled by the light-rays from the mind-vajra seed-syllable of the disciple; and having visualized on the tongue the red syllable *ĀḤ* resting upon a moon, surrounded by a garland of flames, one should say, "Speak, O Vajra! Thus, he will truthfully declare the auspicious or inauspicious deed of himself or another.

Then, having drawn in the descended deity with rays from one's own heart and causing her to be absorbed within the seed-syllable at one's heart, and holding a vajra over the head of the disciple, one should dismiss [the deity] with "Oṃ kṛto vaḥ" and so forth, followed by "Hūṃ Haḥ Āḥ Jhaiḥ Mur. Alternatively, [one may do so] according to what was written by Ghaṇṭāpāda.
Taking a cloth from a woman stained with dust and smeared with feces, urine, and so forth— crushed, smeared with urine and excrement, and mixed with *guggulu*—
one should take it to a *preta*-fire and place it in a lotus-shaped vessel.

Having cast all of that there, standing in the *ālīḍha* posture, the Vajra-holder—possessing the nature of the three wheels and seized by wrath—should then offer incense to that one who embodies the three wheels; he will undoubtedly become possessed. (2–3)

"Stay! Greatly enter with wrath! HŪṂ! To Śrī Heruka we pay homage; to the King of Vidyās we meditate; svāhā! With this, one should impel the hero. Thus, one should effect the descent [of the deity] according to the procedure stated in the *Lakṣābhidhāna-tantra*. Sprinkled with the ten "lights of nectar," such as feces, urine, and so forth, the Guru, in the form of Saṃvara, standing in the *ālīḍha* posture, [should treat] the disciple—who is himself the essence of Saṃvara and stands in the *ālīḍha* posture with palms joined at the heart—by fumigating him with his right hand while sounding a bell with his left hand and reciting the mantra beginning with "Stay! with great majesty. Then, it should be understood that [the signs of] being possessed have occurred, and so forth.

22.2.4 (p.405) Although it is stated in some tantras that one should cause the deity to descend by placing before [the altar] a maiden of twelve years of age, whose virginity is intact and whose major and minor limbs are unimpaired, and a youth of the same age, who is ignorant of the female sphere and whose major and minor limbs are unimpaired, as the vessel;

Nevertheless, because it is proclaimed many times in other tantras that a deity may descend into a vessel—even one who is advanced in years, possesses all limbs intact, has known sexual intercourse, yet whose capacity for firm meditative cultivation (*dṛḍhabhāvanā*) has suddenly been strengthened by a Guru from whom the form of the Vajra-holder manifests at every moment through accumulated merit—one should strive for the purpose of the disciple’s possession (*āveśa*). This is the procedure for possession (*āveśavidhi*).
22.3 The Procedure for the Entry of the Disciple behind the Veil (*sāndhapaṭa-śiṣyapraveśavidhi*). (p. 406)

Then, having asked the disciple facing the maṇḍala, "What kind of appearance do you perceive with your eyes? and having ascertained his fitness for the accomplishments of pacification, enrichment, subjugation, or wrathful rites according to the sequence of the appearances he describes—whether white, yellow, red, or black—the master should take him by both thumbs with his right hand holding a vajra. Performing the vajra-step dance and reciting the *kuṇḍali* mantra, he should cause him to circumambulate three times to the right and perform the empowerment of truth (*satyādhiṣṭhāna*), saying:
"Thus, this disciple has been properly introduced into the maṇḍala by me."
May the lineage of these deities be as meritorious as this. // 1 //
Whatever kind of accomplishment may arise for him, in whatever lineage he is a vessel, and whatever the power of his merit may be—let that same [attainment] be his within this mandala. //2//
Thus concludes the procedure for the entry of the disciple behind the curtain into the maṇḍala.
23. The Procedure for the Garland Initiation (Mālābhiṣeka-vidhi) 23.1 The Procedure for the Garland Initiation.

408) Then, having previously taken a single fresh and light flower from the garland that has been consecrated with the syllable *trāṃ*, he should place it in the student's cupped hands. At that time, the student—having visualized himself as the garland of flowers, radiant with the three-syllabled mantra (*tryakṣara*), his defilements washed away, and empowered by the Guru; and having relied upon the Lord of the Maṇḍala together with the members of the assembly as if standing before him with overflowing devotion—should enter that Maṇḍala mentally and cast the flower upon its head.

"Oṃ, remain! O Vajra, be firm for me; be eternal for me; preside over my heart; grant me all accomplishments! Hūṃ ha ha ha ha hoḥ āḥ khaṃ vīra hūṃ! Accept this handful of flowers, O Lord! Hoḥ! Reciting this mantra, one should assign the practitioner's *kula* according to where the flower falls within the five lines, and should bestow the corresponding yoga and observe the signs of accomplishment (*siddhi*).

If a flower falls upon the *ūrṇā*, the crown of the head, or the *uṣṇīṣa* of the Buddhas, there is the accomplishment of the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*). If it falls on the eyes or the mouth, there is the accomplishment of Mantra. On the upper part of the body, the accomplishment is supreme; on the middle part, it is middling; and on the lower part, it is inferior. If it falls at a great distance from the image, the accomplishment comes after a long time; if near, it is swift. As for the deities, their respective places are to be known by the division of the squares and so forth.

If it falls between two deities, then whichever deity the flower is closer to belongs to that family. If it lands exactly on the boundary, the accomplishment of both rites is achieved; in that case, it belongs to whichever one the practitioner prefers. If it falls outside the five lines, one should throw again up to three times. Furthermore, if it falls outside there, the accomplishment is minor. There is no accomplishment if it falls outside the circular lines or beyond the outer vajra-garland. One must not show this mandala to such a person.

Having rendered [the disciple] fit through the recitation of mantras and so forth, he should be introduced on another occasion; for if he were to fall within the interior of the outer vajra-fence, it would be difficult.

Then, taking that flower and binding it upon the garland, one should bind that garland upon the head of the disciple while reciting: "Oṃ, accept this, O being of great power! This is the procedure for the garland initiation (mālābhiṣeka). 23.1.3 (p. 411)

In this context, even when flowers fall upon deities made of colored powder (*rajomaṇḍala*), there is no fault for one who possesses a virtuous mind; thus, there is no defect whatsoever. However, regarding one who is unacquainted [with this], it is stated in the *Vimalaprabhā* that because the colored powder might be disturbed by the falling of flowers, demerit would ensue; therefore, a flower should be cast upon the insignia located on the *vijaya-kalaśa*. Here, once possession has occurred, after the declaration of auspiciousness and so forth, [one recites]: *oṃ tiṣṭha vajra*.

Having thus strengthened the possession (*āveśa*), and having performed the sequence beginning with the inquiry regarding the appearance of the eyes and ending with the binding of the head, one should dismiss the descended deity. However, they say that if one is unable to perform the rite of possession, one should perform the inquiry regarding the appearance of the eyes and so forth immediately after the offering of the water of the pledge (*samayodaka*).
23.2 The Procedure for Entry Consisting of Vision;
Thereafter, having visualized the Lord upon the moon at the disciple’s heart, the letter *ra* on his forehead, and two blazing *oṃ*s in his two eyes, [the master recites]:
“Vajrasattva himself, intent today upon opening your eyes, opens for you the unsurpassed Vajra-eye, which perceives all. (1)

Reciting "Oṃ jñānacakṣuḥ hūṃ āḥ svāhā," one should remove the blindfold. Because it possesses all eyes and the quality of seeing everything, it is the "vajra-eye"—an eye unimpeded toward all forms, being unsurpassed like that of the Buddhas due to the removal of obscurations. Then, having said, "O Vajra, look! and having first stated the names of the deities, one should show them starting from the Lord of the Maṇḍala down to the Guardian of the Northern Gate, or as far as Sumbharāja, according to what is appropriate.
Behold now this maṇḍala with the force of your faith!
You have been born into the family of the Buddhas and are empowered by mudrās and mantras. Through the accomplishment of all siddhis, you shall become the foremost of those bound by the samaya.
"Perform the propitiation through mantras with the graceful union of the vajra and the tip of the lotus.

(3) Having recited this, [the teacher says]: "I have entered the great mandala of the Vajra-maṇḍala; I have beheld the great mandala of the Yoga-maṇḍala; I have been initiated into the great mandala of the Guhya-maṇḍala. Having caused [the disciple] to recite this, he should cause him to recite the pledge (*samaya*): "Hoḥ! Hoḥ! Hoḥ! This is the procedure for the entry consisting of the vision of the disciple into the maṇḍala.
24. The Procedure for the Water Initiation (*udakābhiṣeka*).

24.1 (p.414) Then, having given a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to the guru according to his means for the purpose of the water-consecration, with his knees placed upon the ground and palms joined in reverence, [he should say]:
"Just as the Great Festival was bestowed upon the Buddhas by Bodhivajra..."
"O Khavajra, grant this to me now for the sake of my protection as well!
Reciting thus, one should make the request.

Then, outside the root mandala, so that it is not touched by the bathing water, the guru should perform the *nīrājana* for the disciple—who has been visualized in the form of Vajradhara and is facing the mandala—at the previously described image-bathing site, beginning with "a universal lotus (*viśvapadma*) in the eastern direction facing the entrance door" and ending with "the mandala visualized on the pedestal," etc., using the previously mentioned *nīrājana* sequence: *oṃ āḥ vighna...* and so forth.

Thereafter, having worshipped the Tathāgatas and the Vidyā-devis residing in the infinite directions with rays from the seed-syllable in the heart, [he should pray] for the sake of the disciples' consecration:
"The Buddhas, the Wielders of the Vajra, bestowed the consecration upon Guṇākara for the protection of the world; likewise, please bestow it upon this one. (2)

Having thus supplicated with this verse, those Tathāgatas, having entered into wisdom and melted through great passion, entered within by way of the Vairocana-gate; emerging through the path of the vajra, they were introduced into the lotus of the Goddess by her mouth with those fluids.

Instantly, immediately after [the realization of] emptiness, the disciple is consecrated as the form of Akṣobhya together with Prajñā, born from the *hūṃ*-vajra, inseparable from the Jñānasattva. Then, emerging from the lotuses by way of their bodies with arms, faces, and so forth, they fill the sky. With steady eyes, accompanied by the Vidyās such as Locanā and others, they shower down parasols, banners, flags, garments, musical instruments, songs, dances, flowers, saffron, and the like. With white vases filled with the nectar of bodhicitta poured from hands like tender sprouts, they consecrate that disciple who has emerged from the lotuses, while being attended by goddesses such as Rūpavajrā.

Whatever auspiciousness belongs to the Great Bliss— the Lord of all excellent families, the soul of all, who dwells in the hearts of all sentient beings, and who is the progenitor of all beings— may that auspiciousness be yours today at this sublime consecration.
(3) Lakṣmīdhara, resembling a mountain of gold, Lord of the three worlds, has abandoned the three stains.
May that Buddha, whose eyes are like the petals of a fully blossomed lotus, bring auspiciousness and peace to you today!

(4) May that supreme Dharma taught by him—unshakable, renowned throughout the three worlds, honored by men and gods, the highest truth that brings peace to all beings—bring auspiciousness and peace to you today! (5)

May that Saṅgha— endowed with the True Dharma, rich in the auspiciousness of learning, worthy of offerings from humans, gods, and asuras, the abode of glory, and the most excellent of assemblies— be an auspicious cause of peace for you today. (6) 24.4 (p.419)

Thus, while auspiciousness was being brought forward by these songs of benediction, he himself sang them aloud; then, drawing small amounts from the *vijaya* and other jars, or using what was held in a lotus-bowl or a conch shell—first from the *vijaya* kalaśa—he uttered: "Oṃ! By means of the empowerment of Vajrasattva of Great Bliss, I empower you as the sovereign of all Tathāgatas; be firm! Having thus spoken, even if one does not recite [the rest] due to a preference for brevity.

Then, with water from the vases of the four Tathāgatas, then from the vases of the four Goddesses, and then from the vases of the mandala deities as appropriate—or, if these are unavailable, from the water of the *vijaya* vase, which consists of Akṣobhya in the form of the nectar of bodhicitta, flowing from the tip of a vajra with leaves—[one should perform the consecration]:
"I bestow the Great Vajra consecration, honored by the three realms, which arises from the abode of the secrets of all Buddhas. (7)

Reciting "Oṃ āḥ, consecrate with the vajra-water, hūṃ; you are I, the one of great bliss," one should perform the consecration. One should contemplate that at that time [the disciple] has entered into great bliss. This is the procedure for the water consecration. 25. The Procedure for the Crown Consecration (p. 421).

Then, one should visualize the Guru—who has been entreated with the words "therefore, by means of the Bodhi-vajra," and so forth—as having the form of Āṃ-Ratnasambhava, merged into a single unity with the Jñānasattva, being consecrated with vases by the Tathāgata goddesses stationed in the sky, and having auspicious songs presented to him by Rūpavajrā and the others. This same procedure applies to the consecrations of the Vajra-lordship and the Name.

Then, a crown fashioned from gold, cloth, and other materials, originating from the Ratna-sambhava family and possessing its nature, empowered by the five Tathāgatas in the form of Jñānasattvas who preside over the central disciple and the [other] Kuleśas, is placed respectively upon the center of his head, the forehead, the two sides, the crown, and the back. *Oṃ vajradhātvīśvary abhiṣiñca hūṃ!* *Oṃ sattvavajry abhiṣiñca bhrūṃ!* *Oṃ ratnavajry abhiṣiñca āḥ!* *Oṃ dharmavajry abhiṣiñca hrīḥ!*

"Oṃ karmavajri abhiṣiñca tāṃ [trāṃ]. Having thus established [the disciple] with these five mantras, one should place the *mahāvajra* consecration upon the head while reciting the verse beginning with "The great vajra consecration... and also recite: "Oṃ āḥ, consecrate me with the vajra-crown, hūṃ; you are passion, I am passion. Then, reciting "Vajra tuṣya hoḥ," one should cause [the disciple] to rejoice. This is the procedure for the crown consecration (*mukuṭābhiṣeka*).
Thereafter, one should bind the turban on the forehead with the mantra "Oṃ hūṃ trāṃ hrīḥ aḥ.
26. The Procedure for the Vajra Consecration (*vajrābhiṣeka*).

Then, having visualized the disciple—who has thus requested [initiation]—as Amitābha transformed from the lotus of shame (*hrī*), inseparable from the Knowledge-Being (*jñānasattva*), and likewise the *vajra* as being of the nature of Amitābha, one recites the verse beginning with "The Great Vajra Initiation" (*abhiṣekaṃ mahāvajram*):
"Today you are consecrated by the Buddhas through the vajra-consecration.
Take up this vajra, which is the state of all Buddhas, for the sake of perfect accomplishment. (1)
Reciting this, and having touched the disciple’s heart, throat, and head with the vajra, he should place it in the disciple’s right hand. This is the procedure for the vajra-consecration. 27.
The Procedure for the Bell-Consecration (p. 424).

Thereafter, having given to him who has thus requested the bell—which is the transformation of Amoghasiddhi—into his left hand [the master], as well as the bell that is non-different from the Jñānasattva [Amoghasiddhi] himself, and having caused him to perform the gesture of embracing the mudrā with both hands holding the vajra and the vajra-bell, [the master] recites the following verse beginning with "The empowerment... and then says: "Oṃ, I empower you as the Lord of Vajras; abide, O Vajra, you are the Samaya. Having recited this, he says: "Oṃ vajraghaṇṭa aḥ aḥ!
You are accepted, O Blessed One; be present within me!"
Thus one should recite. This concludes the ritual for the bell-consecration, which is another name for the consecration of sovereignty.
28. The Ritual for the Name-Consecration.

Thereafter, having visualized that [disciple] who has thus requested [initiation] as the form of Vairocana born from the *oṃ*-syllable and *cakra*, who is of one flavor with the Jñānasattva, and while placing the vajra and bell upon his head (*samanvāharayan*—*saman dhārayan* according to the Sakurai edition), one should recite the verse beginning with "The initiation... and so forth. Then, one should confer initiation in the nature of Vairocana, using either the name "Oṃ, Vajrasattva, I initiate you by means of the vajra-name initiation; you are the Vajra of Hatred" or "you are the Vajra of Delusion," and so on, or else by means of the name of one's own family determined by the falling of the flower.
In that regard, the names of Vajrasattva are Paramādya, Anupama, Surata, Samarasa, Vijaya, Alala, Sattva, Mahāsukha, Anaṅga, Jñāna, Sahaja, and Vajra;
the word "Vajra" is to be connected with each [of these]. Regarding the names of the six Tathāgatas themselves:
those of Akṣobhya are Hāsa, Vilāsa, Rati, Līlā, Lalita, Svayaṃbhū, Dveṣa, He, Karuṇācitta, Hūṃkāra, and Akṣobhyavajra.
Of Vairocana: Vairocana, Oṃkāra, Śāśvata Tathāgata, Māyābuddha, Rūpakāya, and Vajra;
of Ratnasambhava: Ratna, Cintāmaṇi, Kha, Gaganatejas, Mārtaṇḍa, Bhāskara, and Mānavajra;
of Amitābha: Rāga, Avalokita, Dharma, Padma, Vajrāṅkura, Padmāṅkura, Suratāṅkura, Karuṇāṅkura, Paramānanda, Suratānanda, and Amitavāgvajra.
From Amoghasiddhi arise Amoghaparamāśva, Samayapāramitā, Karmānila, Sparśavajrā, and Īrṣyāvajrā.

28.2 (p.428) For Vajrasattva, there are Vajravegī, Vajravilāsinī, Vajramadā, Vajrakoṅkaṇā, Vajrānanā, Vajrapatākā, Vajramālā, and Vajrodayā. For Akṣobhya, there are Vajranairātmyā, Vajrahastā, Vajrāvalī, Vajrakarā, Vajramāmakī, and Dveṣarati.
Of Vairocana are Vajraḍākinī, Vajragaurī, Vajralāsyā, Vajralocanā, and Moharati;
of Ratnasaṃbhava are Vajrahārā, Vajrāśvāsā, Vajrajvālā, Vajramālā, Vajrākāśā, and Ākāśarati;
of Amitābha are Vajrarāgā, Vajragītā, Vajrāhosukhā, Vajravetālī, Vajramatī, Vajrahāsyā, Vajrapāṇḍarā, and Rāgarati.
Of Amoghasiddhi, there are Vajragarvā, Vajramāyā, Vajravaḍabā, Vajratārā, Vajranarteśvarī, Samayavajrā, and Vajrarati. This is the ritual for the name-consecration.

These six consecrations, beginning with the garland and water, are called the "consecrations of knowledge" (*vidyābhiṣeka*) because they produce the fitness that is the antidote to ignorance. A disciple consecrated by these [six] becomes authorized to hear, explain, and practice the mantras of the *Kriyā* and *Caryā* tantras. As for the *Yoga* and *Yoginī* tantras, the opinion of those who consider themselves masters (*ācārya*) is that [the disciple is authorized] even there; however, this is not based on scripture (*anāgama*). For nowhere did the Blessed One teach that it is possible to describe the true nature of those [higher tantras] without the vow of the innate consecration (*sahajaseka-saṃvara*), nor was such a teaching improper.
These consecrations are bestowed upon those who do not seek the master’s consecration (ācāryābhiṣeka) after first granting them the common vows;
however, for those who do seek it, they are bestowed preceded by both sets of vows.
29. The Ritual Procedure for Granting the Three Samayas.
29.1 Then, to that disciple who has offered the ritual fee and joined his palms in reverence, [the master says]:
"O treasure of compassion, please grant me the initiation of the Vajrācārya."
"May I become capable of accomplishing the welfare of both myself and others through your grace.
Having recited this, one should meditate on the *vajra*—which was requested by the guru—as being born from the syllable *hūṃ* and having the form of Vajrasattva:
"The Being who is without beginning or end, Vajrasattva, the Great Joy."

"Samantabhadra, the self of all, the Lord of Vajragarva, the Lord, the Blessed One, the Primordial Supreme Person"—reciting thus, one should cause [the disciple] to grasp this through its true nature. This is the Vajra-samaya; he is the Lord of the World.
29.2 Then, having meditated upon the bell as born from the syllable ĀḤ, [one should recite]:
"This is the bell of all Buddhas, known as Ghoṣānugā."
"For you too must always uphold the supreme enlightenment regarded as such by the Victors.
Reciting this, he should cause [the student] to grasp it in its true nature. Following after the sound flowing effortlessly, the bell is like the wisdom of the Buddha;
the disciple, however, [should grasp] that [sound].
"Existence is indeed pure by its own nature, yet it is made into non-existence by [conceptual] natures;

by beings who are truly existent and pure by their own nature, supreme existence is brought about. Speaking thus, one should play [the bell]. "By superimposed natures, it is made into a contradictory existence"—this is the *ghaṇṭā-samaya* (bell commitment).
29.3 (p.432) Following that,
he [should visualize] him; for the mudrā is said to be the commitment (samaya), because of its firmness as a mental form.
That by which all forms are made firm is proclaimed as the *mudrā*.
(5) Having thus empowered the *jñānamudrā*, through the enjoyment of all desires...
Accomplish all siddhis!

Having thus established the form of Vajrasattva as the *jñānamudrā* through the sequence of union (*sampuṭakrama*), one should perform the gesture of embracing. As it is said in the *Paramādya-tantra*:

"Grasping the *vajra* with its essential reality (*tattva*) and sounding the *ghaṇṭā* with the Dharma, and having empowered the *mahāmudrā* with the Samaya, one should recite the mantra from the heart. (6)
Thus is the pledge of the mudrās; thus is the ritual procedure for taking up the three pledges.
30. The Ritual for the Master’s Initiation (Ācāryābhiṣekavidhi) 30.1 (p. 434):

Thereafter, having had [the candidate]—who has undertaken the three samayas—seated either in the bathing mandala as before or elsewhere, and having visualized him in the form of Vajrasattva, [the master] should perform [the initiation] according to the procedure stated for the water initiation, from the seed-syllable in the heart onwards, with [water] dripping from the tip of the vajra.

"I bestow the great vajra consecration, honored by the three realms, which arises from the abode of the three secrets of all Buddhas. (1) Reciting "Oṃ āḥ sarvatathāgatābhiṣeka samaya śriye hūṃ svāhā," one should perform the consecration.
Then, having visualized [the deity] with Akṣobhya as his crown-ornament, one should cause the other Tathāgatas and their goddesses to enter into that very form of the Jñānasattva.
Having empowered it with the mantra: *oṃ supratiṣṭhita vajre svāhā*, one should offer flowers and so forth to him. And thus it has been said:
"Embracing the sixteen-year-old Prajñā with both hands..."
Through the union of the bell and the vajra, the consecration of the master is considered [to be performed].
(2) Thus it is said.
435) Therefore, in brief, this nature of Vairocana, namely the peaked pavilion (*kūṭāgāra*), is the reality (*tattva*) and purification (*viśuddhi*) of the mandala.
In summary, the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) are the five Buddhas.

By such statements, the reality (*tattva*) and purification (*viśuddhi*) of the deities are established. However, from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), because even the mandalas and so forth are characterized by the absence of intrinsic nature (*naiḥsvābhāvya*) in both stages [of generation and completion], suchness (*tathatā*) alone is the reality and purification. One should also explain the preliminary preparations of the master (*ācārya-parikarman*), such as the drawing of the mandala together with its peripheral equipment.

Thus, the attainment of knowledge regarding the reality of the mandala and so forth, as well as the fulfillment of the vow (*saṃvara*) consisting of what is to be done and what is not to be done—characterized by a form of commitment (*samaya*) that must not be transgressed—is declared to be "fitness" (*bhavyatā*). However, the reality of the mandala and other such matters have been described by us in detail in the *Āmnāyamañjarī*. This concludes the procedure for the Master’s Initiation (*ācāryābhiṣeka*), which is also known by the name "Irreversible Initiation.
31. The Procedure for the Bestowal of Mantras (p. 437):
Thereafter, one should personally recite three times the Heart-mantra and other mantras, having performed the recitation one hundred and eight times.
"You have been given by me, O Blessed One; be present here."
Saying this, he should give [the mantra] to the disciple. The disciple also [should say]:
"O Blessed One, you have been received by me; remain present within me."
Having grasped [the bell] with this [verse], one should recite it three times. This is the procedure for the offering of the mantra.
This very [procedure] is called the "mantra-consecration" (mantrābhiṣeka) in other tantras, such as the *Buddhakapāla*, and by Ghaṇṭāpāda.
32. The Ritual of Collyrium (Añjanavidhi):

Thereafter, having placed collyrium made of ghee and honey into a vessel of gold or silver, and having visualized the syllable *praṃ* in the eyes of the disciple with a golden probe, one should apply the collyrium while reciting: *Oṃ vajranetrāpahara paṭalaṃ hrīḥ*. Then one says:
"O child, the veil of ignorance has been removed from you by the Victors."

One should say: "Just as the king of physicians with his probes [removes] the cataract of the world. This means it has been removed because its fitness for removal has been brought about. Thus ends the procedure for the collyrium. 33.
The Procedure for the Consecration of the Mirror (p. 438).
Then, taking up a mirror and consecrated with the syllable *Āḥ*, he shows it to the disciple:
"All phenomena are like reflections; they are transparent, pure, and unclouded;
they are ungraspable and inexpressible, arising from causes and karma. (1)
Like a mirror, O Vajrasattva, you are clear, pure, and undisturbed;
for within your heart, my child, dwells the Lord of all Buddhas himself.
Having thus understood that all phenomena are without intrinsic nature and without abode, (2).
"Perform the incomparable benefit of sentient beings; you have been born upon the chest of the Protectors. Thus one should say.

It is *accha* (clear) because it is free from the turbidity of the afflictions (*kleśa*); it is *śuddha* (pure) because it is devoid of the veil of the knowable (*jñeyāvaraṇa*); it is *anāvila* (unclouded) because the latencies (*vāsanā*) of those two have departed. The first verse refers to natural purity (*prakṛtiviśuddhi*), while the second refers to purity through the removal of stains (*vaimalyaviśuddhi*). He abides in those qualities by way of empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*), as an object of attainment (*prāpyatva*), and as an objective support (*ālambana*) through his capacity. This is the ritual procedure for the mirror consecration (*darpaṇābhiṣeka*).

While explaining two methods for viewing the mirror, the *Āryanāgabuddhipādīya-maṇḍalopāyikā* has not been seen at all. However, some have stated that the method of viewing twice was taught because of a lack of intention to describe the consecration (*abhiṣeka*).
34. The Ritual for Shooting Arrows (p. 440).

Then, having given the bow born from the syllable *hoḥ* while reciting "Hoḥ!", one should say: "Make all the Tathāgatas impassioned. And at the time of shooting the arrows, the disciple, reciting "I make all the Tathāgatas impassioned," should shoot four arrows in the four directions with the intention of piercing away obstacles—one upward, one downward, and the others [in the cardinal directions]. This is the procedure for shooting the arrows. 35.
The Procedure for the Secret Empowerment (Guhyābhiṣeka-vidhi) 35.1 (p. 441)

Then, once the area has been made secluded by means of a curtain or similar screen, the disciple, having presented to the Guru for the sake of the secret initiation a Wisdom Consort (*prajñā*) endowed with fresh youth and other qualities—or another woman if such a consort is unavailable—and having joined his palms in reverence while visualizing the Guru as Vajrasattva, says:
"By the grace of your feet, I have attained the unsurpassed practice;
therefore, O Lord, grant me your favor through the secret initiation. (1)
Thus one should request with this verse.

Then the Guru, possessing the ego-identity (*ahaṃkāra*) of the Lord of the Mandala (*cakreśa*), having first performed the consecration of the vajra and lotus, enters into union with her—who has been manifested in the form of a goddess immediately following the emptiness of the ordinary female form—reciting: *Oṃ, I am of the nature of the vajra which is the passion of all Tathāgatas.*

Reciting thus, one should visualize the Tathāgatas such as Vairocana, who have entered through the eyes and other sense-faculties by means of the rays of light from the heart-seed syllable, and having caused them to enter oneself through the gate of Vairocana, one should contemplate them melting through great passion and emerging via the *avadhūtī*. Having stabilized that innate [bliss] within the vajra-jewel, one should press the jewel with the thumb and ring finger, lift it from the lotus, and—imagining that the liquid of the Tathāgata is non-different from one’s own bodhicitta—show it to the mouth of the disciple in the form of the Speech-Vajra; because there might be a fear of lack of faith upon seeing it, it is kept beyond the range of vision by having the blindfold tied on.

"Just as the sons of the Buddha were sprinkled by the past Vajradhara and others, so do I sprinkle you, O child, with the beautiful *bodhicitta*. (2) Reciting the mantra of the Lord of the Maṇḍala, beginning with "Oṃ Āḥ Vajradhṛk Hūṃ," according to the respective tantra, one should pour [the water]. He too, with the perception that he is the assembly of all Tathāgatas such as Vairocana, exclaims: "Aho! Great Bliss!"
Speaking thus, he should drink.

Having awakened the consort (*prajñā*), he should rise and, remaining naked, place drops of the nectar of the *tathāgata* situated upon his own lotus into her mouth. She too should drink in that same manner. This is the procedure for the secret initiation (*guhyābhiṣeka*), which is the initiation by means of the two secrets—the concealed bodhicitta of both wisdom (*prajñā*) and method (*upāya*).
36. The Procedure for the Initiation of the Wisdom-Knowledge (*prajñājñānābhiṣeka*)

36.1 (p.444) Thereafter, when the disciple has requested—either that [consort] or another woman who abides by the pledges and vows, or another woman endowed with beauty and youth—with the verse beginning "By means of the Bodhi-vajra," [the teacher says]:
"This delightful dhāraṇī of yours is to be cultivated; it was devised by the Buddhas."
Through the application of the sequence of the wheel, taste the true bliss.
"Beholding the mind within the jewel from the vajra-paryaṅka posture," having thus established [this], one should offer it.
She too, displaying a lotus flower—an unblemished garment made fragrant with saffron and other perfumes—said to the disciple:
"Aha! My lotus is endowed with every bliss;
for him who serves it according to the prescribed rite, I stand before him. (2)
"O Padme, perform the necessary tasks such as the propitiation of the Perfectly Awakened One;
for the King of Great Bliss himself is always present right here.
(3) One should say: "Embrace liberation! Hoḥ!"

He himself, as the form of the deity, having generated Prajñā in the form of a goddess, visualizes the filaments and jewels of the lotus and vajra produced from *hrīḥ* and *hūṃ*, and the yellow syllable *phaṭ* produced from *āḥ* and *oṃ* at the opening of the vajra. Then, having drawn in the channel located in the left-left limb by means of the tongue and the forefinger marked with a red *hrīḥ* at its tip—preceded by the sound *śīṭ*—he recites: *oṃ śī śī śī ha ha ha svāhā*. And: *oṃ sarvatathāgatānurāgaṇavajrasvabhāvātmako ’ham*.

Thus reciting the mantra and having experienced the various forms of bliss through the teacher’s instruction, his body being empowered by the Tathāgatas and others drawn forth by the rays from the seed-syllable in his own heart, and having become of one flavor with the infinite Vairocana, Locanā, and the rest who have been introduced by the teacher, he should begin the rati.
Through contact with the Prajñā, the glorious one should perceive the reality (*tattva*), while gazing at the mind within the jewel [of the *vajra*] from the *vajraparyaṅka* posture. (4)

Having reflected thus, and having maintained [the practice] according to one's ability, one should gradually release [the tongue] and, having extracted [the substance] from the lotus with the tongue itself, one should drink the *bodhicitta* in its form as the *samaya* by means of the vision of reality (*tattvadṛṣṭi*).

"Cakra" refers to the mandala (*cakra*) of deities such as Vairocana together with their vidyās; its "application" (*prayoga*) consists of the sequential process of summoning, entering, and emerging via the path of the vajra. "Ritual procedure" (*vidhāna*) refers to the production of the forms of the goddesses and so forth. Regarding "liberation" (*mokṣa*), the Guru must explain liberation as being free from all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) and as the supreme form of the deity. "Reality" (*tattva*) is the inconceivability of all phenomena; because it conforms to the reflection of that [reality], the wisdom-knowledge (*prajñājñāna*) whose nature is innate bliss (*sahajānanda*) is called reality. "Mind" (*citta*) is the bodhicitta. "Jewel" (*maṇi*) refers to the [tip of] the vajra.

If a woman is being consecrated, then the jewel is that of the lotus. "Gazing" (*īkṣayan*) means looking at the gaze; "making [her] gaze" (*īkṣan*) is the meaning of "gazing" (*īkṣamāṇa*). Thus ends the procedure for the consecration of wisdom-knowledge (*prajñājñāna*).
37. The Fourth Consecration (p. 448).

Immediately after that, one should bestow the fourth consecration by means of speech alone. One should explain that very same wisdom-knowledge (*prajñājñāna*), which is the sprouted *bodhicitta*, as it increases through meditative cultivation and attains freedom from obscuration; it is reality (*tattva*) whose nature is the inconceivability of all phenomena, possessing the seven limbs, having the nature of the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*), and being the essence of the Great Vajradhara—this is the form of the fourth consecration. Thus concludes the procedure for the fourth consecration.
38. The Procedure for Bestowing the Vidyā-vow (p. 448).

Immediately after that, having placed the hand of that Prajñā into the hand of the disciple and holding those two with his own left hand, he places his right hand, together with the vajra, upon the head of the disciple and says: "You are witnesses here; she has been offered by me to him."
Thus, having taken the Tathāgatas as witnesses:
"Buddhahood is not attained by any other means, and these three worlds are pure; therefore, never be separated from this [wisdom]. (1)
"This is that unsurpassed vidyā-vow of all the Buddhas;
for the fool who transgresses it, there shall be no supreme accomplishment.
(2) Speaking thus, one should bestow the vidyā-vow. This is the procedure for the bestowal of the vidyā-vow.
39. The Ritual of the Vajra Vow (Vajravratavidhiḥ).
Thereafter, having visualized the disciple in the form of Vajrasattva, [the master says]:
"This very state of all Buddhas resides in the hand of Vajrasattva."

"For you too, the firm vow of Vajrapāṇi must always be maintained. (1) Reciting this, he should cause [the disciple] to take up the vajra. He, however, should take it up while reciting: "Oṃ! O Vajrasattva, you who are the accomplishment of all Tathāgatas, remain as the vajra-samaya! I maintain you! Hīḥ! Hi hi hi hi hūṃ! This is the procedure for the Vajra-vow. 40. The Procedure for Bestowing the Conduct-Vow (*caryāvratadānavidhi*).
450) Then, having recited three times over the khaṭvāṅga, the ḍamaru, and the lotus vessel the heart-mantra of any one of the deities such as Buddhakapāla, Saṃvara, or Hevajra, [the preceptor] says:
"O Hero, take this khaṭvāṅga and the ḍamaru vessel."
"This is the mudrā of Śrī Vajrasattva, abiding both externally and internally.

Reciting this verse, he should cause [the disciple] to take [it]. Or else, as stated in another tantra, he should cause him to take another limb of conduct (*caryāṅga*) other than the skull-topped staff (*khaṭvāṅga*) and so forth, by saying, "Take that which has been consecrated by the heart-mantra of each respective Lord of the Mandala," and so on. And likewise in the *Śrīsamāja*:
"The great image, bearing a crown of matted hair, resembling white in color..."
One should cause everything to be performed according to the rules, fully restrained by the vows of mantra.
"One should partake of all food and edibles consisting of bulbs, roots, and fruits.
By such statements, the *caryāvratam* (observance of conduct) is taught for the purpose of undertaking the *vidyāvrata* (observance of knowledge).

Whichever woman or man requests the vow of conduct (*caryāvrata*), one should visualize her in the form of Vajravārāhī or Nairātmyā, or in the form of whichever Family Goddess corresponds to the [result of] the flower-fall; and the man as any one of the forms such as Saṃvara-Hevajra. Then, having caused the Wisdom Deity (*jñānadevatā*)—summoned by rays from the seed-syllable in the heart of that [deity] or him—to enter, [one should know:
Akṣobhya is in the form of the wheel, Amitābha is the nature of the earrings, Ratneśa is in the necklace around the neck, and Vairocana is said to be in the hand.

"Amoṣa resides in the girdle. (3) Having spoken thus, one should instantly visualize the wheel, earrings, necklace, bracelets, and girdle as being, respectively, the forms of Akṣobhya, Amitābha, Ratnasaṃbhava, Vairocana, and Amoghasiddhi. Then, having caused the respective Jñānasattvas to enter them as they have been invited, and having resolved that the mudrās—the wheel and so forth—which are transformations of Akṣobhya and the others, are themselves of the very nature of Akṣobhya and the rest, [one recites]: *oṃ dhara dhara dhāraya dhāraya marda marda vajradhṛk phaṭ svāhā*.

Having recited this mantra three times, one should place a *cakrī* (crown) upon the head of that [disciple] or herself, while reciting the verse beginning with "Take hold" (*gṛhṇa*). In the case of a female, having substituted the reading "O Goddess" (*devī*) for "O Hero" (*vīra*), one should place it on while reciting. With the mantra: *oṃ vajradharma samayas tvaṃ hulu hulu ārolik phaṭ svāhā*, one should place two earrings (*kuṇḍala*) upon the ears after reciting it three times. With the mantra: *oṃ vajrasūrya tamovidhūnana samayas tvam ahaṃ ratnadhṛk phaṭ svāhā*, one should place a necklace (*kaṇṭhikā*) around the neck after reciting it three times.

"Oṃ śāśvata paramaśāśvata ehy ehi jinajik phaṭ svāhā. Having recited this three times, one should place two bracelets (*rucaka*) on the hands like bangles. "Oṃ phu phu hi hi hi prajñādhṛk phaṭ svāhā. Having recited this three times, one should place a girdle (*mekhalā*) on the hips. Then, according to the sequence—whether [referring to] the Goddess (*devī*) or the Hero (*vīra*)—one should assign them as follows: "the Cakrī who has the form of Akṣobhya," "the two earrings (*kuṇḍala*) of Vāgvajra," "the necklace (*kaṇṭhikā*) of Ratnasaṃbhava," "the bracelet (*rucaka*) whose nature is Śāśvata," and "the girdle (*mekhalā*) of Amoghasiddhi. Having added these, one should recite the words beginning with "grasp" (*gṛhṇa*).

40.3 However, if a woman or a man who has attained the capacity for vision and so forth wishes to undertake the vow of the Hero’s Conduct (*vīracaryāvrata*) for the sake of others, one should visualize her in the form of Vajravārāhī and him in the form of Saṃvara, as having a single flavor with the Jñānasattva. Having resolved upon the wheel and so forth as before, and the garland of severed heads and so forth as being the nature of their respective mantra-deities, one should recite three times: *Oṃ vajravairocanīye hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*. With this, one should place the wheel upon him in the same manner. Furthermore, there are five skull-cups representing the five Buddhas, as it has been said:
"Vairocanī is the mantra for one whose head is adorned with a skull-cup.
Here, "skull-cup" (*kapāla*) also refers to the form of a wheel (*cakrī*). *Oṃ hrīḥ ha ha hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ*—this, recited three times, is the two earrings. As it has been said:
"The earring that beautifies the ear is made with the seven-syllable mantra."
Thus, with the root mantra of Vajravārāhī, or with the mantra beginning "Oṃ sarvabuddha... and so forth, one should recite [the mantra] three times over a necklace (kaṇṭhikā). As it has been said:
"Whatever mantra of Vajravārāhī adorns the neck, it is the necklace."

Thus: *oṃ hanamahi svāhā hūṃ vauṣaṭ he hūṃ hūṃ ho phaṭ hūṃ*. This mantra, recited three times, consecrates two bracelets (*rucaka*). As it is said: "O Hero, this mudrā, which beautifies the limbs, belongs to the Armor [mantra] by means of the six [syllables]."

Thus: *oṃ vaṃ hāṃ yoṃ hrīṃ moṃ hroṃ hrīṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ*. Having recited this mantra three times over the girdle, it is as stated: "The girdle is made into an ornament by means of the mantra of the Six Yoginīs."
Thus:
*Oṃ śrīvajra he he ru ru kaṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ ḍākinījālasaṃvaraṃ svāhā*. Having recited this three times, one should place a garland of fifty severed heads around the neck. As it has been said:
The heart-mantra of the deity is indeed a garland adorned with fifty [syllables].
Thus: *Oṃ sarvabuddhaḍākinīye vajravarṇanīye hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*. This should be recited three times, and one should wear a tiger skin as clothing. As it is said:
"The supreme [attainment] of the Ḍākinī of all Buddhas consists in wearing garments of skin."

Thus, with the thirty-six mantras beginning with *oṃ pracaṇḍe hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ* and ending with *oṃ rūpiṇīye hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ*, the vessel for drinking the nectar of gnosis (*jñānāmṛta*) is recited over three times and placed in the hand. As it is said:
"The yoginīs of the entire wheel [hold] the skull-cup for drinking the mantra."
Thus: having consecrated the khaṭvāṅga and the ḍamaru three times with the root mantra of the Bhagavān, one should take them up with the verse beginning "gṛhṇa" (take hold).

With the root mantra of Śrī Saṃvara, one should recite [the mantra] three times over the sacred thread (*brahmasūtra*), the necklace suspended from the neck, and the vajra ornament; likewise, the crown made of the hair of a thief, the double-wrapped hair-braid, the ash, the armlet, the anklet, and the *ghurghurā* bell, each in its respective place. As it is said: "The hero of the root mantra is fashioned as the sacred thread and so forth."
Thus it is said.

In that regard, the *brahmasūtra* (sacred thread) should be made with one string; the girdle (*mekhalā*) with eight strings; that same [girdle] on the waist of a woman with sixteen strings; and the necklace (*hāra*) with twenty-five strings. As it has been stated:
"The sacred thread should consist of a single strand, while the girdle consists of eight strands."
The *rasanā* is to be known as sixteenfold, while the *mālinī* is twenty-fivefold.
(4) Thus [it is said]. 40.5 (p. 458)

Alternatively, the sacred thread (*brahmasūtra*) may be made of human bone or hair; herein, the wheel and other [ornaments] should be fashioned from human bone as appropriate, along with the vajras for the jewelry. That single [thread] is worn on the topknot; it is said that having cut it into five-finger-width sections, it is worn upon the crown.

Thus: other ornaments for the ears, neck, heart, secret place, and arms are to be worn as they appear beautiful. The thirty-six mantras and the two root mantras have been described by us in the *Śrīsaṃvarābhisamayopāyikā*.

The vow of the conduct of heroes (*vīracaryāvratam*) is indeed called the conduct of the vow of the crown prince (*yauvarājyavratacaryā*), and it is also called the vow of the conduct of the Vajra-Kāpālika, as stated in the *Śrīsaṃpuṭatantra*.
Following that, one should worship the five mudrās and so forth. This is the ritual procedure for bestowing the vow of conduct (*caryāvratadānavidhiḥ*).
41. The Procedure for Prophecy (Vyākaraṇavidhi).
Then, having assumed the *tathāgata-īrṣyā* posture, placing the left fist—holding the corner of the saffron robe—at the heart, and with the right hand in the *abhaya-mudrā*, [the Tathāgata says]:
"I, Vajrasattva, the Tathāgata, hereby prophesy you."
"Having extracted [the disciple] from the miserable states of existence (*durgati*), for the sake of the ultimate pacification of existence (*bhava*):

'O Amukavajra Tathāgata, may you attain accomplishment; you are the *samaya*; Bhūr Bhuvaḥ Svaḥ! Reciting this mantra, one should perform the prophecy (*vyākaraṇa*). The disciple is to be prophesied as having the form of whichever Tathāgata corresponds to the falling of the flower. It should be believed that whoever is thus prophesied is prophesied by all the Tathāgatas for perfect enlightenment (*saṃbodhi*). This is the procedure for the prophecy.

These—namely, the knowledge (*vidyā*), the vajra-conduct (*vajracaryā*), the vow (*vrata*), and the prophecy—are in some instances designated as consecrations (*abhiṣeka*) at the beginning of certain tantras."
42. The Ritual of Authorization 42.1 (p.
460) Thereafter:
"That fourth [empowerment] is likewise again," as stated immediately thereafter;
[it is given] to the disciple whose defilements have been removed by the empowerment of the awakening mind (bodhicitta).
Then, however, one should grant permission.

Thus, according to the *Saṃpuṭa*, [the preceptor] should place the syllable *bhrūṃ* on a seat somewhere in front of the disciple’s seat as the Wheel of Dharma (*dharmacakra*). Reciting “*oṃ vajrahetu maṃ*,” he places [an implement] in the right hand; reciting “*oṃ vajrabhāṣa raṃ*,” he places a conch born from the syllable *āḥ* in the left hand; and while reciting the first vowel (*a*), he gives a book born from that same [first] vowel, and while reciting the final vowel (*aḥ*), he gives a bell born from the final vowel, making the disciple ring that bell:
“Everything has the characteristic of space, and space itself is without characteristics.
Through the union with the equality of space, the supreme equality of all things is made manifest. (1)
"From this day forward, by the mere arising of the thought [of awakening], turn the wheel of Dharma;
for you have completely filled the unsurpassed conch of Dharma in every direction.
Thus he should say.

"Foremost of all" means that the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*)—the pinnacle of all phenomena due to its being free from obscuration—is clearly and directly perceived through meditative cultivation; you too should do likewise. Now, furthermore, by resolving upon that [nature], the bell indicates: "Turn the Wheel of Dharma.
462) Having thus granted general permission, in order to grant specific permission, one should visualize the disciple in the form of Vairocana and so forth, in due order.
For the sake of the welfare of all sentient beings, throughout all worlds and in every way, turn the wheel of Dharma for the entire universe according to their respective dispositions. You,
whose very nature is wisdom and skillful means, are like a supreme wish-fulfilling gem.
"Unwearied and free from attachment, act now for the sake of sentient beings.
(4) Thus, by substituting the word "Dharma" with the words "Vajra," "Ratna," "Padma," and "Karma," one should grant permission through these fivefold recitations.
Having prostrated, he should say:
"I shall do exactly as my lord commands."
Thus ends the procedure for permission.
43. The Procedure for Consolation.
Thereafter,
holding a parasol over his head and having performed a circumambulation,
he should speak while joining his palms at the entrance of the mandala and lowering the parasol.
"This disciple who has been introduced shall become a holder of the tantra.
(1) Having thus petitioned the Lord of the Maṇḍala and set aside the parasol, he should speak words that reach the heart of the disciple:
"Now you are the master of the maṇḍala and a holder of the mantra-tantra."
It is esteemed by the Buddhas, the Bodhisattvas, and the deities.
Out of compassion for sentient beings, you should diligently draw the maṇḍala according to the prescribed rite, and practitioners should be applied to the tantra.
Having seen and entered this supreme, most secret, and excellent maṇḍala,
you are today liberated from all sins and are well-established.
There shall be no further falling away for you from this vehicle of great bliss.
The suffering of existence has ceased for you, for the sake of the ultimate accomplishment of liberation from existence.
(5) O Long-lived One, today you have been consecrated by all the Buddhas together with the Vajra-holders;
it is certain that you are the sovereign lord of the great kingdom of the three realms. (6)
There is no other evil in the three realms equal to dispassion;
therefore, you must never again practice detachment from sensual desires. Instead, take delight in the enjoyment of all pleasures, free from fear of anything whatsoever. (7)
The nectar of the five meats is to be consumed; this is the samaya for one other than a rākṣasa.
(8) Indeed, one must not commit the killing of living beings, nor should one abandon the jewel of a woman.
One must not forsake the master; the vow is difficult to transgress. (9)
There is nothing that cannot be accomplished by a mind endowed with wisdom and skillful means;

do not fear, for there is no sin in you, according to the word of the Tathāgata. (10) Thus, make your mind a diamond of clarity; cultivate your own commitment (*svasamaya*), which bestows inexhaustible bliss.
"In this world of fleeting pleasures, you have today attained the eternal state that is equal to Vajrasattva.

(11) Moreover, this is the very nature of things (*dharmatā*): one who has been consecrated according to the ritual rules is attended by all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas with clear minds, as if toward a beloved son, solely for the sake of his welfare. Thus is the procedure for consolation.
And the disciple, having thus received initiation, being confident and joyful, thinks:
"I shall act in this way;
today my birth has become fruitful, and my life has become fruitful."

"Today I am born into the family of the Buddha; I am now a son of the Buddha"—thus he should say. And he should respectfully give to the Guru as an offering, according to his ability, elephants, horses, jewels, gold, silver, clothing, ornaments, cows, buffaloes, male and female slaves, laborers, and so forth, as well as his beloved wife, daughters, sons, and others. He should also perform offerings of oblations (*bali*), fire-sacrifices (*homa*), communal feasts (*bhojya*), and so on.

"Completely liberated" means being well-established through the restraint of non-virtuous actions, and being perfected through the attainment of the *dharmakāya* by way of the certainty of a happy rebirth. "Ultimately" refers to existence being without end; the *saṃbhogakāya* is eternal because it is non-decaying. "Vajra" refers to the indivisible clarity of mind toward the Guru, the Buddhas, and so forth. "One's own commitment" (*svasamaya*) refers to one’s own deity and so forth. Although you were born into a world of little happiness and much suffering, you have attained the eternity of faultless great bliss.
44. The Ritual for One’s Own Initiation (Svasyābhiṣekavidhi) 44.1.1 (p. 468)

In this context, there is the consecration with a garland upon the head in order to illuminate the natural purity of the disciple, who possesses the nature of a Tathāgata as indicated by the falling of the flower;
and there is the water consecration in order to instill the capacity for the cleansing of the stains of ignorance.

The crown consecration (*mukuṭābhiṣeka*) is for the purpose of applying the refinement of the Tathāgata’s sealing and for the fitness to accomplish the *uṣṇīṣa*. The binding of the hero’s ribbon (*vīrapaṭṭabandha*) is for the uprooting of the enemies such as the afflictions; it is an accessory to the crown consecration. In some places this is treated as a separate consecration, but in others the binding of the ribbon is not mentioned, because its purpose is accomplished by the crown consecration alone due to a particular intention. The vajra consecration (*vajrābhiṣeka*) is for the sake of instilling the fitness for the arising of indivisible gnosis.

The empowerment by means of the ringing bell, which indicates the source of phenomena (*dharmodayā*), is for the purpose of awakening [the disciple] through the sovereign power of the arising of non-dual gnosis that is inseparable from unsurpassed emptiness and compassion. Because it is an empowerment for the sake of that sovereignty, it is called the "empowerment of sovereignty" (*ādhipatyābhiṣeka*).
The name-empowerment (*nāmābhiṣeka*) is for the purpose of implanting the seed of the name suitable for the future station of a Lord of Sages.

Furthermore, these five—beginning with the sprinkling of water—should be resolved upon as being of the nature of the perfectly pure *dharmadhātu*, equality, discernment, performance of duty, and mirror-like gnosis (*ādarśajñāna*), through the nourishment of their respective seeds. That the sprinkling of water is of the nature of mirror-like gnosis is also stated in the *Tattvasaṃgraha*: "Akṣobhya is also of the nature of mirror-like gnosis.

From this point forward, "vajrasamaya" is the binding through the act of binding by means of maintaining the nature of that [reality]— which is the intent to become resolute in attaining the awakening of the pure union (*viśuddhayuganaddhabodhi*)—
and "ghaṇṭāsamaya" is for the purpose of enjoining the attainment of suchness (*tathatā*), which is the source for teaching the eighty-four thousand aggregates of Dharma (*dharmaskandha*).

The *mudrā-samaya* is for the purpose of instilling a firm capacity for the nature of a perfectly awakened Buddha, which consists of great bliss (*mahāsukha*) and is composed of wisdom (*prajñā*) and skillful means (*upāya*). For this very reason, the *Ḍākinīvajrapañjara* states that the consecration of a perfectly awakened Buddha (*sambuddhābhiṣeka*) is precisely the *mudrā-samaya*, as it is encompassed by the two [other] *samayas*. However, in other tantras, a triad of *samayas* is said to be the prerequisite for the master’s consecration (*ācāryābhiṣeka*). As was stated previously in the passage beginning with "by the two hands," etc., there is no contradiction because the capacity for the cleansing of impurities exists within both systems of *samaya* establishment.

Just as on the tenth stage (*bhūmi*), the great Bodhisattvas who are non-retrogressive (*avaivartika*) are consecrated by the Tathāgatas of the ten directions, so too this [practitioner], surrounded by the three pledges, is consecrated into the Dharma-kingdom of the triple world by those [deities] and by the Guru, through immeasurable teachings for the sake of the infinite mass of sentient beings, in order to act as their preceptor (*ācārya*). Thus, it is the "Preceptor Consecration" (*ācāryābhiṣeka*), and because it is like that of the non-retrogressives, it is also the "Non-retrogressive Consecration" (*avaivartikābhiṣeka*).
Furthermore, the seed of non-retrogression is thus implanted.

For this very reason, with respect to that [attainment], the consecration for non-retrogression (*avaivartya*) and the consecration for non-reversal (*avivarta*) are called the "consecration of non-retrogression" (*avaivartyaseka*) and the "consecration of non-reversal" (*avivartaseka*). For this very reason, what is known as the Master (*ācārya*) is here said to be threefold by virtue of the Vajra, the Secret, and the Knowledge [consecrations].
Such is the view of the wicked-minded alone.

471) The recitation of mantras is for the sake of being free from obstacles, for planting the seeds of accomplishments such as peace (*śānti*), and for purifying the field of ultimate mantra-accomplishment.
The ointment is for the arising of the superknowledge of the divine eye through the removal of the film of ignorance.
And the mirror consecration is for the purpose of instilling the refinement that perceives the entire universe as a reflection by means of that [divine eye].
The casting of the arrow is for the purpose of implanting the seed for penetrating the objective of the extremely subtle dharmadhātu through the victory over the four Māras.

The secret initiation (*guhyābhiṣeka*) is for the purpose of making faith and wisdom into a field, for the purpose of guarding the commitments (*samaya*), and for the purpose of purifying speech. Wisdom (*prajñā*) is that in which there is preeminent knowledge; it refers to the external consort. Knowledge (*jñāna*) is the mind that has become pure through the departure of conceptual construction; it is innate bliss (*sahajānanda*). This is the initiation of the knowledge of wisdom (*prajñājñānābhiṣeka*). That very same knowledge, when attained through stainless and complete purity, is the fourth initiation.
These two are also consecrations (*abhiṣeka*) because of the sprinkling of the mind with the essence of great bliss.

Connected to this very point, wisdom alone is the "observance of knowledge" (*vidyāvrata*), for it is the direct means for the perfection of the stainless, true bliss; thus, it must not be abandoned even during the initial stages.
"When one performs all activities with skillful means while remaining in a non-conceptual state, that is the most supreme of all vows through its non-conceptual nature.
From this statement of the *Vajraḍāka*, the "vajra-vow" is taught in order to strictly enjoin one to the vow of bodhicitta consisting of the five wisdoms, [asking]: "What is the use of other vows?"

And because the realization of the mind of awakening (*bodhicitta*) does not occur without conduct (*caryā*), there is the vow of conduct (*caryāvratam*) for the purpose of training. It has three types.
Among them, the first is devoted to the application of the three internal seals (*mudrā*). As it has been said:
"The skull-topped staff (*khaṭvāṅga*) is the form of the deity; the hand-drum (*ḍamaruka*) is conceived as wisdom (*prajñā*)."
Thus ends the skull-cup for drinking mantra-liquor.

And thus: [this text] teaches three things—the deity’s body, the unstruck sound (*anāhatanāda*) of the *caṇḍālī* in its subtle form, and the conventional bodhicitta which is the basis for the experience of non-dual great bliss.

The second [part] is devoted to the application of generating the fivefold perfectly pure wisdoms, such as the wisdom of the sphere of phenomena (*dharmadhātu-jñāna*), for both the yoginī and the practitioner of the conduct vow (*caryāvratī*).

The third [type] consists of the application of the arising of the bodhicitta—which consists of emptiness and great compassion—by a male or female yogin who, possessing the power of the fourfold vision, the superknowledges (*abhijñā*), and so forth, is devoted to accomplishing the welfare of sentient beings and has transcended the world, and who is intent upon establishing the purpose of universal adornment within (or, according to the Sakurai edition, both externally and internally).
Thus it is said in the *Yoginīsañcāra-tantra*:
"First, the yogin, being composed in meditative absorption, should diligently generate the power (*śakti*)."
Thereafter, having attained the necessary capacity, one who desires the practice of the vow should—
while maintaining the conduct of the five colors yet conceiving them as a single color, with a nature of non-conceptual, single-mindedness— enjoy the five objects of desire. (2–3)
Thus, the knower of Śrī Heruka fulfills all hopes;
that one of great wisdom maintains the excellent vow of non-dual gnosis.
For one engaged in the observance of the conduct, the yoga should be known as well-ascertained. (4)
Thus,
this prophecy is given to illuminate the fact that you are fit for the sequence of realizing the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) which does not transcend the three realms (*traidhātuka*).

For instance, *bhūḥ* refers to the netherworld (*pātāla*) together with its retinue of the wind-maṇḍala and so forth; *bhuvaḥ* refers to the mortal world (*martyaloka*); and *svaḥ* refers to the heavenly realm (*svarga*), extending up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*). Since you are the *samaya*—the one who, through your capacity, shall realize the reality whose nature is that triad by means of the sequence of the stages beginning with *pramuditā*—the meaning of "You are the *samaya* of *bhūḥ*, *bhuvaḥ*, and *svaḥ*" is this.
The permission is: "Having accomplished perfection according to the ritual rules, perform the welfare of sentient beings through the teaching of the Dharma and other means."

"Even while enjoying sensual pleasures, you are today itself a Buddha, liberated from all obscurations"—this is "consolation," because it awakens [the disciple] with the underlying intention that they have become fit for nourishment through such acts as entering the maṇḍala.

476) Some maintain that these five, beginning with the Vajra-vow, are permitted for those who are satisfied with only that [specific initiation], either following the Master-initiation or following the Knowledge-initiation. Furthermore, the mantra, the ointment, the mirror, and the arrow-throwing may also follow the Knowledge-initiation; and in some cases, the Knowledge-vow follows even the Wisdom-consort initiation.

In some instances, however, the mantra and so forth, the conduct-vow (*caryāvrata*), the general permission (*sāmānyānujñā*), the three pledges (*samaya*), and the capacity (*bhavyatā*) are not mentioned, because they are intended to be included within those respective other meanings according to their application during the various consecrations. In some cases, the permission and the encouragement (*āśvāsa*) are included within the "non-retrogression" (*avivarta*). Here, however, everything is stated separately. As it is said in the *Ḍākinīvajrapañjara-tantra*: "The first is by the water-consecration; the second is from the crown-consecration (*mauliseka*)."
The third is by means of the vajra-consecration, and the fourth is self-sovereignty;
one should perform the fifth with the name-consecration, and the sixth is indeed the perfect Buddha-consecration;
the seventh is the flask-consecration, and the eighth is by means of the secret-consecration.
The ninth [empowerment] is from the wisdom empowerment.
"By means of the application of the *tattvavajra*, one should bestow the *vajravratābhiṣeka* upon all;
the Teacher himself grants the prophecy—this is the sequence of the procedure for consecration.

(7) Thus it is said. In this regard, the *mālābhiṣeka* is not explicitly mentioned because it serves as the cause for the *udakābhiṣeka* and so forth, while the *mantra* and other consecrations are to be understood, according to their respective applications and based on statements in other tantras, as being ancillary to the *ācāryābhiṣeka* or sometimes to the fourth consecration (*caturthābhiṣeka*).
And for this very reason it is said in the *Śrīsamāja*:
"In this tantra, initiation is conceived as divided into three types:
the first is the vase initiation, and the second is from the secret consecration."
"The third is indeed the gnosis of wisdom (*prajñājñāna*), and the fourth is likewise that. Thus it is said in the *Śrīsaṃpuṭa*,
and that initiation is of four kinds.
"First is the vase consecration; second is from the secret consecration;
the third is the wisdom-knowledge [consecration], and the fourth is likewise again. Thus it is stated in the *Dvikalpatantra*.
The teacher’s secret [empowerment] and the wisdom [empowerment], and the fourth is likewise.

Thus, in that regard, the vase initiation (*kalaśābhiṣeka*) is sixfold due to the distinctions among the water, crown, and vajra-lord preceptors (*ācārya*). This is because in all cases one is consecrated with vases by means of the vidyās such as Tathāgatalocanā and others; and because the preceptor initiation (*ācāryābhiṣeka*) is especially superior due to its being an exceptionally excellent sprinkling. Furthermore, it is said that the "seventh" is the vase-sprinkling (*kalaśaseka*); however, since the five initiations beginning with the water-sprinkling serve as the causal basis for the arising of that preceptor initiation, they too are called the "preceptor initiation"—thus, everything is consistent. Such is this procedure for the initiation of another.
44.2. *Svasyābhiṣekavidhi*:

If one has violated the commitments (*samaya*) oneself, one should likewise receive such an initiation as was prescribed for the procedure of the master’s entry; however, this is only if the true guru resides in a very distant place, in a region inaccessible due to obstacles such as difficult paths, and not otherwise.

However, by means of always undertaking the yoga of one’s chosen deity—the single flavor of wisdom and skillful means—one should receive from the Lord of the Mandala within the mentally constructed mandala the water initiation and so forth, up to the secret, wisdom, and fourth initiations, as well as the [initiation] ending with the inhalation; such is the procedure for one’s own initiation.

Furthermore, for this Vajrasattva-vow-holder, there are two categories of transgressions: root transgressions (*mūlāpatti*) and gross transgressions (*sthūlāpatti*). These have been explained in the *Āmnāyamañjarī*. Regarding faults such as disrespecting the guru, one should give gifts and food according to one's ability, and having first confessed before the guru, one should take the vow (*saṃvara*) as before. This is the consecration ritual (*abhiṣekavidhi*) together with its traditional instructions and auxiliary practices.
45. Homavidhi 45.1 (p. 480)
In this context, it was previously stated that one should offer oblations for the sake of pacifying obstacles and so forth. Therefore:
"Without the performance of oblations, success in ritual acts does not arise at all;
for the sake of accomplishing pacification, nourishment, and other such goals, one should undertake the rite of oblation."
Since it has been stated thus, the fire-oblation (homa) should be performed at the appropriate time;
therein,
due to the diversity of sentient beings, there are infinite [varieties], yet fivefold according to the distinction of families (kula).
The fire-pits are of four kinds according to the division of ritual action; such is the determination.
Thus it was said by the Blessed One.

However, in the *Vajrakrodhasamāpattiguhyatantra*, one hundred and ten types of fire-pits (*kuṇḍa*) are specified according to the differentiation of ritual actions (*karman*). They are as follows: for pacification (*śāntika*), it is circular; for enrichment (*pauṣṭika*), it is square; for malevolent sorcery (*abhicāra*), it is triangular; for summoning (*ākarṣa*), it is shaped like a hook; for subjugation (*vaśīkaraṇa*), it is shaped like a vajra; for summoning wealth and grain, it is shaped like a jewel; for assuming any form at will (*kāmarūpitva*), it is shaped like a phallus; for invisibility (*antardhāna*), it is shaped like a bow and arrow; and for commanding (*ājñāpana*), it is shaped like a sword.

For the destruction of sins, the ground should be in the form of a gateway (*toraṇa*). For the host of Vidyās, it should be in the form of the mudrā of one’s own family. For traveling through the sky, it should be in the form of the circle of the sky. For the blazing of the Vidyā, it should be in the form of a flame. For the accomplishment of the Great Maṇḍala, it should be in the form of a wheel. For all rites, having first traced the outer maṇḍala as a square with four gates—one studded with vajras in the east, one studded with jewels in the south, one studded with lotuses in the west, and one studded with action-vajras (*karmavajra*) in the north—and so forth;
furthermore, for subjugation (*vaśya*), it is triangular, and for malevolent rites (*abhicāruka*), it is a half-moon.

In the *Susiddhikara*, the *Vajrāmala*, the *Vairocanābhisambodhi*, the *Trisamayārāja*, the *Samantābhiṣekajanana*, the *Vajrapāṇigarbhasambhava*, and the *Vajrābhyudaya* tantras, it is stated that for rites pertaining to all activities (*sārvakarmika*), the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) should be square, one cubit (*hasta*) in depth, with its upper surface measuring half a cubit, and so forth.

In the *Subāhuparipṛcchā*, the *Padmasambhava*, and the *Supratiṣṭhita* tantras, it is stated that for all rites (*sārvakarmika*), the fire-pit (*kuṇḍa*) should be lotus-shaped and circular, measuring one cubit (*hasta*) in circumference and half a cubit in depth. It should be surrounded at its base by eight lotuses, with a central lotus in the middle. Leaving a space of four finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) above the pit, there should be an altar (*vedī*) extending four finger-breadths both in width and height, shaped like fully blossomed petals protruding from the pit.

Outside the altar-railing (*vedikā*), the pit (*kuṇḍa*) is surrounded by a garland of lotuses. In the center of the pit, upon the lotuses of the cardinal directions, are a vajra, a jewel, a lotus, and a double-vajra (*viśvavajra*); upon the lotuses of the intermediate directions are a pair of Locanās, a three-pronged vajra, a lotus, and an utpala. In the central lotus is an eight-spoked wheel.
Inside, along the edge of the pit, the pit is encircled by a garland of vajras; such is described as the "all-purpose" (*sārvakarmika*) pit, and so forth. 45.4 (p. 483)
