In the *Kālacakra*, however, for pacification (*śānti*), the fire-pit (*kuṇḍa*) is circular and one cubit; for enrichment (*puṣṭi*), it is square and two cubits; for malevolent rites (*abhicāra*), it is shaped like a bow and half a cubit; for attraction (*ākarṣaṇa*), it is triangular and twenty finger-breadths; for creating enmity (*vidveṣa*), it is pentagonal with the same measurement as the circle; for deluding (*mohana*), it is hexagonal and thirty finger-breadths; for subjugation (*vaśya*), it is heptagonal and forty finger-breadths; and for paralyzing (*stambhana*), it is octagonal and sixty finger-breadths. In all cases, the depth of the pit is half the measurement of the pit; it is stated that the universal-purpose (*sārvakarmika*) pit is circular, and so forth. However, in the *Śrī-Buddhakapāla-tantra*:
For pacification (śāntika), the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) is square, measuring one span (vitasti) in both height and width;
for enrichment (pauṣṭika), the pit is circular, measuring three spans in both height and width.
For subjugation (*vaśya*), the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) is triangular, measuring eight finger-breadths in both height and width;
for malevolent rites (*abhicāra*), the pit is crescent-shaped, measuring one cubit in both height and width.
Thus it has been stated [in verse 45.5, p. 484].

Likewise, although the accomplishment of pacification (*śānti*), enrichment (*puṣṭi*), subjugation (*vaśya*), malevolent rites (*abhicāra*), and so forth may occur in a single all-purpose hearth (*sārvakarmika-kuṇḍa*), separate individual hearths are also prescribed in the tantras for each of these. Furthermore, regarding the specific rites of the hearths for pacification and the others, as well as the all-purpose hearth, there exist—in the center, on the rim, on the altar, and outside thereof—distinctions in configuration, color, and the arrangement of symbols; distinctions in the specific ground, the specific direction, and the variations in the dress, seat, position, and facing direction of the officiant and the fire-deity; and distinctions in the specific time for the performance of the oblation (*homakriyā*) in certain cases.
What is taught in the tantras is taught otherwise in the non-tantras.

For a yogin (or yoginīs, according to Sakurai’s edition) who possesses firm conviction and has the form of Vajrasattva, because of the firmness of the manifestation of the universe as having a single flavor with emptiness—like an illusion—and because one who consists of compassion engages for the sake of others, all this is capable of accomplishing the desired goal; thus, due to the diversity of the dispositions of those to be trained, this manifold arrangement of forms consisting of compassion exists.

Thus, having understood everything in this way, we have clearly and definitively established the complete ritual tradition—including the characteristics of the fire-pit (*kuṇḍa*) and the procedure for the fire-oblation (*homavidhāna*)—in accordance with the *Tattvasaṃgraha* and other Yoga and Yoginī Tantras, which are widely practiced. Therefore, one should ascertain all of that from the *Jyotirmañjarī* itself and perform the oblation; what further need is there to state it here? Thus, the procedure for the fire-oblation according to the *Jyotirmañjarī* should be understood. 46. Procedure for the Conclusion of the Mandala, etc.

Then, having performed the *pauṣṭika* and *śāntika* fire offerings (*homa*) according to the ritual rules and having personally worshipped the mandala, he should have the disciples and others perform worship, saying, "May you all worship the Tathāgatas and the rest according to your capacity. Having satisfied those who have entered with foods to be chewed, eaten, licked, and drunk offered by the circle, and having honored them through a night vigil with dance, song, and so forth, as well as through the practice of the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*), he should say, "You must not speak of what has occurred here to anyone," and then request a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).
The disciple should also give it with devotion.
A jewel, a most beloved wife, one's own body, and the earth.
In brief, one should perform such action as will please the true guru;
for when the guru is pleased, success is attained, and not otherwise—so the Sage has declared.
What merit has not been performed by him, or what austerity has not been practiced,
through the worship of the Teacher Vajrasattva, the achiever of the unsurpassed?

Thinking thus, he then dispatched his disciples; having performed the offerings and worship to the directions outside, he entered within, prostrated before the *cakra*, offered the *argha* and other honors to the Lord of the *cakra*, and dedicated the merit. Having circumambulated the maṇḍala three times, he stood at the eastern gate facing the Blessed One, recited the hundred-syllable mantra three times, and asked for forgiveness with the words beginning "apratyā" and so forth. Then, with "oṃ kṛto vaḥ" and so on, and "oṃ āḥ hūṃ vajra muḥ," he dismissed the *jñānacakra* and internalized the maṇḍala created by himself into his own being.

Reciting "Oṃ, the letter A is the gateway to all phenomena because they are unproduced from the beginning; Oṃ Āḥ Hūṃ Phaṭ Svāhā! Oṃ Āḥ Hūṃ Muḥ! and resolving upon the non-arising of all phenomena while ringing the bell, one should erase [the lines] starting from the eastern gate along the path of the Brahma-thread up to the position of the central deity using the vajra held in the hand. Having placed a speck of powder the size of a grain of dust on one's own head, one should erase the lotus and other [designs]. Then, one should carve out the gates and the corners with lines of the vajra held in the hand.

Thereafter, having raised the stakes with the four-hūṃ mantra: *oṃ vajrakīla utkīlaya sarvakīlān vajradharājñayā hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ hoḥ*, one should bathe them with milk over which the mantra *oṃ ru ru sphuru jvala tiṣṭha siddhalocane sarvārthasādhanani svāhā* has been recited one hundred and eight times. One should then dismiss the deities of the stakes and fill in the pits.

Having given a small amount of the *rajas* to one who requests it for the sake of pacification and other rites, [the officiant] should take all the remaining *rajas* and, having adorned another new jar with cloth, place it upon an elephant or in a palanquin. It should be carried by a Yoginī dressed in the garments provided by the patron (*dānapati*), accompanied by the ringing of bells, auspicious songs, musical instruments, parasols, banners, and worship, either for the Ācārya or the disciple seated in the palanquin. Having reached a great river, a large lake, or deep water, and having sat down on the bank smeared with cow dung and white perfumes...

Having constructed a maṇḍala, one should worship Vajrasattva in the pericarp of the lotus and the nāgas upon the petals as before. Having offered a milk oblation with the *nāgabali* mantra and performed worship, one should offer colored powder (*rajas*) to the nāgas and cause it to flow away. One should visualize that the nāgas, with great honor, lead the powder down to the subterranean realm (*pātāla*). Wherever the powder has been led, one should fill that jar with water, bring it back in the same manner, and sprinkle it for the sake of pacification (*śānti*) within the maṇḍala house and other areas.
In a maṇḍala house smeared with cow dung, one should feed milk-rice (*pāyasa*) to virgins.
Then, having collected all the necessary wealth, the preceptor himself should enjoy it; nothing at all should be used by the disciples and others.
This applies to the wealth acquired during the filling of a pit (gartāpūra), the consecration (pratiṣṭhā), the fire-oblation (homa), and the ritual circle (cakra).
"The Master alone possesses all of that," said the Holder of the Excellent Vajra.

The patron, however, for the sake of moving the installed images and so forth, should lead them back to their own place with the worship of musical instruments and other offerings, and then perform worship. Through the medium of the preceptor (*ācārya*), he should satisfy the door-preceptors (*dvārācāryas*), the ritual-vajra-holders (*karmavajrin*), the yoginīs, and the artisans with garments and the like, as well as with betel and other gifts, according to their merit and his capacity. He should provide a communal meal (*saṃghabhojya*) and a feast-circle (*gaṇacakra*), and satisfy the poor and the destitute. This is the procedure for the conclusion of the mandala and so forth.
47. The Mandala Procedure of the Mental [Mandala] (p. 492).

Such is the procedure for the painted mandala. Furthermore, this procedure for painting bears fruit only when performed mentally; therefore, the mental procedure alone is superior. Consequently, one should perform everything mentally—from the seizing of the site in the form of the lord of the mandala, up to the consecration of the images, the initiation of the disciples, the dismissal, and the concluding rites of pacification and fire-offerings.

Therefore, when all this cannot be performed, is not appropriate, or is not obtained due to some deficiency, one should perform it by means of meditation (*dhyāna*). For even though external objects exist, meditation alone is primary; external ritual is desired only for the sake of increasing merit through the world’s seeing, giving, and faith. However, due to the incompleteness of the necessary conditions (*sāmagrī-vaikalya*), every rite must be performed by meditating alone—so it was stated by the ancient masters.
Therefore, even a beginner, with a steady mind, should perform the consecration as before within a mentally emanated maṇḍala, and should also confer initiation upon worthy persons.
Thus it is said in the *Śrī Buddhakapāla Tantra*:
"In the center of the interior of the lotus of wisdom is a maṇḍala ten million yojanas in extent."
Within that, in the center of the mandala, the wise one should consecrate the excellent disciple with the triple-vow (tripuṭa).
Thus it is said; and elsewhere it is stated:
"In some cases, the Victors have prescribed the performance of the true maṇḍala ritual by means of the mind alone."
Thus concludes the mental procedure for the mandala.

In this regard, if an obstacle or affliction arising from the underworld—such as water, fire, wind, clouds, predatory beasts, humans, gods, armies, elephants, and so forth—is anticipated, whether caused by fate or by humans and others, during the drawing of a colored powder mandala (*rajomaṇḍala*) or similar rites, then one should repeatedly [visualize] the mandala-palace in the form of a peaked house situated in the center of the hub of a yellow, ten-spoked wheel that rotates clockwise. One should resolve with firm conviction that all obstacles are warded off by means of [the visualization of] being composed of vajra and so forth. Furthermore, for one who practices incessantly the samādhi of emptiness, whose sole flavor is vast compassion, even immeasurable obstacles are pacified; thus, this procedure does not apply to him. In this context, it is stated that all the ritual actions, such as the purification of the ground for the *bali* mandala, are preceded by the holding of the *vajra* and other implements; thus, their characteristics are described. Therein, the five-pronged *vajra* has equal three parts; the central hub (*varaṭaka*) is one-third of the third part [of the total length]; the prongs are one-eighth [the length of the hub]; they are bent at the tips by four parts; from the middle of the prongs downward, it is circular; the central prong is square, sharp, endowed with three girdles (*mekhalā*), and filled with barley; the distance between its tip and the tips of the directional prongs is one barley-corn (*yava*) each; all the prongs are equal to one another, while the middle one is slightly longer.

The middle of the needles is slightly slender at the bottom, then thick, and from the lower part it becomes slender again; the center of the middle section is thick, and both ends are then slender. With the exception of the central needle, whose base is encircled by three folds like the moon, the eastern and other needles are situated between the teeth of the *makara*. Its nose measures half the height of a grain husk; the *makara* face is one-fourth of the needle's size; and the rim (*nemi*) consists of lines for the rays and the surrounding halo above the moon.

The middle portion of this girdle (*mekhalā*) should be made slightly wider; the remaining two portions should be equal to one another and gradually double in height. The encircling band (*veṣṭana*) is made with half the measure of the diamond (*vajra*). Indeed, the length of the diamond is twice the measure of the encircling band. Below the moon is a lotus, below the lotus is a circle of fine jewel garlands, and below that is the cord of the girdle; the ray (*raśmi*) should be understood according to its proper application. It is of two kinds, distinguished by being sharp, very sharp, fierce, or gentle.

The *vajra* is well-known to be from four finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) up to twenty finger-breadths; some say it may be according to one's preference. The bell (*ghaṇṭā*) has three equal parts corresponding in size to the *vajra*. Its lower third, starting from the mouth, should be made of pure bell-metal (*kāṃsya*); the two upper parts are to be made of gold or other precious materials. The middle part, which is the hollow space within the bell-metal, is equal in its width and length. Above the rim, within the two bands (*mekhalā*), there is a garland of *vajras* and so forth.

Below the Amṛtakumbha is a square altar; below that, three folds (valīs); below that, a lotus; and below that, between the two girdles (mekhalās), there are garlands of vajras and other symbols as appropriate. Below that are various jewels, necklaces (hāra) and half-necklaces (ardhahāra). Within the eight central spaces of the necklaces are eight emblems: the wheel, jewel, lotus, and sword in the directions starting from the east; the eye, vajra, lotus, and blue lotus in the intermediate directions starting from the southeast. And in various places, according to what is beautiful, there are white water-lilies, blue lotuses, lotuses, jewel petals, sprouts, and so forth.

By the measurement of a *kumbha*, the face of the Prajñā [bell] is above the mouth, like half a vajra as before; here, some bells have faces slightly blossoming like lotuses, some are lotus-shaped, and some are cow-faced.

Here, one should meditate upon Akṣobhya, Vairocana, and the others upon the spokes of the vajra, beginning with the center and extending to the eastern spoke and so forth, up to the central hub (*varaṭaka*). Alternatively, one may meditate upon Vairocana in the center, and Maitreya, Kṣitigarbha, Vajrapāṇi, Gaganagañja, Lokeśvara, Mañjuśrī, Sarvanivaraṇaviṣkambhin, and Samantabhadra on the petals in the east and other directions. In the eighth part, one should place Vajrasattva. On the other lotus, one should place Vajrāṅkuśī, Vajrapāśī, Vajrasphoṭā, and Vajrāveśā on the petals in the east and other directions.

In the directions starting from the southeast (āgneyī) are Cundā, Ratnolkā, Vajraśṛṅkhalā, and Aparājitā. In the intermediate directions and at the center are Jñānaḍākinī, Vajraḍākinī in the east, Ghoraḍākinī in the north, Vetālī in the west, and Caṇḍālī in the south. Above the bell, upon downward-facing lotus petals, are Locanā, Māmakī, Pāṇḍarā, and Tārā, arranged clockwise in the cardinal directions; and in the intermediate directions are Vasudhārā, Cundā, Bhṛkuṭī, and Vajramālā. In the center of the vase is the body of Prajñāpāramitā, facing upward; above that is a lotus and a vajra as before.
The seed-syllables, emblems, arms, and so forth of these deities, Akṣobhya and the others, are described in the *Niṣpannayogāvalī*.

Then, having generated the deity as the *samayasattva*, one should summon the *jñānasattva* deity by means of light rays from the seed-syllable in the heart; having caused it to enter into those [samayasattvas] preceded by the offering of water for the feet (*pādya*) and so forth, and having installed them according to the ritual rules, one performs the worship and other rites. Having transformed the deities into the form of the needle and so forth, one should develop firm conviction that the vajra is the nature of skillful means (*upāya*), the bell is of the nature of wisdom (*prajñā*), and both are the essential nature of ultimate bodhicitta. Then, recite: *oṃ sarvatathāgatasiddhi vajrasamaye tiṣṭha eṣa tvāṃ dhārayāmi*.

Reciting "hiḥ hi hi hi hi hi hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā," one should hold the vajra with both hands using the thumbs and ring fingers. Reciting "oṃ vajraghaṇṭā hūṃ," one should hold the bell with the left hands, place it upon the left hip, and while visualizing, "I delight Vajrasattva and the others," preceded by the utterance of the syllable *hūṃ*, one should brandish the vajra while reciting: "soha i vajjam ullālutāri asattva vimokkha dhamma vimokkhye vajja tuṅga vajjaṅ gacchā adharantu / hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ ho ho ho. Thus one should brandish the vajra.

Then, having placed the vajra on the right hip or brandishing it, one should ring the bell while reciting: *oṃ vajradharma raṇita praraṇita saṃpraraṇita sarvabuddhakṣetrapracāline prajñāpāramitānādasvabhāve vajrasattvahṛdayasaṃtoṣaṇi hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ ho ho ho svāhā*. Thus, while moving the handle through the eight directions of the bell's interior, one should sound it. As for the detailed characteristics and so forth of the various types of bells and vajras, they have been explained in the *Āmnāyamañjarī*; such is the procedure regarding the characteristics of the vajra and bell. 51. (p.516)
Thus, while the words of the supreme sages are cast into the unfathomable [ocean],
some do not even reach the shore of the Śruti, while others float upon it; yet,
by the greatness of our compassionate mind, we have dived deep within.
May they partake of this nectar brought forth for your delight.
May they quickly enjoy that well-performed and exalted light which blazes within, having spread forth from those two who are a mine of glories.
May my beloved Vajra sport within the mandala of the Universal Form, the Lord who bestows fearlessness upon the three worlds, which is the abode of bliss.
The *Vajrāvalī*, a manual for the mandala rites composed by the great scholar Abhayākaragupta, is completed.
